But the Lord, in the knowledge of His own majesty, has compassion on their human errors, and knowing how great the joy that would follow these torments, while He yet endured them, forgives the crime of those who were crucifying Him: willing that His death would give life to His slayers, and be the condemnation of those who willed to perish. Returning from hades, He seeks His Apostles, so that He might show them that within Him there was both the power of divinity and the reality of our flesh*. Because of this, Brethren, let us rejoice in Christ, now risen from the dead. Let us hold firmly, that He has recalled this flesh* from the sepulchre that we may merit to have part in that wondrous common heritage: namely, the grace of the Apostles and the Resurrection of the Lord, by the help of this Same Lord Who with the Father and the Holy Ghost lives and reigns unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: The suffering of the cross was a stumbling block to many, as the apostle says. "We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles."The penitent thief considered the cross of Christ not to be a stumbling block but power rightly merits paradise. The same apostle says, "To those Jews who have been called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." The Lord also correctly gives paradise to him, because on the gibbet of the cross the thief confesses the one whom Judas Iscariot had sold in the garden. This is a remarkable thing. The thief confesses the one whom the disciple denied! This is a remarkable thing, I say. The thief honors the one who suffers, while Judas betrayed the one who kissed him! The one peddled flattering words of peace, and the other preached the wounds of the cross. He says, "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom."

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Someone might say of last Sunday's sermon, in which we preached that there was no less glory in Joseph's grave receiving the Lord than in holy Mary's womb begetting him, "What comparison can there be between the womb and the grave, since the one brought forth a son from its innermost bowels while the other only gave him a place of burial?" But I say that Joseph's love was no less than Mary's, since she conceived the Lord in her womb and he did so in his heart. She offered the secret place of her inmost members to the Savior; he did not deny him the secret place for his own body. She wrapped the Lord in swaddling clothes when he was born; he wrapped him in linen cloths when he died. She anointed his blessed body with oil; he honored it with spices. Each one's service is similar and each one's love is similar; hence each one's reward must also be similar. But there is this difference: an angel called Mary to her service, but righteousness alone persuaded Joseph.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Let us see, then, what happens to the Lord's body after they take it down from the cross. Joseph of Arimathea, a righteous man, as the Evangelist says, took it and buried it in his new tomb in which no one had ever been laid. Blessed is the body of the Lord Christ, which in birth comes forth from a virgin's womb and in death is placed in the grave of a righteous man! Clearly this body is blessed. Virginity brought it out, and righteousness held it! Joseph's grave held him incorrupt, just as Mary's womb preserved him inviolate. In the one, a man's impurity does not touch him; in the other, death's corruption does not hurt him. In every way, holiness and virginity are bestowed on that blessed body. A new womb conceived him, and a new grave enclosed him. The womb is the Lord's womb. It is virginal. The tomb is virginal. Should I not rather say that the tomb itself is a womb? There is, in fact, a great similarity. Just as the Lord came out from his mother's womb living, so also he rose living from Joseph's tomb. Just as he was born from the womb in order to preach, so also now he has been reborn from the tomb in order to evangelize. The last birth is more glorious than the first. The first conceived a mortal body, but the last brought out an immortal one. After the first birth, he descends to hell, but after the last birth, he returns to the heavens. The last birth is more religious than the first. The first kept the Lord of the whole world locked in the womb for nine months, but the last held him in the belly of the grave for only three days. The first offered hope to all rather slowly, but the last raised salvation for all quite quickly.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Let us see why they placed the Savior in someone else's grave instead of his own. They placed him in another person's grave because he died for the salvation of others. They did not impose death on him. He endured death for us. Death did not just happen to him, but it benefited us. Why should he, who did not have his own death in himself, have his own grave? Why should he, whose dwelling remained in heaven, have a burial place on earth? Why should he have a grave? For only three days, he did not so much lie as one dead in a tomb as rest as one sleeping in a bed. The brief period of time itself certainly indicates sleep rather than death. A tomb is the dwelling of death. Christ who is life did not need a dwelling for death, nor did he who is always living require a habitation of the deceased. We have correctly laid up this life in our own tomb so that as he gives life to our death, we may rise with him from the dead.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: US; But if perhaps the swaddling clothes are mean in your eyes, admire the Angels singing praises together If you despises" tile manger, raise your eyes a little, and behold the new star in heaven proclaiming to the world the Lord's nativity. If you believe the mean things, believe also the mighty. If you dispute about those which betoken His lowliness, look with reverence on what is high and heavenly.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (lib. Ascet.) The fruit of repentance is an equanimity of soul, which we do not fully obtain, as long as we are at times affected by our passions, for not as yet have we performed the fruits worthy of repentance. Let us then repent truly, that being delivered from our passions we may obtain the pardon of their sins.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote:
(lib. ad. piet. ex. 12.) Or the devil had prompted Christ in the desert to prefer the things of the world to the love of God. The Lord commanded him to leave Him, (which itself was a mark of Divine love.) It was afterwards then enough to make Christ appear the false advocate of love to His neighbours, and therefore while He was teaching the paths of life, the devil stirred up the Gentiles and Pharisees to lay traps for Him that He might be brought to hate them. But the Lord, from the feeling of love which He had towards them, exhorted, reproved, ceased not to bestow mercy upon them.

(ut sup.) But the reason why one Evangelist places this event first, and another that, is because vain-glory and covetousness give birth in turn to one another.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (non occ.) But it is worthy of remark, that seven resurrections are related before our Lord's, of which the first was that of the son of the widow of Sarepta, (1 Kings 17) the second of the Shunamite's son, (2 Kings 4) the third which was caused by the remains of Elisha, (2 Kings 13) the fourth which took place at Nain, as is here related, the fifth of the ruler of the Synagogue's daughter, (Mark 5) the sixth of Lazarus, (John 11) the seventh at Christ's passion, for many bodies of the saints arose. (Mat. 27.) The eighth is that of Christ, who being free from death remained beyond for a sign that the general resurrection which is to come in the eighth age shall not be dissolved by death, but shall abide never to pass away.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (Quæst. in Script. 63.) Or perhaps the Lord calls Himself a light shining to all who inhabit the house, that is, the world, since He is by nature God, but by the dispensation made flesh. And so like the light of the lamp He abides in the vessel of the flesh by means of the soul as the light in the vessel of the lamp by means of the flame. But by the candlestick he describes the Church over which the divine word shines, illuminating the house as it were by the rays of truth. But under the similitude of a vessel or bed he referred to the observance of the law, under which the word will not be contained.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (Ep. ad Georgium.) Now the Lord ordains for each class of sinners an appropriate punishment. The fire of Hell unquenchable for fleshly burnings, gnashing of teeth for wanton mirth, intolerable thirst for pleasure and revelry, the worm that dieth not for a crooked and malignant heart, everlasting darkness for ignorance and deceit, the bottomless pit for pride. Hence the deep is assigned to the devils as unto the proud, it follows, And there was there an herd of swine, &c.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (Cap. Theol. 191.) Which it is said is come nigh, not to show the shortness of time, for the kingdom of God cometh not with observation, but to mark the disposition of men towards the kingdom of God, which is indeed potentially in all believers, but actually in those who reject the life of the body, and choose only the spiritual life; who are able to say, Now I live, yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. (Gal. 2:20.)

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (Cap. Theol. 191.) Which it is said is come nigh, not to show the shortness of time, for the kingdom of God cometh not with observation, but to mark the disposition of men towards the kingdom of God, which is indeed potentially in all believers, but actually in those who reject the life of the body, and choose only the spiritual life; who are able to say, Now I live, yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. (Gal. 2:20.)

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: To this end then the law commanded a threefold love to God, that it might pluck us away from the threefold fashion of the world, as touching possessions, glory, and pleasure, wherein also Christ was tempted.

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: (in Orat. Dom.) Or, the Lord commands us to pray, Lead us not into temptation, let us not have experience of lustful and self-induced temptations. But James teaches those who contend only for the truth, not to be unnerved by involuntary and troublesome temptations, saying, My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations. (James 1:2.)

author: Maximus the Confessor
quote: Or, he teaches us to keep our lamps burning, by prayer and contemplation and spiritual love.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
In order that by the miracle of these the hearts of the fathers might be turned to the children, and the disobedient unto the wisdom of the just.
...
O ye disobedient as regards the wisdom of the just, turn your hearts to your children. Learn the mysteries of God; the very thing itself which is being done bears witness that it is God that is thus hymned by uninstructed tongues. Search the Scriptures, as ye have heard from the Lord; for they are they which testify of Him, and be not ignorant of this miracle. Hear ye men without grace, and thankless, what good tidings the prophet Zechariah brings to you. He says, Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; behold thy King cometh unto thee: just and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon the foal of an ass. Why do ye repel the joy? Why, when the sun shineth, do ye love darkness? Why do ye against unconquerable peace meditate war? If, therefore, ye be the sons of Zion, join in the dance together with your children. Let the religious service of your children be to you a pretext for joy. Learn from them who was their Teacher; who called them together; whence was the doctrine; what means this new theology and old prophecy. And if no man hath taught them this, but of their own accord they raise the hymn of praise, then recognise the work of God, even as it is written in the law: "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast Thou perfected praise." Redouble, therefore, your joy, that you have been made the fathers of such children who, under the teaching of God, have celebrated with their praises things unknown to their seniors. Turn your hearts to your children, and close not your eyes against the truth. But if you remain the same, and hearing, hear not, and seeing, perceive not, and to no purpose dissent from your children, then shall they be your judges according to the Saviour's word.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
For what is more splendid for a king than a purple robe embroidered around with flowers, and a shining diadem? Or what for God, who delights in man, is more magnificent than this merciful assumption of the manhood, illuminating with its resplendent rays those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death?.
But by means of that light, which is of one substance with Thee, Thou hast given light to those that sat in darkness.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Tremendous, verily, is the mystery connected with thee, O virgin mother, thou spiritual throne, glorified and made worthy of God. Thou hast brought forth, before the eyes of those in heaven and earth, a pre-eminent wonder. And it is a proof of this, and an irrefragable argument, that at the novelty of thy supernatural child-bearing, the angels sang on earth, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good-will towards men," by their threefold song bringing in a threefold holiness.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Hence it was that the ark of God removed from the inn at Bethlehem, for there He paid to the law that debt of the forty days, due not to justice but to grace, and rested upon the mountains of Sion, and receiving into His pure bosom as upon a lofty throne, and one transcending the nature of man, the Monarch of all, she presented Him there to God the Father, as the joint-partner of His throne and inseparable from His nature, together with that pure and undefiled flesh which he had of her substance assumed. The holy mother goes up to the temple to exhibit to the law a new and strange wonder, even that child long expected, who opened the virgin's womb, and yet did not burst the barriers of virginity; that child, superior to the law, who yet fulfilled the law; that child that was at once before the law, and yet after it; that child, in short, who was of her incarnate beyond the law of nature.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Upon all this that righteous man, waxing bold and yielding to the exhortation of the mother of God, who is the handmaid of God in regard to the things which pertain to men, received into his aged arms Him who in infancy was yet the Ancient of days, and blessed God, and said, "Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace, according to Thy word: for mine eyes have seen Thy salvation, which Thou hast prepared before the face of all people; a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel." I have received from Thee a joy unmixed with pain. Do thou, O Lord, receive me rejoicing, and singing of Thy mercy and compassion. Thou hast given unto me this joy of heart. I render unto Thee with gladness my tribute of thanksgiving.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: And in addition to this, when besides the spectacle, and even beyond the spectacle, they heard an old man, very righteous, very worthy of credit, worthy also of emulation, inspired by the Holy Spirit, a teacher of the law, honoured with the priesthood, illustrious in the gift of prophecy, by the hope which he had conceived of Christ, extending the limits of life, and putting off the debt of death—when they saw him, I say, leaping for joy, speaking words of good omen, quite transformed with gladness of heart, entirely rapt in a divine and holy ecstasy; who from a man had been changed into an angel by a godly change, and, for the immensity of his joy, chanted his hymn of thanksgiving, and openly proclaimed the "Light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel."
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: When, then, to these sacred rites, prophecy and the priesthood had been jointly called, and that pair of just ones elected of God—Simeon, I mean, and Anna, bearing in themselves most evidently the images of both peoples—had taken their station by the side of that glorious and virginal throne,—for by the old man was represented the people of Israel, and the law now waxing old; whilst the widow represents the Church of the Gentiles, which had been up to this point a widow,—the old man, indeed, as personating the law, seeks dismissal; but the widow, as personating the Church, brought her joyous confession of faith and spake of Him to all that looked for redemption in Jerusalem, even as the things that were spoken of both have been appositely and excellently recorded, and quite in harmony with the sacred festival. For it was fitting and necessary that the old man who knew so accurately that decree of the law, in which it is said: Hear Him, and every soul that will not hearken unto Him shall be cut off from His people, should seek a peaceful discharge from the tutorship of the law; for in truth it were insolence and presumption, when the king is present and addressing the people, for one of his attendants to make a speech over against him, and that to this man his subjects should incline their ears. It was necessary, too, that the widow who had been increased with gifts beyond measure, should in festal strains return her thanks to God; and so the things which there took place were agreeable to the law.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For these thankless men saw, and by means of His miracles handled the wonder-working God, and yet remained in unbelief. They saw a man, blind from his birth, proclaiming to them the God who had restored his sight. They saw a paralytic, who had grown up, as it were, and become one with his infirmity, at His bidding loosed from his disease. They saw Lazarus, who was made an exile from the region of death. They heard that He had walked on the sea. They heard of the wine that, without previous culture, was ministered; of the bread that was eaten at that spontaneous banquet; they heard that the demons had been put to flight; the sick restored to health. Their very streets proclaimed His deeds of wonder; their roads declared His healing power to those who journeyed on them. All Judea was filled with His benefit; yet now, when they hear the divine praises, they inquire, Who is this?

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Tell us, then, O children, whence is this, your beautiful and graceful contest of song? Who taught it you? Who instructed you? Who brought you together? What were your tablets? Who were your teachers? Do but you, they say, join us as our companions in this song and festivity, and you will learn the things which were by Moses and the prophet earnestly longed for.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord: the Lord to save man who had wandered in error; to put away error; to give light to those who are in darkness; to abolish the imposture of idols; in its place to bring in the saving knowledge of God; to sanctify the world; to drive away the abomination and misery of the worship of false gods. Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord: the one for the many; to deliver the poor out of the hands of them that are too strong for him, yea, the poor and needy from him that spoileth him. Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord, to pour wine and oil upon him who had fallen amongst thieves, and had been passed by. Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord: to save us by Himself, as says the prophet; no ambassador, nor angel, but the Lord Himself saved us.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: It became indeed the Lord of the law and the prophets to do all things in accordance with His own law, and not to make void the law, but to fulfil it, and rather to connect with the fulfilment of the law the beginning of His grace. Therefore it is that the mother, who was superior to the law, submits to the law. And she, the holy and undefiled one, observes that time of forty days that was appointed for the unclean. And He who makes us free from the law, became subject to the law; and there is offered for Him, who hath sanctified us, a pair of clean birds, in testimony of those who approach clean and blameless.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Hail to thee, thou Catholic Church, which hast been planted in all the earth, and do thou rejoice with us. Fear not, little flock, the storms of the enemy; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom, and that you should tread upon the necks of your enemies. Hail, and rejoice, thou that wast once barren, and without seed unto godliness, but who hast now many children of faith. Hail, thou people of the Lord, thou chosen generation, thou royal priesthood, thou holy nation, thou peculiar people -- show forth His praises who hath called you out of darkness into His marvellous light; and for His mercies glorify Him.
source_title: Methodius Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ commands in the Gospels, thus directing: "Let not your lights be extinguished, and let not your loins be loosed. Therefore also be ye like men who wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that, when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately. Blessed are ye, when he shall make you sit down, and shall come and serve you. And if he come in the second, or in the third watch, ye are blessed." For consider, O virgins, when He mentions three watches of the night, and His three comings, He shadows forth in symbol our three periods of life, that of the boy, of the full-grown man, and of the old man; so that if He should come and remove us from the world while spending our first period, that is, while we are boys, He may receive us ready and pure, having nothing amiss; and the second and the third in like manner.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote:
For the flesh is truly, as it were, our five-lighted lamp, which the soul will bear like a torch, when it stands before Christ the Bridegroom, on the day of the resurrection, showing her faith springing out clear and bright through all the senses, as He Himself taught, saying.
Wicked demons who once fell from light; but when the Creator and Framer of all things had, as the most divine Paul says, laid hold of the seed of Abraham, and through him of the whole human race, He was made man for ever, and without change, in order that by His fellowship with us, and our joining on to Him, the ingress of sin into us might be stopped, its strength being broken by degrees, and itself as wax being melted, by that fire which the Lord, when He came, sent upon the earth.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: For the mind being cleansed by laborious exercises from the distracting thoughts which darken it, quickly perceives the truth; as the widow in the Gospels found the piece of money after she had swept the house and cast out the dirt, that is, the passions which obscure and cloud the mind, which increase in us from our luxuriousness and carelessness.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: Hence the Word has with deep perception called the souls of the prophets concubines, because He did not espouse them openly, as He did the Church, having killed for her the fatted calf.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: As also the Lord showed, when He said: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations." For what the Lord then called "habitations," the apostle here calls "clothing." And what He there calls "friends" "of unrighteousness," the apostle here calls "houses" "dissolved." As then, when the days of our present life shall fail, those good deeds of beneficence to which we have attained in this unrighteous life, and in this "world" which "lieth in wickedness," will receive our souls; so when this perishable life shall be dissolved, we shall have the habitation which is before the resurrection-that is, our souls shall he with God, until we shall receive the new house which is prepared for us, and which shall never fall.
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: And there may be a doubt concerning Lazarus and the rich man. The simpler persons think that these things were spoken as though both were receiving their due for the things which they had done in life in their bodies; but the more accurate think that, since no one is left in life after the resurrection, these things do not happen at the resurrection. For the rich man says: "I have five brethren; ... lest they also come into this place of torment, " send Lazarus, that he may tell them of those things which are here.
source_title: Methodius From the Discourse on the Resurrection

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: -Let no one amongst us be found to receive Him with a sad countenance, lest he be condemned with those wicked citizens-the citizens, I mean, who refused to receive the Lord as King over them.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: But while these things were doing, and the disciples were rejoicing and praising God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, saying, Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven, and glory in the highest; the city began to inquire, saying, Who is this? stirring up its hardened and inveterate envy against the glory of the Lord. But when thou hearest me say the city, understand the ancient and disorderly multitude of the synagogue. They ungratefully and malignantly ask, Who is this? as if they had never yet seen their Benefactor, and Him whom divine miracles, beyond the power of man, had made famous and renowned; for the darkness comprehended not that unsetting light which shone in upon it.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: And therefore it is ordered that a virgin shall not taste of this vine, so that she may be sober and watchful from the cares of life, and may kindle the shining torch of the light of righteousness for the Word. "Take heed to yourselves," says the Lord, "lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares, as a snare."

author: Nicetas of Remesiana
quote: That which was spiritual in the Old Testament, for example, faith, piety, prayer, fasting, patience, chastity and psalm singing—all this has been increased in the New Testament rather than diminished. Therefore you will find in the Gospel Zechariah, the father of John, who uttered a prophecy in the form of a hymn after his long silence.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (Hom. i. in Luc.) The effect upon his own mind, St. Luke explains by the expression, of the things which have been fully accomplished among us, i. e. have had their full manifestation among us, (as the Greek word peplerophoremenon signifies, which the Latin cannot express in one word,) for he had been convinced of them by sure faith and reason, and wavered not in any thing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Just as of old among the people of the Jews many laid claim to prophecy, and some were false prophets — of whom one was Hananiah, the son of Azor —, while others were true prophets, and there was in the people the grace of discerning spirits, by which some were received among the prophets, while a few were rejected as though by "the most experienced money-changers", so also now, in the new covenant, "many have attempted" to write gospels, but not all have been received. And that you may know that not only four gospels, but very many, have been composed, out of which these that we have were chosen and handed down to the churches, let us learn from the very preface of Luke, which runs thus: "Forasmuch as many have attempted to set in order a narrative". In this that he says, "they have attempted", there lies a hidden accusation of those who, without the grace of the Holy Spirit, leapt forward to write gospels. For Matthew and Mark and John and Luke did not "attempt" to write, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, they wrote the gospels. "Many" therefore "have attempted to set in order a narrative concerning those things which have been most clearly known among us". The Church has four gospels, heresy has very many, of which one is written according to the Egyptians, another according to the Twelve Apostles. Basilides too dared to write a gospel and to entitle it with his own name. "Many have attempted" to write, but only four gospels are approved, from which the doctrines concerning the person of our Lord and Savior are to be brought forth. I know a certain gospel which is called "according to Thomas", and one "according to Matthias"; and we have read many others too, lest we should seem to be ignorant of anything on account of those who think they know something if they have come to know these things. But in all these we approve nothing else except what the Church does, namely that only four gospels are to be received. This is so, because at the beginning it was read: "many have attempted to set in order a narrative concerning those things which have been confirmed among us". Those men tried and "attempted" to write concerning those things which have been most clearly ascertained by us. Luke indicates his own disposition by the words in which he says: "have been most clearly shown among us", that is "πεπληροφορημένων" (fully assured), which the Latin tongue does not render in a single word. For with sure faith and reason he had come to know them, and he wavered in nothing as to whether it was so or otherwise. But this befalls those who have believed most faithfully and have obtained that which the prophet implores, and who say: "confirm me in your words". Whence the Apostle also says of those who were firm and strong: "that you may be rooted and grounded in faith". For if anyone is rooted and grounded in faith, though a storm arise, though the winds blow, though the rain pour down, he shall not be torn away, he shall not fall, because the building has been founded with solid mass "upon the rock". And let us not think that the firmness of faith, which mind and reason bestow, is given by these carnal eyes. Let all the unbelieving believe in signs and portents which the human eye beholds. But let the faithful and prudent and strong man follow reason and the word, and thus judge what is true and what is false.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 1

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It is plain that of one kind of knowledge, the end is in the knowledge itself, as in geometry; but of another kind, the end is counted to be in the work, as in medicine; and so it is in the word of God, and therefore having signified the knowledge by the words were themselves eyewitnesses, he points out the work by what follows, and were ministers of the word.

It is written in Exodus, The people saw the voice of the Lord. (Exod. 20:18.) Now a voice is rather heard than seen. But it was so written, to show us that men see the voice of the Lord with other eyes, which they only have who are worthy of them. Again in the Gospel, it is not the voice that is perceived, but the Word, which is more excellent than the voice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "As they have handed down to us, who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word". In Exodus it is written: "the people saw the voice of God". And surely a voice is heard rather than seen; but it was written thus for this reason, that it might be shown to us that with other eyes one may "see the voice of God" — those eyes with which they behold who are worthy. Moreover in the Gospel not a voice is perceived, but a word, which is more excellent than a voice. Whence it is now said: "as they have handed down to us, who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word". Therefore the apostles themselves saw the word, not because they had looked upon the body of the Lord and Savior, but because they had seen the Word. For if to have seen Jesus according to the body is this, namely to have seen the word of God, then Pilate too, who condemned Jesus, saw the word of God, and Judas the traitor, and all who cried out: "crucify, crucify him, take such a one from the earth", saw the word of God. But far be it that any unbeliever should see the word of God. To see the word of God is such a thing as the Savior speaks of: "He who has seen me has seen also the Father, who sent me". "As they have handed down to us, who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word". Secretly, by Luke's words, we are taught that the end of one kind of teaching is the teaching itself, but that the end of another kind of teaching is reckoned to lie in the work. For example: the science of geometry has as its end only the science and the teaching itself. But there is another science whose end demands a work, such as medicine. I must know the theory and the doctrines of medicine, not only that I may know what I ought to do, but that I may do it, that is, that I may cut wounds, prescribe a moderate and disciplined diet, feel the heat of fevers by the beating of the veins, so that by cyclical treatments I may dry up, temper, and restrain the abundance of humors. And if anyone should only know these things and not follow them up with work, his knowledge will be empty. Something like this, holding between the knowledge of medicine and its practice, exists also in the knowledge and the ministry of the word. Whence it is written: "as they have handed down to us, who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word", so that we may recognize that by what he said, "themselves saw", teaching and knowledge are signified, but by what he says, "were ministers of the word", works are demonstrated.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 1

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: St. Luke hereby explains to us the source of his writing; seeing that what things he wrote, he gained not from report, but had himself traced them up from the beginning. Hence it follows, It seemed good to me also, having carefully investigated every thing from the very first, to write to thee in order, most excellent Theophilus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "It seemed good to me also, having followed from the beginning". He impresses and repeats that the things he is about to write he had not come to know by rumor, but that he himself had followed them from the beginning. Whence he is also deservedly commended by the apostle Paul, who says: "whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches". For this is said of no one else, but is handed down as said of Luke. "It seemed good to me also, having followed from the beginning, to write all things diligently in order to you, most excellent Theophilus". Someone may suppose that he wrote the gospel to a certain Theophilus. All of you who hear us speaking, if you are such that you are loved by God, you too are "theophili" (lovers/beloved of God), and to you the gospel is written. If anyone is "theophilus", he is both most excellent and most strong, for this is what is more significantly expressed in the Greek word: "κράτιστος" (most excellent). No "theophilus" is weak. And just as it is written of the people of Israel, when it was going out of Egypt, that "there was not among their tribes one that was weak": so I will boldly say that everyone who is "theophilus" is robust, having strength and vigor both from God and from his word, so that he may be able to know the truth of those words in which he has been instructed, understanding the word of the gospel in Christ: to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 1

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Those who wish to spread over their sins some excuse suppose that no one is without sin, and they make use of the testimony written in Job: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life upon the earth should be but of a single day; his months, moreover, are numbered". Of this passage they bring forward only the sound, being wholly ignorant of its interpretation. Against them we shall reply briefly, that to be without sin is understood in the Scriptures in two ways: the one, never to have sinned at all; the other, to have ceased from sinning. If, then, they say that he is called without sin who has never sinned, we too agree that no one is without sin, since all of us as human beings have at some time sinned, even though afterward we have pursued virtue. But if they so understand a man not to be without sin as to deny that anyone, after his vices, so betakes himself to the virtues that he never sins at all, then their opinion is false. For it can come about that one who has sinned before, when he ceases from sinning, is said to be without sin. Thus also our Lord Jesus Christ "presented to himself a glorious Church, not having spot", not because the churchly man has never had a spot, but because he is by no means spotted any longer: "not having wrinkle", not that the wrinkle "of the old man" was never at some time in him, but that he has ceased to have it. In this manner also that which follows is to be understood: "that it may be holy and unspotted", not that from the beginning it was unspotted — for this indeed cannot be supposed of a man, that his soul was not spotted — but that it is reckoned pure and sincere, having ceased to be spotted any longer. We say these things for this reason, that we might teach that a man can, on the ground that he has ceased to sin, be called without sin and "unspotted". Hence also it is most plainly written concerning Zechariah and Elizabeth: "they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach". Let us more carefully contemplate the praises of Zechariah and Elizabeth which holy Luke writes in his history, not only that we may know that they were praiseworthy, but that, taking up their holy zeal, we too may be made worthy of praise. He could have written simply: "they were both righteous, walking in all the commandments"; but now it is necessarily added: "they were both righteous before God". For it can indeed come about that someone is righteous before men, but is not so "before God". For example: when a man has nothing evil that he might speak about me, and, considering everything about me, finds nothing to disparage, I am righteous "in the sight" of men. Suppose that all hold the same opinion of me, and seek what they might disparage, and yet cannot find it, but praise me with one accord — I am righteous "in the sight" of very many men. But the judgment of men is not certain: for they do not know whether in the hidden part of my heart I have at some time sinned, whether I have looked upon a woman to lust after her, and adultery has been born in my heart. Men are ignorant, when they have seen me give alms according to my means, whether I did it because of God's commandment or sought the praise and favor of men. It is a difficult thing to be righteous "before God", so that you do some good for no other cause than for the sake of the good itself, and seek God alone as the rewarder of your good work. Something like this the Apostle also says: "whose praise is not from men, but from God". Blessed is he who is righteous and praiseworthy "before God". For men, although they may seem to have a certain judgment, nevertheless cannot pronounce with clarity. For it happens sometimes that they praise one who is not praiseworthy, and disparage one who is by no means worthy of disparagement. God alone is a righteous judge both in praise and in blame.

Hence worthily now also it is added in the praise of the righteous: "they were both righteous before God". To something like this Solomon too exhorts us in the Proverbs, saying: "provide good things in the sight of God and of men". There follows another commendation of Zechariah and Elizabeth: "walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord". When we judge well and rightly concerning any matters, we walk "in the ordinances of the Lord"; when we do this or that, we walk "in his commandments". Hence I think that holy Luke also, wishing to proclaim them with perfect praise, said: "they were both righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord". Let someone say to me: if this praise is perfect, what does this mean, that it is said: "without reproach"? For it was enough to say: "walking in all the ways and ordinances of the Lord", unless it could come about that one walks in all the commandments of God, and yet does not walk "without reproach". And how can it happen that one walking "in all the commandments and ordinances of God" should be under reproach? To this I shall briefly say: unless this were so, we should never know it recorded, written in another place: "justly pursue that which is just". For unless there were something just which we might pursue not justly, it would by no means be enjoined upon us that we should justly pursue that which is just. For when we do the commandment of God and in our conscience are bespattered with the filth of vainglory, so as to please men, or some other cause which does not please God goes before as the motive of the good work, then, although we do the precept of God, nevertheless we do not do it "without reproach", and we pursue unjustly that which is just. It is therefore difficult to walk "in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach", according to the testimony and praise of God in Christ Jesus, which is to be rendered on the day of judgment by him before whom "all of us must be made manifest before his tribunal, that each one may receive the things he has done through the body, whether good or evil". "For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God", that we may receive what we deserve in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 2

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: First of all, consider what this means, that very many of the holy women in the scriptures are said to have been barren, as Sarah herself, and behold now Rebekah as well. But Rachel too, beloved of Israel, was barren. Hannah also, the mother of Samuel, is written to have been barren. But in the Gospels too Elizabeth is recorded to have been barren. And in all these women this one heading is signified: that after barrenness they all brought forth a holy childbirth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And we speak thus not only of the present time, but also of the future. When we shall have passed from the world, God will not appear unto all men, nor will the angels, but unto him only who has a clean heart. The place will neither hinder nor serve any one.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Concerning what is written: "an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right of the altar of incense".

Things that are corporeal and lacking in sense-perception, so as to be seen by another, contribute nothing of themselves, but only the eye of another, intent upon them—whether they will it or not—sees them, wherever it has directed its gaze and contemplation. For what can a man, or any other thing surrounded by a gross body, do, when it is present, to keep from being perceived? On the contrary, those things which are heavenly and divine, even when they are present, are not seen unless they themselves will it; and it lies in their will to be seen or not to be seen. It was the grace of God that He appeared to Abraham or to the rest of the prophets—not because the eye of Abraham's heart alone was the cause of his beholding God, but because the grace of God freely offered itself to be looked upon by the just man. And this you are to understand not only concerning God the Father, but also concerning the Lord the Savior and concerning the Holy Spirit and—to descend to lesser beings—concerning the Cherubim and Seraphim. For it can happen that even now, while we are speaking, an angel is present, and yet, because we do not deserve it, we are unable to see him. For although the eye whether of our body or of our soul strains itself to contemplate, unless the angel appears of his own accord and offers himself to be seen, the one who desires to see will not see. And so, wherever it is written: "God appeared" to this or that person, and, as now: "an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right of the altar of incense", understand it as I have said. Whether God or an angel, to Abraham or to Zechariah, whether he is unwilling or willing, either will not be seen or will be seen. And this we say not only in the "present age", but also in the age to come, when we shall have departed from the world: that not to all do either God or the angels appear—that is, that he who has gone out from the body should straightway deserve to see both the angels and the Holy Spirit and the Lord the Savior and God the Father Himself; rather, he alone will see who has a clean heart and has shown himself such as to be worthy of the sight of God. And although he who is clean of heart and he who is still bespattered with some filth may be in the same place, the one place will be able neither to harm nor to help anyone, because he who has a clean heart will see God, but he who is not such will not see that which is beheld by another. Something of this kind I think must also be understood concerning Christ, when He was seen in the body: that not all who saw Him were able to see Him. For they saw only His body, but according to that which Christ was, they could not see Him. The disciples, however, saw Him and contemplated the greatness of His divinity. On which account I think that to Philip too, who entreated and said: "show us the Father, and it is enough for us", the Savior replied: "am I so long a time with you, and you have not known me? Philip, he who sees me sees also the Father". For neither did Pilate, who was seeing Jesus, behold the Father, nor did the traitor Judas—since neither Pilate himself nor Judas saw Christ according to that which Christ was, nor did the multitude that pressed upon Him. Those alone saw Jesus whom He judged worthy of His sight. Let us therefore, we also, labor that even in the present God may appear to us—for the holy word of the Scriptures has promised: "because He is found by those who do not tempt Him, and He appears to those who are not unbelieving toward Him"—and that in the age to come He may not be hidden from us, but that we may see Him "face to face" and have confidence of a good life and enjoy the sight of Almighty God in Christ Jesus and the Holy Spirit: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 3

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
A new face suddenly presenting itself to the human eye, troubles and startles the mind. The angel knowing this to be the nature of man, first dispels the alarm, as it follows, But the angel said unto him, Fear not.

The angel not only soothes his fears, but gladdens him with good tidings, adding, For thy prayer is heard, and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear a son.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Zechariah, when he had seen the angel, was terrified. For indeed a strange countenance, presenting itself to human sight, disturbs the mind and dismays the spirit. Hence the angel, knowing that this belongs to human nature, first remedies the disturbance, saying: "fear not, Zechariah", and revives the trembling man and gladdens him with new tidings, adding: "your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth shall bear a son, and you shall call his name John; and he shall be to you a joy and an exultation". When some righteous person arises in the world and enters the course of this life, the ministers of his birth rejoice and lift themselves up on high. But when one is born who is destined for an evil life, and is consigned, as if for punishments, to the workhouse, the minister is dismayed and falls down. Do you wish to receive an example of a holy man, whose every fruit lies in praise? Look at Jacob, who begot twelve male children, who all came forth as the people of God and as the patriarchs and princes of that portion: in all these Jacob the father rejoiced, just as now too joy is announced to all concerning the birth of John; and whoever has once, for the benefit of others, descended to the works of begetting children and has willed to bind himself to this ministry, let him beseech God that such a one from among his sons may enter the world, over whose birth he may be the more glad.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For when a just man is born into the world, the authors of his birth rejoice; but when one is born who is to be as it were an exile to labour and punishment, they are struck with terror and dismay.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It is written, then, of John: "he shall be great in the sight of the Lord". This, which is said—"he shall be great in the sight of the Lord"—shows the greatness of John's soul, which lies open to the eyes of God; and there is something lesser, which is properly beheld in the virtue of the soul. Thus I understand also that which is said in the Gospel: "do not despise one of these least ones", who are in the Church. "Least" there is understood in distinction from the greater. I am not commanded not to despise the one who is great, because he who is great cannot be despised, but it is said to me: "do not despise one of the least". And that you may know that "least" and "little" is not said by chance, but with the reasoning we have set forth, it is written: "whoever shall scandalize one of these least ones".

The "least" one is scandalized; the great one cannot sustain a scandal. There follows concerning John: "and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit while yet in his mother's womb". And the birth of John is full of miracle. For just as an Archangel announced the coming of our Lord and Savior, so also an Archangel announces the birth of John. "He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit while yet in his mother's womb". The people of the Jews in no way saw our Lord working "signs and wonders" and healing their infirmities; but John, still set in his mother's womb, exults and cannot be contained, and at the coming of the mother of Jesus longs to burst forth from the womb. "For behold", says Elizabeth, "as your greeting was made in my ears, the infant exulted for joy in my womb". John was still in his mother's womb and already he had the Holy Spirit. For that was not the beginning of his substance and nature.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: John indeed turned many, but it is the Lord's work to turn all to God their Father.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then Scripture says that "he shall convert very many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God". John converts "very many", but the Lord not many, rather all. This is his work, that he should convert all to God the Father.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In the spirit and power of Elijah.—He says not, in the mind of Elijah, but in the spirit and power. For the spirit which was in Elijah came upon John, and in like manner his power.

This sacrament of preparation is even now fulfilled in the world, for even now the spirit and power of John must come upon the soul, before it believes in Jesus Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And he shall go before Christ in the spirit and power of Elijah". He does not say: in the soul of Elijah, but: "in the spirit and power of Elijah". There was in Elijah a power and a spirit, as in all the prophets, and, according to the dispensation of the body, in the Lord and Savior himself also, of whom a little later it is said to Mary: "the Holy Spirit shall come upon you and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you". The spirit, therefore, which had been in Elijah, came into John, and the power which was in him appeared in this one also. The former was translated, but the latter was the forerunner of the Lord and died before him, so that, descending also to the lower regions, he might there proclaim his coming.

I think that the mystery of John is fulfilled in the world down to this very day. Whoever is to believe in Christ Jesus, first the spirit and power of John comes to his soul and "prepares for the Lord a perfect people", and in the ruggednesses of the heart makes the ways level and straightens the paths. Not at that time only were the ways prepared and the paths made straight, but down to this very day the spirit and power of John goes before the coming of the Lord and Savior. O the great mysteries of the Lord and of his dispensation! Angels run before Jesus, angels daily either ascend or descend upon the salvation of men in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Zechariah the priest, while he offers incense in the temple, is condemned to silence and holds his peace; indeed, he speaks only by nods, and remains mute right up to the birth of his son John. To what does this history point? The silence of Zechariah is the silence of the prophets among the people of Israel. In no way does God speak to them, and "the word, which in the beginning was God with the Father", has passed over to us, and Christ is not silent to us, though among them he is silent even to this day: for which reason also the prophet Zechariah kept silent. For it is most clearly proved from his very words that he was both a prophet and a priest. But what does this mean, which follows: "he was making signs to them" and made up for the loss of his voice by nods? I think that such works are those which, being without speech and reason, differ in nothing from nods. But where reason and speech have gone before and the work has thus followed after, they ought not to be reckoned mere nods, which are adorned with speech and reason. If therefore you see the manner of life of the Jews to be without reason and speech, so that they cannot render a reason for the things they do, understand that what then took place in Zechariah is even now being fulfilled in them as in an image. Their circumcision is like nods. For unless a reason for circumcision be rendered, circumcision is a nod and a mute work. The Passover and the other solemn feasts are nods rather than truth. To this day the people of Israel is deaf and "mute"; for it could not be otherwise than that he should be deaf and "mute" who had cast speech away from himself. And of old indeed Moses said: "but I am ἄλογος (without speech or reason)" — which, though the Latin has rendered it otherwise, can nevertheless be more properly translated: "without speech or reason" —, and after he said this, he received reason or speech, which he had confessed that he did not before possess. But the people of Israel in Egypt, before it received the law, was in a certain way "mute", without speech and reason; then it received speech, of which Moses was an image. This people, therefore, does not now confess what it then confessed in Moses, namely that it is "mute" and ἄλογος, but by nods and silence indicates that it does not have speech and does not have reason. Does it not seem to you to be a confession of foolishness, when none of them can render a reason for the legal precepts and the prophetic oracle? Christ has ceased to be in them, speech has abandoned them, and that has been fulfilled which is written in Isaiah: "the daughter of Zion shall be left like a booth in a vineyard, and like a lodge in a cucumber-field, like a city that is stormed". These being abandoned, salvation has been transferred to the nations, that those others might be stirred up to jealousy. Beholding, therefore, the dispensation and the hidden purpose of God, how Israel has been cast off unto our salvation, we ought to take care lest perhaps those others have been cast out for our sake, and we be worthy of greater punishment — we for whose sake others also have been abandoned, and we have done nothing worthy of God's adoption and of his mercy, who adopted us and reckoned us among his own sons in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 5

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And therefore he says, Five months, that is, until Mary should conceive, and her babe leaping with joy should prophesy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "When Elizabeth conceived, she hid herself for five months, saying: for thus has the Lord done for me in the days in which he looked upon me to take away my reproach among men". I ask for what reason, after she understood that she was pregnant, she withdrew from the public eye? Unless I am mistaken, this is the reason: Even those who are joined in marriage do not have every time free for intercourse between themselves, but there is a time when they withdraw from the work of marriage. For if a man be old and a woman aged, it is a matter of the greatest shame for them to be slaves to lust, to be slaves to the conjugal act, when they seem, by the decay of the body and by old age and by the will of God, to have been lifted above such things. But this woman, because at the word of the angel and by the dispensation of God she had again been joined to her husband, was ashamed that, being aged and almost decrepit, she had returned to the work of the young. Hence too she "hid herself for five months" — not until the ninth month, until the birth pressed upon her, but until such time as Mary also should conceive. For when Mary conceived and came to her, and "the greeting was made in" her "ears", "the infant leapt for joy in the womb" of Elizabeth, and she prophesied. And, filled "with the Holy Spirit", she spoke those things which the Gospel narrative describes. And "these words were spread abroad throughout all the hill country". For when a rumor went out among the people that she had a prophet in her womb, and that what she carried was greater than a man, then she is no longer hidden, but with all freedom she reveals herself and rejoices that she has in her womb the forerunner of the Savior.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For if she had had no husband, soon would the thought have stolen into the Devil's mind, how she who had known no man could be pregnant. It was right that the conception should be Divine, something more exalted than human nature.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then Scripture recalls that "in the sixth month" of Elizabeth's conception "the angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee, whose name was Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary". Again, turning it over in my mind, I ask why God, when once he had determined that the Savior should be born of a "virgin", did not choose a girl without a betrothed, but rather her especially who had already been "betrothed". And unless I am mistaken, this is the reason: He ought to be born of that virgin who not only had a betrothed, but, as Matthew writes, had already been handed over to a man, although the man did not yet know her, lest her very condition should display the shame of a virgin, if she were seen to be a virgin with a swelling womb. Hence I found it elegantly written in the letter of a certain martyr — I mean Ignatius, the second bishop of Antioch after Peter, who in the persecution at Rome fought against the beasts: "the virginity of Mary was hidden from the prince of this world"; it was hidden because of Joseph, hidden because of the marriage, hidden because she was thought to have a husband. For if she had not had a betrothed and, as was supposed, a husband, she could in no way have been hidden from "the prince of this world". For at once a silent thought would have crept upon the devil: how is this woman, who has not lain with a man, pregnant? This conception must be divine, it must be something loftier than human nature. On the contrary, the Savior had arranged his dispensation and the assumption of a body so that the devil should not know it: hence in his birth he concealed him, and afterward he charged his disciples "not to make him manifest". And when he was tempted by the devil himself, he nowhere confessed himself to be the Son of God, but answered only: it is not fitting that I should worship you, nor that I should make these stones into bread, nor that I should cast myself down from on high. And while he said these things, he was always silent that he was the Son of God. Look also in another Scripture, and you will find that it was Christ's will that the devil should not know the coming of the Son of God. For the Apostle, affirming that the opposing powers did not know his passion, says: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the princes of this world, who are brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this world knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory". The mystery of the Savior, therefore, was hidden from the princes of this world. But as for what can be objected on the contrary, it seems to me it must be resolved before it is put forward by another — namely, by what reasoning that which was hidden from the princes of this world was not hidden from the demon who spoke in the Gospel: "have you come here before the time to torment us? we know who you are, the Son of God". But consider that the lesser in malice knew the Savior; whereas he who is greater in wickedness and crafty and vile, by that very fact that he is greater in evil, is hindered from knowing the Son of God. We ourselves too, if we have less of evil, can more easily advance to virtue; but if there be more of evil in us, we must sweat with immense labor to be freed from the greater malice. So much concerning the fact that Mary had a betrothed.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But because the angel greeted Mary with a new form of speech, which I could not find in all of Scripture, a few things must be said about this also. For what he says, "Hail, full of grace", which in Greek is "κεχαριτωμένη" (one filled with grace), where I have read it elsewhere in the Scriptures I do not recall; nor is such a form of speech addressed to a man — "hail, full of grace". This greeting was reserved for Mary alone.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For if Mary had known that similar words had been addressed to others, such a salutation would never have appeared to her so strange and alarming.
When the angel saw that she was troubled at this unusual salutation, calling her by her name as if she was well known to him, he tells her she must not fear, as it follows; And the angel said, Fear not, Mary.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For if Mary had known that such a word had been spoken to any other as well — for she had knowledge of the Law and was holy and had come to know the oracles of the prophets by daily meditation — the greeting would never have terrified her as something strange.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For if Mary had known that similar words had been addressed to others, such a salutation would never have appeared to her so strange and alarming.
When the angel saw that she was troubled at this unusual salutation, calling her by her name as if she was well known to him, he tells her she must not fear, as it follows; And the angel said, Fear not, Mary.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: See then the greatness of the Saviour, how it is diffused over the whole world. Go up to heaven, see there how it has filled the heavenly places; carry thy thoughts down to the deep, behold, there too He has descended. If thou seest this, then, in like manner, beholdest thou fulfilled in very deed, He shall be great.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
On account of this the angel says to her: "fear not, Mary! for you have found grace before the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High". Of John also it is said, "he shall be great", and Gabriel the angel testifies to this very thing; but when Jesus came, truly great, truly exalted, he who before had been "great" was made lesser. For "he", he says, "was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light". The greatness of our Savior did not appear then, when he was born, but now — after he seemed to be crushed by his adversaries — it has shone forth.

See the greatness of the Lord: "into all the earth has the sound of his teaching gone out, and his words unto the ends of the world". Our Lord Jesus, because he is the power of God, has been poured out over the whole world, and at the present moment is with us according to that which is read in the Apostle: "when you are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of the Lord Jesus". The power of the Lord and Savior is both with those who are separated from our world in Britain, and with those in Mauritania, and with all who under the sun have believed in his name. See, then, the greatness of the Savior, how it has been poured out over the whole world — and certainly I have not yet set forth his true greatness. Ascend into the heavens and see him, how he has filled the heavenly places: for indeed "he appeared to the angels". Descend in thought into the depths, and you will see that he descended there also. For "he who descended is the same also who ascended, that he might fill all things", "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and things on earth and things under the earth". Consider the power of the Lord, how he has filled the world — that is, the heavenly and the earthly and the infernal things — how he has penetrated heaven itself and ascended to the things above. For we read that the Son of God passed through the heavens. If you see these things, you will likewise perceive that it was not said in passing, "he shall be great", but that the word was fulfilled in deed. Great is our Lord Jesus, both present and absent, and he grants a share of his strength even to this gathering and assembly of ours; and that we each may deserve to receive it, let us beseech the Lord Jesus: to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 6

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For Jesus who was in her womb hastened to sanctify John, still in the womb of his mother. Whence it follows, with haste.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It was fitting also that Mary, most worthy of the offspring of God, should after the angel's address go up into the hill country and dwell in the loftier places. Whence it is written: "Mary, rising up in those days, went into the hill country". It was fitting too that she, since she was not sluggish in her earnestness, should hasten with earnest care, and, being full of the Holy Spirit, should be led up to the loftier places and be protected by the power of God, by which she had already been overshadowed. She came therefore "into a city of Judah and into the house of Zechariah, and greeted Elizabeth. And it came to pass, when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, that the infant leaped in her womb, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Those who are better come to those who are worse, in order to grant them some benefit by their coming. So too the Savior came to John, that he might sanctify John's baptism; and Mary, as soon as she heard the angel announcing that she had conceived the Savior and that her kinswoman Elizabeth had a child in her womb, "rose up and went with haste into the hill country, and entered the house of Elizabeth". For Jesus, who was in her womb, was hastening to sanctify John, still set within his mother's belly. Indeed, before Mary came and greeted Elizabeth, the "infant did not leap in the womb"; but as soon as Mary spoke the word which the Son of God had prompted in the belly of His mother, "the infant leaped for joy", and then for the first time Jesus made His forerunner a prophet.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (vid. etiam Tit. Bos.) He was not filled with the Spirit, until she stood near him who bore Christ in her womb. Then indeed he was both filled with the Spirit, and leaping imparted the grace to his mother; as it follows, And Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. But we cannot doubt that she who was then filled with the Holy Spirit, was filled because of her son.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is therefore no doubt that she who then "was filled with the Holy Spirit" was "filled" on account of her son! For the mother did not first merit the Holy Spirit, but rather, when John, still enclosed in the womb, had received the Holy Spirit, then she too, after the sanctification of her son, "was filled with the Holy Spirit". You will be able to believe this if you learn something similar also concerning the Savior. Blessed Mary is found—as we have discovered in a good number of copies—to prophesy. For we are not unaware that, according to other manuscripts, it is Elizabeth who utters these words in prophecy. Mary, then, was filled with the Holy Spirit at that time when she began to have the Savior in her womb. For as soon as she received the Holy Spirit, the fashioner of the Lord's body, and the Son of God began to be in her womb, she herself too was filled with the Holy Spirit.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The "infant", then, "leaped in the womb of Elizabeth, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out with a loud voice and said: Blessed art thou among women". In this place we must, lest any of the simple be deceived, refute the objections that heretics are accustomed to raise. For a certain man—I know not who—broke out into such madness as to assert that Mary was disowned by the Savior, on the ground that after His birth she was joined to Joseph; and he spoke words which, with what sort of mind he uttered them, he himself who spoke them knows. If therefore heretics should ever bring some such objection against you, answer them and say: Surely Elizabeth, full "of the Holy Spirit", says: "blessed art thou among women". If Mary is proclaimed blessed by the Holy Spirit, how did the Savior disown her? Furthermore, as for their assertion that she married after the birth, they have no source from which to prove it; for those sons who were called Joseph's were not born of Mary, nor is there any Scripture which mentions such a thing.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" This which she says, "whence is this to me?" she does not say out of ignorance—and least of all when full of the Holy Spirit, as though she did not know that according to the will of God the mother of the Lord had come to her; but she speaks in this sense: what good have I done? what works of mine are so great that the mother of the Lord should come to me? through what righteousness, by what good deeds, by what fidelity of mind have I merited this, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (non occ. vide Theoph. et. Tit. Bost.) Now in saying this, she coincides with her son. For John also felt that he was unworthy of our Lord's coming to him. But she gives the name of "the mother of our Lord" to one still a virgin, thus forestalling the event by the words of prophecy. Divine foreknowledge brought Mary to Elisabeth, that the testimony of John might reach the Lord. For from that time Christ ordained John to be a prophet. Hence it follows, For, to, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "For behold, as soon as thy greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for exultation in my womb". Holy was the soul of blessed John, and while still enclosed in his mother's womb and yet to come into the world he knew Him whom Israel did not know; whence he "leaped", and not simply "leaped", but "for joy". For he had perceived that his Lord had come to sanctify His servant, before he came forth from his mother's belly.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Would that it might befall me to be called a fool by the unbelieving, I who have believed such things. The work itself and the truth show that I have believed not in folly but in wisdom, since this which is reckoned foolishness among them becomes for me the occasion of salvation. For unless the nativity of the Savior had been heavenly and blessed, unless it had had something divine and surpassing the humanity of men, His teaching would never have penetrated throughout the whole world. If there had been only a man in Mary's womb and not the Son of God, how could it have come to pass that both at that time and now the manifold diseases not only of bodies but also of souls should be cured? Which of us was not foolish, we who now through the mercy of God have understanding and know God? Who was not without faith in righteousness, we who now for Christ's sake have righteousness and follow after righteousness? Which of us was not wandering and astray, we who now, on account of the coming of the Savior, are not tossed about and troubled, but are on the way—namely, in Him who says: "I am the way"? We can also, gathering together the rest, see that all the things which have been written concerning Him are reported as worthy of divine wonder, since both His nativity and His nurture and His power and His passion and His resurrection work in us not only at that time but even now. Who gathered you, O catechumens, into the church? What goad drove you to leave your homes and come together into this assembly? For we do not go around your houses one by one, but the almighty Father by an invisible power lays upon your hearts—upon those whom He knows to be worthy—this ardor, so that as though unwilling and drawing back you come to the faith, especially at the beginning of religion, when, as though trembling and fearful, you take up the faith of salvation with fear. I beseech you, O catechumens: do not draw back, let none of you dread and be afraid, but follow Jesus who goes before you. He draws you to salvation, He gathers you into the church—now indeed upon the earth, but, if you bring forth worthy fruits, into the "church of the firstborn, who are written in the heavens". "Blessed is she who believed", and blessed is he who believed, because there will be a fulfillment for these things "which have been spoken" to her "by the Lord". Over these things Mary also "magnifies" the Lord Jesus. And "the soul magnifies the Lord, the spirit magnifies God". What interpretation these words have, if the Lord grants that we be gathered together again into the church—so that you may come joyfully to the house of God and lend your ears to the divine reading—we shall inquire, we shall sift, we shall discourse, in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 7

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now if the Lord could neither receive increase or decrease, what is this that Mary speaks of, My soul doth magnify (magnificat) the Lord? But if I consider that the Lord our Saviour is the image of the invisible God, and that the soul is created according to His image, so as to be an image of an image, then I shall see plainly, that as after the manner of those who are accustomed to paint images, each one of us forming his soul after the image of Christ, makes it great or little, base or noble, after the likeness of the original; so when I have made my soul great in thought, word, and deed, the image of God is made great, and the Lord Himself, whose image it is, is magnified in my soul.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Before John, Elizabeth prophesies; before the birth of the Lord and Savior, Mary prophesies. And just as sin began from a woman and thereafter proceeded onward to the man, so too the beginning of salvation took its origin from women, that other women also, laying aside the frailty of their sex, might imitate the life and manner of conduct of these holy women, and above all of those who are now described in the Gospel. Let us therefore examine the virgin's prophecy. "My soul", she says, "magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior". Two things, "the soul" and "the spirit", discharge a twofold praise. The soul proclaims the Lord, the spirit God: not that the praise of the Lord is one thing and the praise of God another, but because he who is God is the same as the Lord, and he who is the Lord is the same as God. It is asked how "the soul magnifies the Lord". For if the Lord can receive neither increase nor diminishment and is what he is, on what account does Mary now say: "My soul magnifies the Lord"? If I consider the Lord and Savior to be "the image of the invisible God", and see that my soul was made "according to the image of its Creator", so as to be an image of the Image — for my soul is not specifically an image of God, but was made after the likeness of the prior Image — then I will see that, after the example of those who are accustomed to paint images, and, having received (for instance) the single face of a king, to apply the diligence of their art to expressing the principal likeness, each one of us, forming his soul according to the image of Christ, sets in it either a greater or a lesser image, whether faded or dirty, or bright and shining and answering to the likeness of the principal Image. When therefore I have made the image of the Image, that is, my soul, great, and have magnified it by deed, by thought, by word, then the image of God is made great, and the Lord himself, whose image it is, is magnified in our soul. And just as the Lord grows in our image, so, if we are sinners, he is diminished and decreases. Or rather, the Lord is neither diminished nor decreases, but we, in place of the image of the Savior, put on other images for ourselves; in place of the image of the Word, of wisdom, of justice, and of the other virtues, we assume the form of the devil, so that it is said of us: "serpents, brood of vipers".
