But we are also clothed with the persona of a lion and of a dragon and of foxes, when we are venomous, cruel, cunning, and also of a he-goat, when we are more prone to lust. I remember once, when discoursing on Deuteronomy at that place where it is written: "do not make any likeness of male or of female, the likeness of any animal", that I said that it is "the spiritual law" that some make themselves the image of a male, others of a female, that this one has the likeness of birds, that one of reptiles and serpents, and that another makes himself the likeness of God. How these things are to be understood, he will know who has also read those passages. "The soul" of Mary, then, first "magnifies the Lord", and afterward "the spirit exults in God"; for unless we have first believed, we cannot exult.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 8

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the soul first magnifies the Lord, that it may afterwards rejoice in God; for unless we have first believed, we can not rejoice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But why was she lowly and cast down, who carried in her womb the Son of God? Consider that lowliness, which in the Scriptures is particularly praised as one of the virtues, is called by the philosophers "modestia." And we also may paraphrase it, that state of mind in which a man instead of being puffed up, casts himself down.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Because he has looked", she says, "upon the lowliness of his handmaid". Upon what lowliness of Mary did the Lord look? What did the mother of the Savior have that was lowly and cast down, she who bore the Son of God in her womb? So then, when she says: "he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid", it is as though she had said: "he has looked" upon the justice of his handmaid, "he has looked" upon her temperance, "he has looked" upon her fortitude and wisdom. For it is fitting that God should look upon the virtues. Let someone answer and say: I understand how God looks upon the justice and wisdom of his handmaid; but how he regards her lowliness is not sufficiently clear. Let him who inquires into such things consider that in the Scriptures, properly speaking, one of the virtues is proclaimed as "lowliness" (humility). For the Savior says: "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls". But if you wish to hear the name of this virtue, how it is called even by the philosophers, listen — that it is the same "lowliness" upon which God looks, which is called by them ἀτυφία (freedom from vanity) or μετριότης (moderation). But we too can name it by a certain circumlocution, when someone is not puffed up, but casts himself down. For he who is puffed up falls, according to the Apostle, "into the judgment of the devil" — since he too began from inflation and pride —; "lest", he says, "being puffed up he fall into the judgment of the devil". "He has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid". God, she says, has looked upon me as lowly and pursuing the virtue of gentleness and of self-abasement. "For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed". If I understand "all generations" simply, I interpret it of those who believe.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 8

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if I have searched out something more deeply, I will observe how great is the advance signified by saying: "because he who is mighty has done great things for me": for since "everyone who humbles himself will be exalted", and God "has looked upon the lowliness" of blessed Mary, therefore "he who is mighty has done" for her "great things, and holy is his name".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 8

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the mercy of God is not upon one generation, but extends to eternity from generation to generation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And his mercy is unto generations of generations". The "mercy" of God is extended not unto one generation, nor unto two, nor unto three, nor even unto five, but forever "from generation unto generation".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 8

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But to those that fear Him, He hath done mighty things with His arm; though thou comest weak to God, if thou hast feared Him thou shalt obtain the promised strength.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "For those who fear him he has done a mighty deed with his arm". Though you come to the Lord weak, if you have feared him, you will be able to hear the promise which the Lord pledges to you on account of your fear of him. What is this promise? "For those who fear him", she says, "he has done a mighty deed". A mighty deed, or dominion, is royal power. For indeed κράτος, which we may call "dominion", is so named from the fact that it holds command, or contains all things under itself. If therefore you have feared the Lord, he gives you strength or dominion, he gives you a kingdom, so that, made subject to the "King of kings", you may possess "the kingdom of heaven" in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 8

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Both of the things that are said and of those that are reported as done, the account ought to be worthy of the Holy Spirit and of the faith of Christ, to which we who believe are called. Hence now too the reason must be sought why Mary, after her conceiving, came to Elizabeth and "remained with her three months"; or what the reason was that Luke, who was writing the history of the Gospel, should also insert this, that she "remained with her three months, and afterwards returned to her own house". Surely there ought to be some reason which, if the Lord opens our heart, the discourse that follows will show. For if from the mere fact that Mary came to Elizabeth and greeted her, "the infant leaped for joy", and "Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit", prophesied those things which are written in the Gospel, and in a single hour made such great advances, it is left to our conjecture how much John advanced in three months, with Mary sitting beside Elizabeth. For it would be exceedingly unfitting that in a mere point and moment of an hour the infant should have leaped and in a manner frolicked with joy, and Elizabeth should have been filled with the Holy Spirit, but that in three whole months neither John nor Elizabeth should have advanced from the nearness of the Lord's mother and the presence of the Savior himself. Therefore John was being exercised, and in a manner anointed as in an athletic arena, throughout those three months, and was being prepared in his mother's womb, so that, having been born wonderfully, he might more wonderfully be nourished. For because he was nourished in an unaccustomed way, it is not recorded in writing how he was suckled at his mother's breasts, how he was placed in the bosom of a nurse, but at once there follows: "and he was in the deserts until the day of his showing forth to Israel".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 9

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Next we read: "But for Elizabeth the time was fulfilled that she should bring forth, and she bore a son". Many think it is said superfluously: "But for Elizabeth the time was fulfilled that she should bring forth, and she bore a son". For what woman can bring forth unless she has first fulfilled the time of bringing forth? But whoever contemplates the Scriptures most diligently and hears Paul saying: "attend to the reading", observing both in the Old and in the New Testament, if anywhere he might find it written at the birth of a sinner: "the time was fulfilled that she should bring forth", he will never at all find it. But wherever a just man is born, there the days are fulfilled, there the coming into the world is fulfilled. The birth of the just has fullness, but the nativity of a sinner has, so to speak, emptiness and hollowness. So much for what is written: "the time was fulfilled that she should bring forth".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 9

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then it follows that, when John was born, "the neighbors and kinsfolk congratulated" his mother, and they wished to impose on the boy a name in honor of his father, so that he should be called Zechariah. But Elizabeth, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, said: "John is his name". Then when they sought just reasons why he should be called John of all names, since in his family no one bore this name, they ask his father, who, being unable to answer, spoke with his hand and with letters. For he "wrote" on a tablet: "John is his name". And at once, as the stylus was pressed into the wax, "the tongue", which before had been bound, "was loosed" and recovered speech that was not human. As long as his tongue was bound, it was human; for unbelief had bound it. As soon as it was loosed, it ceased to be human, "and he spoke, blessing God" and prophesied those things which are written in the Gospel, about which, with the Lord Jesus Christ granting it, we shall discourse when the time comes: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 9

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (non occ.) Zacharias is by interpretation "remembering God," but John signifies "pointing to." Now "memory" relates to something absent, "pointing to," to something present. But John was not about to set forth the memory of God as absent, but with his finger to point him out as present, saying, Behold the Lamb of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now Zacharias being filled with the Holy Spirit utters two prophecies, the first relating to Christ, the second to John. And this is plainly proved by those words in which he speaks of the Saviour as present and already going about in the world, saying, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he hath visited, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zechariah announces two prophecies in a general way, the first concerning Christ, the second concerning John. This is plainly borne out from his own words, in which he speaks of the Savior as though already present and dwelling in the world, and then afterward of John. For "being filled with the Holy Spirit he prophesied, saying: Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought the redemption of his people". For when God was visiting and willing to redeem his people, "Mary remained" with Elizabeth, after the angel had spoken to her, "three months", so that by a certain ineffable power the Savior, being present, might instruct not only John, as we said a while ago, but also Zechariah, as the Gospel word now declares. For here too, little by little through three months, he was receiving the increases of the Holy Spirit, and, while he does not know it, he was being taught, and he prophesied concerning Christ, saying: "who gave redemption to his people, and raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David", because Christ was born "of the seed of David according to the flesh". And truly he was "a horn of salvation in the house of David", because this prophecy is sung in harmony: "For a vineyard was made on a horn". On what horn? On Christ Jesus, on him of whom it is now written: "he raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Because Christ was born of the seed of David, according to the flesh, it is said, A horn of salvation to us in the house of his servant David; as it has also elsewhere been said, A vineyard hath been planted in a horn, (Is. 5:1.) i. e. in Jesus Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us not suppose that this refers to our bodily enemies, but our ghostly. For the Lord Jesus came mighty in battle (Ps. 24:8) to destroy all our enemies, that He might deliver us from their snares and temptation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Salvation from our enemies". Let us not now suppose that this is said of bodily enemies, but of spiritual ones. For the Lord Jesus came, "mighty in battle", to destroy all our enemies, that he might free us from their snares: from the hand of all our enemies "and from the hand of all who hate us".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us not suppose that this refers to our bodily enemies, but our ghostly. For the Lord Jesus came mighty in battle (Ps. 24:8) to destroy all our enemies, that He might deliver us from their snares and temptation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "To show mercy toward our fathers" — I think that at the coming of the Lord the Savior both Abraham and Isaac and Jacob enjoyed the mercy of God. For it is not credible that those who earlier saw his day and rejoiced should afterward, at his coming and his birth from the Virgin, have received no benefit. And why do I speak of the patriarchs? Following the authority of the Scriptures, I will boldly ascend to higher things, since the presence of the Lord Jesus and his dispensation profited not only things earthly but also things heavenly. Whence the Apostle also says: "making peace through the blood of his cross, whether upon the earth or in the heavens". But if in heaven and on earth the presence of the Lord was of profit, why should you be afraid to say that his coming profited even the greater ones, so that this might be fulfilled which is said: "to show mercy toward our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore to Abraham our father", that he might grant us to be freed "without fear from the hand of the enemies"?
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I think that at the coming of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, both Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, were partakers of His mercy. For it is not to be believed, that they who had before seen His day, and were glad, should afterwards derive no advantage from His coming, since it is written, Having made peace through the blood of his Cross, whether in earth or in heaven. (Coloss. 1:20.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or in another way; Frequently are men delivered from the hands of the enemy, but not without fear. For when fear and peril have gone before, and a man is then plucked from the enemies' hand, he is delivered indeed, but not without fear. Therefore said he, that the coming of Christ caused us to be snatched from the enemies' hands without fear. For we suffered not from their evil designs, but He suddenly parting us from them, hath led us out to our own allotted resting place.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Frequently some are freed from the hand of foes, but not "without fear". For when dread and danger have first gone before, and thus one has been rescued from the hand of enemies, he is indeed freed, but not "without fear". But the coming of the Lord Jesus rescued us "from the hand of the enemies without fear". For we did not perceive our enemies nor see them fighting against us, but, while we knew it not, we were suddenly snatched from their jaws and their snares. "In a point and a moment" he transferred us "into the inheritance and the portion of the just", and we have been freed "from the hand of the enemies without fear, that we may serve God in holiness and justice before him all our days".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or in another way; Frequently are men delivered from the hands of the enemy, but not without fear. For when fear and peril have gone before, and a man is then plucked from the enemies' hand, he is delivered indeed, but not without fear. Therefore said he, that the coming of Christ caused us to be snatched from the enemies' hands without fear. For we suffered not from their evil designs, but He suddenly parting us from them, hath led us out to our own allotted resting place.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The reason I suppose that Zacharias hastened to speak to his son, was because he knew that John was shortly about to be a sojourner in the wilderness, and that he himself should see him no more.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High". Seeking within myself the reason why he prophesies not as though about John, but by speaking to John himself: "and you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High", and the rest — for it was superfluous to speak to one who does not hear and to make an apostrophe to a little one and a suckling — I think I can find this: that just as John was born wondrously and came into the world with an angel proclaiming it, and was poured forth upon the earth while Mary lodged three months beside Elizabeth, so also all the things that are written about him are reported to have been done wondrously. But if you doubt that one just poured forth from his mother's womb could hear his father's words and know what this is which is said to him: "and you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High", consider that what went before was far more wondrous: "behold, as the sound of your salutation came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb". For if, while still enclosed in his mother's belly, he heard Jesus and, hearing, leaped up and rejoiced, why should you not believe that once already born he was able both to hear and to understand his father's prophecy, saying to him: "and you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the Lord, to prepare his ways"? Therefore I think Zechariah hastened to speak to the little one, because he knew that he would after a little while dwell in the wilderness, and that he could not have his presence. "For the child was in the deserts until the day of his showing to Israel". Moses too dwelt in the desert, but only after, when the forty years of his age were completed, he fled from Egypt and for another forty years guarded the flocks of Jethro; John, however, as soon as he was born, passed over to the deserts, and he who "was greater among those born of women" showed himself worthy of a greater nurture. Of him the prophet speaks: "behold, I send my angel before your face". Rightly is he called an angel, who had been sent before the Lord and, as soon as he was born, was able to hear and understand his prophesying father. Wherefore let us, who believe such great wonders, likewise believe in the resurrection, let us believe also in the promises that are to come, of the kingdom of heaven, which the Holy Spirit daily pledges to us. All of which things, as they have been wondrously written, beyond what we are able to perceive, we shall receive in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or he increased in spirit, remaining not in the same measure in which he had begun, but the Spirit was ever growing in him. His will ever tending to better things, was making its own advances, and his mind ever contemplating something more divine, while his memory was exercising itself, that it might lay up more and more things in its treasury, and more firmly retain them. But he adds, And he waxed strong. For human nature is weak, as we learn, the flesh is weak. (Matt. 26:41.) It must therefore be made strong by the Spirit, for the Spirit is ready. Many wax strong in the flesh, but the wrestler of God must be strengthened by the Spirit that he may crush the wisdom of the flesh. He retires therefore to escape the noise of cities, and the thronging of the people. For it follows, And he was in the deserts. Where the air is purer, the sky more clear, and God a closer friend, that as the time had not yet arrived for his baptism and preaching, he might have leisure for praying, and might hold converse with the angels, calling upon God and fearing Him, saying, Behold, here am I.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the holy Scriptures "to grow" is spoken of in two ways: one bodily, where the human will avails nothing, the other spiritually, where the cause of growing rests upon human effort. It is of this, then — the second we set down, that is, the spiritual — that the evangelist now speaks: "but the child grew and was strengthened in spirit". What he says means this: "he grew in spirit", and did not remain in the same measure in which he had begun, but the spirit always grew in him, and, as the spirit increased through each hour and moment, his soul too received its increases. And not only the soul, but the senses and the mind as well followed the growth of the spirit. That which God commands: "increase and multiply" — those who take it simply and according to the letter, I do not know how they can explain it. For granted that "multiply" refers to number, so that, while they become more than they were before, the multiplication has its place: yet what follows, "increase", is not in our power. For what person would not wish "to add to his stature", so as to become taller? If therefore something is commanded for this purpose, that it may come to pass — since it is foolish to command what he to whom you give the command cannot do — and it is commanded us that we should increase, then surely that is commanded which we are able to do. Do you wish to know how "increase" is to be understood? Hear what Isaac did, of whom it is said: "Isaac went forward and became greater, until he became great, or exceedingly great indeed". For his will, ever stretching itself toward better things, had its advances, his mind contemplated something more divine, and he exercised himself in memory, so as to store up more things in his treasury and retain them more firmly. And in this manner it comes about that whoever has cultivated all his virtues in the field of his soul fulfills the commandment enjoining: "increase". Wherefore John too, while still a little one, grew and was multiplied; but it is most difficult, and among mortals most rare, for a little one to grow in spirit. "But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit." "He grew" is one thing, "he was strengthened" another. Human nature is weak and, in order that it may become stronger, needs divine help. We read: "the flesh is weak". By what help, then, is it to be strengthened? By the spirit, surely; "for the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak". He who wishes to become stronger ought to be strengthened by nothing but the spirit. Many are strengthened by the flesh, are made robust in body; but the athlete of God must be made robust by the spirit, and, when he has been thus strengthened, he will strike down the wisdom of the flesh and, made spiritual, will subject the body to the rule of the mind. Let us not think, then, that a plain narrative has been written about John, and one that has nothing to do with us, in what is said: "he grew and was strengthened in spirit", but rather for our imitation, so that, multiplied spiritually according to the sense we have mentioned, we too may receive increases. "And he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel." I said recently that John's very conception had something astounding about it, when "the infant leaped in the womb" and, not yet born, recognized his Lord, and his birth was a miracle no less remarkable, when the word of Zechariah prophesying turns toward him as though he were listening, saying: "and you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High". Worthily, then, he who had been thus conceived and born did not wait to be nourished by his father and mother "until the day of his manifestation to Israel", but withdrew, fleeing the tumult of cities, the throng of the people, the vices of the towns, and went off into the deserts, where the air is purer and the sky more open and God more intimate, so that — since neither the sacrament of baptism nor the time of preaching had yet come — he might be free for prayers and might converse with angels, might call upon the Lord and hear him answering and saying: "behold, I am here". For just as "Moses spoke and God answered him", so I think that John spoke in the desert and the Lord answered him. And this I judge, moved by a sure reasoning from the Scriptures. For if "among those born of women there was none greater than John the Baptist", and God answered Moses, then consequently he answered John as well, who was greater than Moses, who was nourished in the wilderness, whose birth the same Archangel announced as he did the Lord's, whose father, because he did not believe that he would be born, was struck dumb. "John was" therefore "in the desert" and was nourished in a new manner beyond human custom, Matthew himself recording the very thing: "and his food was locusts and wild honey". For because he was the minister of the first coming of the Savior and spoke only of the dispensation of the Lord's flesh, and his prophecy foretold him who had been born of a virgin, he did not have domestic honey refined by human care, but "wild honey" and winged — which was his food — winged, not great, not lifting itself on high, but a small winged thing, scarcely rising from the earth and leaping rather than flying. Why say more? It is said most plainly that "locusts" were his food, a small and clean animal. Consider therefore, dearest brethren, that he who had been born in a new way was in a new way also nourished.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 11

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To those who attentively consider it, there seems to be expressed a kind of sacrament, in its being necessary that Christ should be put down in the registration of the whole world; in order that His name being written with all, He might sanctify all, and being placed in the census with the whole world, He might impart to the world the communion of Himself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After which the Scripture adds: "It came to pass in those days, there went out an edict from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be enrolled. This was the first census, under Quirinius, governor of Syria". Someone may say: evangelist, how does this narrative help me — that the "first census" of the whole world took place under Caesar Augustus, and that among all the rest "Joseph too, with Mary who was betrothed to him and with child", entered his name in the register, and that, before the census was completed, Jesus was born? To one who looks more carefully a certain mystery seems to be signified: that in the enrollment of the whole world Christ too had to be registered, so that, written down with all, he might sanctify all, and, entered in the census with the world, he might offer the world communion with himself, so that after this census he might also enroll from the world, together with himself, "in the book of the living", so that whoever had believed in him might afterward be "written in heaven" with his saints: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 11

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if we would rise to a more hidden meaning, I should say, that there were certain shepherd angels, who direct the affairs of men, and while each one of them was keeping his watch, an angel came at the birth of the Lord, and announced to the shepherds that the true Shepherd had arisen. For Angels before the coming of the Saviour could bring little help to those entrusted to them, for scarcely did one single Gentile believe in God. But now whole nations come to the faith of Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
My Lord Jesus was born, and an angel came down from heaven announcing his birth. Let us see, therefore, whom he sought out, that he might announce his coming. He did not come to Jerusalem, he did not seek out the scribes and Pharisees, he did not enter the synagogue of the Jews, but he found "shepherds keeping watch over their flocks" and spoke to them: "Today there is born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord".

Do you suppose that the word of the Scriptures signifies nothing more divine, but says only this, that an angel came to the shepherds and spoke to them? Hear, you shepherds of the churches, you shepherds of God, that his angel always comes down from heaven and announces to you: "Today there is born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord". For indeed the shepherds of the churches, unless that Shepherd has come, will not be able of themselves to guard the flock well: their guardianship is weak, unless Christ pastures and guards along with them. Some while ago it was read in the Apostle: "We are God's fellow workers". The good shepherd, who imitates the good Shepherd, is a fellow worker of God and of Christ; and for this reason he is a good shepherd, because he has with him the best Shepherd feeding the flock together with him. For "God has placed in the Church apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, teachers, all things for the perfecting of the saints".

And let these things indeed be said in a simpler manner. But if one ought to ascend to a more hidden understanding, I would say that there were certain shepherds — angels who governed human affairs — and that, while each one of these was preserving his own charge and, keeping watch by day and by night, could now no longer bear the labor, and was industriously doing this, that he might govern the nations that had been entrusted to him, an angel came, when the Lord was born, and announced to the shepherds that the true Shepherd had arisen. For example, to come to an illustration, there was a certain shepherd of Macedonia; this one had need of the Lord's help; and therefore there appeared to Paul in his sleep a man of Macedonia, "saying: Cross over into Macedonia and help us". But why do I speak of Paul, when it was not to Paul, but to him who was in Paul, that Jesus spoke this? And so the shepherds have need of the presence of Christ. For which reason the angel came down from heaven and said: "Do not be afraid; for behold, I announce to you a great joy". Truly a great joy for those to whom the care of men and of provinces had been entrusted, that Christ had come into the world. The angel who administered the affairs of Egypt received much benefit, after the Lord came down from heaven, so that the Egyptians might become Christians. It profited all those who held the various provinces — for instance, the governor of Macedonia, the governor of Achaia, and of the remaining regions. For it is not right to believe that evil angels are set over the individual provinces, and that good angels do not have those same provinces and regions entrusted to them. But this, which he says concerning the individual provinces, I think ought to be believed generally concerning all men as well. Two angels attend each person, one of righteousness, the other of iniquity. If there have been good thoughts in our heart and righteousness has sprung up in our soul, there is no doubt that the angel of the Lord speaks to us. But if evil thoughts have been busy in our heart, the angel of the devil speaks to us. Just as, therefore, throughout the individual persons there are two angels, so also I think that in the individual provinces there are differing ones, so that there may be both good ones and evil ones. For example, in Ephesus, on account of those who were sinners in that city, the worst angels presided. Again, because there were many believers in it, there was also the angel of the church of the Ephesians, certainly a good one. But this, which we have said of Ephesus, is to be recognized concerning all provinces. Before the coming of the Lord and Savior, those angels could bring little benefit to those entrusted to them, and their efforts were not able to be followed by any effect. And what is the sign that they could benefit their subjects but little? Listen to what we say: When the angel of the Egyptians helped the Egyptians, scarcely one proselyte believed in God; and this came about while the angel administered the Egyptians. Finally, because most of the proselytes from among the Egyptians and Idumeans received the faith of God, for this reason the Scripture says: "You shall not abhor the Egyptian, since you were sojourners in the land of Egypt, and the Idumean, because he is your brother. If children are born to them, in the third generation they shall enter the Church of God". And so it came about that from all the nations some became proselytes, and this very thing while the angels who had the nations as their subjects strove for it. But now the peoples of believers come to the faith of Jesus, and the angels to whom the churches had been entrusted, strengthened by the presence of the Savior, bring in many proselytes, so that assemblies of Christians may be gathered together in all the world. Wherefore, rising up, let us praise the Lord and become, in place of the carnal Israel, the spiritual Israel. Let us bless almighty God in deed, in thought, in word, in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 12

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But if we would rise to a more hidden meaning, I should say, that there were certain shepherd angels, who direct the affairs of men, and while each one of them was keeping his watch, an angel came at the birth of the Lord, and announced to the shepherds that the true Shepherd had arisen. For Angels before the coming of the Saviour could bring little help to those entrusted to them, for scarcely did one single Gentile believe in God. But now whole nations come to the faith of Jesus.

But in a mystery, the Angels saw that they could not accomplish the work committed to them without Him Who was truly able to save, and that their healing fell short of what the care of men required. And so it was as if there should come one who had great knowledge in medicine, and those who before were unable to heal, acknowledging now the hand of a master, grudge not to see the corruptions of wounds ceasing, but break forth into the praises of the Physician, and of that God who sent to them and to the sick a man of such knowledge; the multitudes of the Angels praised God for the coming of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From this it is shown that, according to the likeness of the legions of worldly warfare, there are also legions of angels of the heavenly warfare, warring against the legions of the demons dwelling in the tombs. For in Luke too "a multitude of the heavenly host" was heard "praising God" on account of Christ's nativity. But if "there was a multitude of the heavenly host praising God", and all warfare is understood to be established on account of adversaries, consequently that host too wars for God on account of adversaries. But Jacob also called a certain place the "camp" of the Lord, since he beheld there the warfare of angels; and wherever there are those who fear God, around them are the camps of angels; for "the angel of the Lord shall send [a host] round about those who fear him and shall deliver them", as the book of Kingdoms relates was the case also around Elisha.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Our Lord and Savior is born in Bethlehem, and "a multitude of the heavenly host" praises God and says: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of good will". Now the "multitude of the heavenly host" speaks these words because it had already failed to furnish men with help, and it saw that it could not fulfill the work that had been entrusted to it apart from him who was truly able to save and even to assist the presiding powers themselves, so that men might be saved. Therefore, just as it is written in the Gospel that certain men, plowing the sea with their oars against contrary winds, were already exhausted and, laboring for twenty-five or thirty stadia, could not reach the harbor, and afterward the Lord came upon them and made the swelling waves grow calm, and freed the ship, whose sides were being flooded on this side and that, from the impending danger — so understand that the angels too indeed wished to furnish men with help and to grant them health from their sicknesses, because "they are all attendant spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who shall obtain salvation", and, as far as lay within their powers, they helped men; yet they saw that their medicine was far inferior to what the cure of those men demanded. Furthermore, that you may understand from an example what we are saying, consider for me a city in which very many are sick and a busy troop of physicians is brought in; let there be diverse wounds, and daily let a creeping rottenness penetrate into the dead flesh, and yet let the physicians who have been brought in to heal be unable to find any further remedies or, by the knowledge of their art, to overcome the greatness of the evil. When things are in such a state, let there come some chief physician who has the highest expertise in the art; and let those who before had been unable to heal, when they behold the rottenness of the wounds cease at the master's hand, not be envious, not be tortured by spite, but burst forth into praises of the chief physician and proclaim God, who has sent both to themselves and to the sick a man of such great knowledge. In this likeness, then, the "multitude of the host" of angels was heard, saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of good will". For after the Lord came to the earth, "he made peace through the blood of his cross, whether for the things that were on earth, or for the things that were in heaven".

Indeed, since the angels wished that men should remember their Creator, when they had done all that lay within their powers that men might be healed, and those men had refused to receive health, they behold him who was able to heal, and glorifying him they say: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 13

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the attentive reader will ask, How then does the Saviour say, I came not to send peace on the earth, whereas now the Angels' song of His birth is, On earth peace to men? It is answered, that peace is said to be to men of goodwill. For the peace which the Lord does not give on the earth is not the peace of good will.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let the diligent reader of Scripture inquire how the Savior can say: "I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword", while now the angels at his nativity sing: "on earth peace". For in another place too it is said in his own person: "My peace I give to you, peace I leave to you: not as this world gives peace, do I give peace". Let him then see whether what we bring forward can resolve the question. If it had been written: "on earth peace", and the sentence had ended at that point, the question would rightly arise. But now that which is added — that is, what is said after "peace": "among men of good will" — resolves the question. The peace too which the Lord does not give "upon the earth" is not the "peace of good will". For he does not say simply: "I came not to send peace", but with an addition: "upon the earth"; nor did he, on the contrary, say: "I came not to send peace upon the earth of good will". These things the angels spoke to the shepherds, who were speaking not only at that time; but even to this day, unless they have spoken to the shepherds and joined their own works to them, it is said to them: "unless the Lord build the house, they have labored in vain who build it; unless the Lord guard the city, in vain does he watch who guards it". If it is expedient to speak boldly, following the meaning of the Scriptures, throughout the individual churches there are two bishops: one visible, the other invisible; the former open to the sight of the flesh, the latter to the perception of the mind. And just as a man, if he has administered well the dispensation entrusted to him, is praised by the Lord, but if badly, lies subject to blame and fault, so also the angel. For it is written in the Apocalypse of John: "but you have there a few names which have not been defiled", or this again: "you have there those who teach the doctrine of the Nicolaitans", and then: "you have those" or "those committing sins", and the angels are accused to whom the churches have been entrusted. But if the angels have such concern how the churches are governed, what need is there to speak of men, how much fear they should have, that they may be able, laboring together with the laboring angels, to obtain salvation? I think that both an angel and a man can be found together as good bishops of a church, and that in a certain way they are sharers of one work. Since this is so, let us beseech Almighty God that the angels and the men who are bishops of the churches may be a help to us, and let us know that both are judged by the Lord on our behalf. But if they have been judged, and the fault and sin has been found not in their carelessness but in our negligence, we shall be reproved and punished. For while they do everything and strive for our salvation, we nonetheless will be at leisure for sins. Moreover it frequently happens that, while we are laboring, they do not fulfill their office and are at fault.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 13

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But in a mystery, the Angels saw that they could not accomplish the work committed to them without Him Who was truly able to save, and that their healing fell short of what the care of men required. And so it was as if there should come one who had great knowledge in medicine, and those who before were unable to heal, acknowledging now the hand of a master, grudge not to see the corruptions of wounds ceasing, but break forth into the praises of the Physician, and of that God who sent to them and to the sick a man of such knowledge; the multitudes of the Angels praised God for the coming of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And it came to pass", he says, "when the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: Let us go over as far as Bethlehem, and let us see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has shown to us. And they came in haste, and found Mary and Joseph and the child". Because they had come in haste, and not step by step nor with weary tread, therefore they found Joseph the steward of the Lord's birth, and Mary who brought forth Jesus in childbirth, and the Savior himself "lying in a manger". That was the manger of which the prophet prophesied, saying: "the ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord". The ox is a clean animal, the ass an unclean animal. "The ass knew the manger of its lord". It was not the people of Israel who knew the manger of their lord, but an unclean animal from among the Gentiles: "but Israel", he says, "has not known me, and my people has not understood me". Understanding this manger, let us strive to know the Lord and to become worthy of the knowledge of him, and to take up not only the nativity and resurrection of his flesh, but also the renowned coming of his second majesty: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 13

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But because they came in haste, and not with loitering steps, it follows, They found Mary, (i. e. her who had brought Jesus into the, world,) and Joseph, (i. e. the guardian of our Lord's birth,) and the babe lying in the manger, (i. e. the Saviour Himself.)

That was the manger which Israel knew not, according to those words of Isaiah, The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib. (Isa. 3:1.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
As we have died with Him at His death, and risen together with Him at His resurrection, so with Him have we been circumcised, and therefore need not now circumcision in the flesh.

But the name of Jesus, a glorious name and worthy of all honour, a name which is above every other, ought not first to be uttered by men, nor by them be brought into the world. Therefore significantly the Evangelist adds, which was called of the Angel, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
In "that he died," Christ "died to sin"; not because he himself had sinned — "for he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" — but he died so that we, who were dead, might, by his dying "to sins," by no means live "to sin" and to vices. Whence it is written: "If we have died together with him, we shall also live together with him"; therefore, just as "we died together" then, when he died, and rose together with him when he rose again, so were we circumcised with him and, after the circumcision, cleansed by the solemn purification. Whence we now have no need whatsoever of carnal circumcision. And that you may know that he was circumcised for our sake, hear Paul preaching most plainly: "in whom," he says, "dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and you are filled in him, who is the head of all principality and power; in whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, buried together with him in baptism, in whom also you rose together with him through the faith of the working of God, who raised him from the dead". Therefore both his death and his resurrection and his circumcision were done for us.

"When," it says, "the days for circumcising the child were fulfilled, his name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived". The name of Jesus, glorious and most worthy of all adoration and worship, "the name which is above every name," was not fitting to be pronounced first by human beings, nor to be brought forth by them into the world, but by some more excellent and greater nature. Whence the evangelist pointedly added, saying: "and his name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For it is not by incantations that Christians seem to prevail (over evil spirits), but by the name of Jesus, accompanied by the announcement of the narratives which relate to Him; for the repetition of these has frequently been the means of driving demons out of men, especially when those who repeated them did so in a sound and genuinely believing spirit. Such power, indeed, does the name of Jesus possess over evil spirits, that there have been instances where it was effectual, when it was pronounced even by bad men, which Jesus Himself taught (would be the case), when He said: "Many shall say to Me in that day, In Thy name we have cast out devils, and done many wonderful works." Whether Celsus omitted this from intentional malignity, or from ignorance, I do not know.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then there follows: "when the days of their purification were fulfilled, according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem". On account of the purification, he says, "of them". Of whom, "of them"? If it had been written: on account of her purification, that is, of Mary, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would boldly say that Mary, who was human, had need of purification after childbirth. But now, in that it says: "the days of their purification", it seems to signify not one, but another or several. Did Jesus, then, have need of purification and was he unclean, or defiled with some filth? Perhaps I seem to speak rashly, but I am moved by the authority of the Scriptures. See what is written in Job: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day". He did not say: "no one is clean from sin," but: "no one is clean from filth". For filth and sins do not signify the same thing; and that you may know that filth means one thing and sin another, Isaiah teaches most plainly, saying: "the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment the filth and by the spirit of burning the blood". Every soul that has been clothed with a human body has its own "filth". And that you may know that Jesus too was made filthy by his own will, because for our salvation he had assumed a human body, listen to the prophet Zechariah saying: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments". And this indeed makes against those who deny that our Lord had a human body, but say it was woven of heavenly and spiritual things. For if his body was of heavenly things and, as they falsely assert, of the stars and some other more sublime and spiritual nature, let them answer why a spiritual body could be filthy, or how they interpret what we have set down: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments". But if they are compelled by necessity to accept that a filthy garment is understood as a spiritual body, they must consequently say that what is set down in the promises has been fulfilled, that is: "an animal body is sown, a spiritual body rises," and that we rise polluted and filthy — which even to think is a sacrilege, especially when one knows it is written: "it is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in strength; an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise". It was necessary, therefore, that for our Lord and Savior, who had been "clothed with filthy garments" and had assumed an earthly body, there should be offered those things which by the law were accustomed to purge filth. What is frequently asked among the brethren I take up again, prompted by the occasion of this passage. Little children are baptized "for the remission of sins". Of what "sins"? Or at what time did they sin? Or how can that reasoning of the washing hold in the case of little children, except according to that sense of which we spoke a little before: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day upon the earth"? And because through the sacrament of baptism the "filth" of birth is laid aside, therefore little children too are baptized: for "unless one be born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven".

"When," it says, "the days of their purification were fulfilled". The "days" are fulfilled also mystically. For a soul is not purified immediately, as soon as it is born, nor can it attain perfect purity in its very origin; but just as it is written in the law: "If she bears a male, the mother shall sit seven days in unclean blood, and then thirty-three days in pure blood, and at the last both she and the infant shall sit in most pure blood", so, because the law is spiritual and "has a shadow of the good things to come", we can understand that true purification comes to us after a time. I think that even after the resurrection from the dead we shall have need of a sacrament that washes and purges us — for no one will be able to rise without filth —, and that no soul can be found which is at once free from all vices. Whence in the regeneration of baptism a sacrament is received, so that, just as Jesus according to the dispensation of the flesh was purified by an offering, so we too may be purified by spiritual regeneration. "They brought him according to the law of Moses to Jerusalem, to present him before the sight of the Lord". Where are those who deny the God of the law, who say that it was not this God, but another different from Christ, who was proclaimed in the Gospel: "God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law"? Are we then to suppose that the good God made his Son under the law of the Creator and under the right of an enemy, a right which he himself had not given? Rather, he was made under the law for this reason, "that he might redeem those who were under the law", and subject them to another law, concerning which it was read a while ago: "Attend, my people, to my law", and the rest.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Where are they who deny that Christ proclaimed in the Gospel the law to be of God, or can it be supposed that the righteous God made His own Son under a hostile law which He Himself had not given? It is written in the law of Moses as follows, Every male which openeth the womb shall be called holy unto the Lord. (Ex. 13:2, 12.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "They brought him" therefore "that they might present him before the sight of the Lord". Fulfilling the precepts of what Scripture? Surely of this one: "as it is written," he says, "in the law of Moses, that every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord", and: "three times a year every male shall appear in the sight of the Lord God". The males which were holy from the fact that they had opened their mother's womb were offered before the altar of the Lord: "every male," it says, "that opens the womb", sounds something sacred. For whatever male you may say has been poured forth from the womb, he does not open his mother's womb as the Lord Jesus does, because in all women it is not the birth of the infant, but the intercourse of the man, that unlocks the womb. But the womb of the Lord's mother was unlocked at that time at which the birth also was brought forth, because before the birth of Christ no male at all touched that holy womb, to be venerated with all reverence. I dare to say something further: that even in what is written, "The Spirit of God shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you", was the beginning of the seed and of the conception, and that without the unlocking of the womb the new offspring grew in the womb. Whence the Savior himself speaks: "but I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people". He saw in his mother's womb the uncleanness of bodies; walled about on this side and that by her inward parts, he endured the confinements of earthly dregs; whence he likens himself to a worm and says: "I am a worm and not a man". For man is wont to be born of male and female, but I was born not of male and female, according to the rite and nature of men, but after the pattern of the "worm", whose seed is not from elsewhere, but whose origin is in the very bodies, and from the very bodies, in which it grows together.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whence it also seems marvelous that Mary's offering did not have the first victim, that is, "a yearling lamb," but the second, as one whose "hand did not suffice" for the first. For thus it is written concerning her: there came, it says, her parents, "that they might offer" for him "a victim, according to that which is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons." But in this too is shown to be true that which is written, that Christ Jesus, "whereas he was rich, became poor." Therefore for this reason he both chose a poor mother, of whom he would be born, and a poor fatherland, of which it is said: "And thou, Bethlehem, art the least among the thousands of Judah," and the rest.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For this reason, because "every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord", he was brought "to Jerusalem", that he might appear before the sight of God, and on account of that which follows: "that a gift might be given for him, according to what is written in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". We see a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons offered for the Savior. I even think those birds blessed, which were offered for the birth of the Lord; and just as I marvel at Balaam's ass and heap up her happiness, because she was worthy not only to see the angel of God, but also, with her mouth unlocked, to break forth into human speech, so much more do I proclaim and exalt these birds, that they were offered for our Lord and Savior before the altar. "That they might offer for him a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". Perhaps I may seem to bring in something novel, but something too little worthy of the majesty of the matter. Just as the generation of the Savior was new, not of man and woman, but of a virgin alone only, so also this "pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons" were not such as we behold with the eyes of the flesh, but such as the Holy Spirit is, who "descended in the form of a dove and came" upon the Savior, when he was baptized in the Jordan. Such too was the "pair of turtledoves": those birds were not, like these, such as flit through the air, but something divine and, for human contemplation, more august, appeared under the form of a dove and a turtledove, so that he who was being born for the whole world and was to suffer might be cleansed before the Lord not with such victims as all men use, but, as his whole dispensation was new, so he might have new victims also, according to the will of Almighty God in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: A reason worthy of God's gift must be sought, as to how "Simeon, a holy man and pleasing to God", as it is written in the Gospel, "awaiting the consolation of Israel, received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not meet death before he saw the Christ of the Lord". What good did it do him to see Christ? Did he have only this in the promise, that he should see him, and gain no benefit from seeing him, or does some gift worthy of God lie hidden here, which the blessed Simeon both deserved and received? "A woman touched the fringe of Jesus' garment and was healed". If she gained so much benefit from the outermost part of the garment, what must we suppose about Simeon, who "received into his own arms" the infant, and holding him in his embrace rejoiced and was glad, seeing carried by himself the little child who had come to release those in bonds and to free his very self from the knots of the body — knowing that no one could send anyone out from the prison of the body with the hope of the life to come except him whom he held in his arms? Hence too he speaks to him: "now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace"; for as long as I was not holding Christ, as long as I was not clasping him with my arms, I was shut in and could not go out from my chains. And this must be understood not only of Simeon, but of the whole human race. If anyone departs from the world, if anyone is released from prison and the house of the bound to go to reign, let him take Jesus in his hands and encircle him with his arms, let him hold him wholly in his bosom, and then, exulting, he will be able to go where he desires. Consider how great a dispensation preceded, that Simeon should deserve to hold the Son of God. First he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit "that he would not see death, unless he had first seen the Christ of the Lord". Then, not by chance and simply did he enter the temple, but "he came to the temple in the Spirit of God"; "for as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God". Therefore the Holy Spirit led him into the temple. You too, if you wish to hold Jesus and to embrace him with your hands and to become worthy to go out of prison, strive with all your effort to have the Spirit as your guide and to come to the temple of God. Behold, now you stand in the temple of the Lord Jesus, that is, in his Church: this is the temple built "of living stones". And you stand in the temple of the Lord when your life and conduct are most worthy of the name of the Church. If you come "in the Spirit to the temple", you will find the little child Jesus, you will lift him up in your arms and will say: "Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace according to your word." And at the same time note that "peace" has been added to the release and dismissal. For he does not say: I wish to be dismissed, but with an addition: to be dismissed "in peace". For this same thing was promised also to the blessed Abraham: "but you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age". Who is it that dies "in peace", except the one who has "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding and guards the heart" of its possessor? Who is it that departs from this world "in peace", except the one who understands that "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself", and has nothing hostile and opposed to God, but has taken up all peace and concord in himself by good works, and so "in peace" is dismissed to go to the holy fathers, to whom Abraham also went forth? Why do I speak of the fathers? One must go also to the very prince and lord of the patriarchs, Jesus, of whom it is said: "it is better to be dissolved and to be with Christ". He has Jesus who dares to say: "I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me". Therefore, that we too, standing in the temple and holding the Son of God and embracing him, may be worthy of release and of departure to better things, let us pray to almighty God, let us pray also to the little child Jesus himself, whom we long to address and to hold in our arms: to whom is glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 15

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If thou wilt touch Jesus and grasp Him in thy hands, strive with all thy strength to have the Spirit for thy guide, and come to the temple of God. For it follows, And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, (i. e. Mary His mother, and Joseph His reputed father,) to do for him after the custom of the law, then took he him up in his arms.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
If we marvel to hear that a woman was healed by touching the hem of a garment, what must we think of Simeon, who received an Infant in his arms, and rejoiced seeing that the little one he carried was He who had come to let loose the captive. Knowing that no one could release him from the chains of the body with the hope of future life, but He whom he held in his arms. Therefore it is said, And he blessed God, saying, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart.

As if he said, "As long as I held not Christ, I was in prison, and could not escape from my bonds."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But who departs from this world in peace, but he who is persuaded that God was Christ reconciling the world to Himself, (2 Cor. 5.) who has nothing hostile to God, having derived to himself all peace by good works in himself?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In my view, and according to the word of God, the soul, released from labors, released from sweats, has been deprived of the flesh and can say: "Now Thou lettest Thy servant depart, O Master, according to Thy word, in peace." It goes forth in peace and reposes with Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Both by the angel and the multitude of the heavenly host, by the shepherds also, and Simeon.

But they who look deeper into the matter may say, that since the genealogy is deduced from David to Joseph, therefore lest Joseph should seem to be mentioned for no purpose, as not being the father of the Saviour, he was called His father, that the genealogy might maintain its place.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And", he says, "his father and mother were marveling over these things, which were said of him". Let us gather together into one the things that were said and written about Jesus at his birth, and then we shall be able to know that each single one is worthy of wonder. For which reason both the father was marveling — for so Joseph too was called, because he was a foster-father — the mother also was marveling over all the things "which were said of him". What then are the things that rumor had spread abroad concerning the little child Jesus? "There were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and observing the night-watches over their flock." At the very hour of Jesus' birth an angel came and said to them: "I announce to you great joy: go, and you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling-cloths and laid in a manger". The angel had not yet finished his words, and behold, "a multitude of the heavenly host" began to praise and bless God. When the shepherds, trembling, had beheld this, and "the angel had departed from them, they said to one another: Let us go to Bethlehem and see this deed which the Lord has shown us". They came and found the little child. Both they and the parents marveled over these things which had been done. And of Simeon it is written that he increased the report and was even a great part of the miracle. For he held the child in his arms and said: "Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation". The summit and, so to speak, the crown of the things that were noised abroad concerning Jesus, at which both his father and mother marveled, was the word of Simeon. For it did not suffice him to hold the little child and to speak out the things that were written concerning himself, but he "blessed" his father and his mother, and prophesied about the infant himself also, saying: "Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. A sword shall pierce through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Luke, who wrote: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also that which will be born holy will be called the Son of God", and who plainly handed down to us that Jesus was the son of a virgin and was not conceived of human seed, this same Luke bore witness that Joseph was his father, saying: "And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were said of him". What reason, then, was there that he should record as father one who was not the father? He who is content with a simple exposition will say: the Holy Spirit honored him with the title of father, because he had nourished the Savior. But he who inquires into something more profound can say: since the order of generation is traced from David down to Joseph, lest Joseph seem to be named in vain — he who had not been the father of the Savior — in order that the order of generation might have its place, he was called the "father" of the Lord. "His father", then, "and mother were marveling at the things that were said of him" both by the angel and by the "multitude of the heavenly host", and also by the shepherds. For hearing all these things they marveled most vehemently.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
They who explain this simply, may say that He came for the fall of unbelievers, and the rising again of believers.

The careful interpreter will say, that no one falls who was not before standing. Tell me then, who were they who stood, for whose fall Christ came?

There is also a deeper meaning aimed against those who raise their voices against their Creator, saying, Behold the God of the Law and the Prophets of what sort He is! He says, I kill, and I make alive. (Deut. 32:39.) If God then is a bloody judge and a cruel master, it is most plain that Jesus is His Son, since the same things here are written of Him, namely, that he comes for the fall and rising again of many.

But we must take care lest by chance the Saviour should not come to some equally for the fall and rising again; for when I stood in sin, it was first good for me to fall, and die to sin. Lastly, Prophets and Saints when they were designing some great thing, used to fall on their faces, that by their fall their sins should be the more fully blotted out. This it is that the Saviour first grants to thee. Thou wert a sinner, let that which is sin fall in thee, that thou mayest thence rise again, and say, If we be dead with Him, we shall also live with Him. (2 Tim. 2:11.)

But all the things which history relates of Christ are spoken against, not that those who believe on Him speak against Him, (for we know that all the things which are written of Him are true,) but that every thing which has been written of Him is with the unbelievers a sign which is spoken against.

Everything that the plain narrative recounts about the Savior is spoken against. The Virgin is a mother. This is "a sign that is spoken against." "The Marcionites speak against this sign and insist that he was not born of a woman." The Ebionites speak against this sign and say that he was born of a man and a woman in the same way as we are born. He had a human body.There is still another "sign that is spoken against." Some say that he came down from heaven. Others say that he had a body like ours, so that he could also redeem our bodies from sin by the likeness of his body to ours and give us hope of the resurrection. He rose from the dead. This is also "a sign that is spoken against." How did he rise? Was he just as he was when he died, or did he surely rise into a body of a better substance?…
I myself think that even the fact that the mouths of the prophets foretold him is a sign that is spoken against.… It does not mean that those who believe in him speak against these signs. We know indeed that everything that Scripture records is true. But, for unbelievers, all things that are written about him are "a sign that is spoken against."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then the Scripture says: "Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted. And a sword shall pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed". In what way the Savior came "for the ruin and for the resurrection of many" is to be contemplated. He who expounds simply can say that he came "for the ruin" of unbelievers and "for the resurrection" of believers. But he who is a careful interpreter says that by no means does one fall who has not first stood. Give me, then, who that one was who stood, and for whose "ruin" the Savior came, and also him who rises up. For surely he rises up who had before fallen. And so we must see whether perhaps the Savior did not come "for the ruin" of some and "for the resurrection" of others, but came for the same persons both "for ruin and for resurrection". "For judgment", he says, "I have come, that those who did not see may see, and those who saw may become blind". For there is in us one thing that saw before and afterward ceased to see, and another thing that did not see and afterward began to see. For example, I wish to see with those eyes with which I did not see before and which were afterward opened to me, since after the disobedience of both Adam and Eve "their eyes were opened", concerning which we treated in the previous discourse. But now we must interpret what this means which he says: "Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel". It is fitting that I first fall, and, when I have fallen, that I afterward rise up well, lest the Savior be to me the cause of an evil ruin. But for this reason he made me fall, that I might rise up, and the ruin has been far more useful to me than that time in which I seemed to stand. For I was standing in sin at that time in which I was living in sin; and because I was standing in sin, the first benefit to me was that I should fall and die to sin. Finally, the holy prophets too, when they contemplated something more august, fell upon their faces; and they fell for this reason, that through this fall their sins might be more fully purged. This very thing the Savior first grants to you as well, that you may fall. You were a heathen — let the heathen fall in you; you loved harlots — let the fornicator first perish in you; you were a sinner — let the sinner fall in you, that you may thereafter rise again and say: "if we have died with him, we shall also live with him", and: "if we have been made conformable to his death, we shall be conformable also to his resurrection". This one, therefore, "is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel", that is, among those who are able to behold with full keenness and reason, and "for a sign that shall be contradicted". Everything that the account relates concerning the Savior is contradicted. The mother is a virgin — it is a sign that is contradicted: the Marcionites contradict this sign and say that he was not at all born of a woman; the Ebionites contradict the sign, saying that he was born of man and woman just as we too are born. He had a human body, and this is a sign that is contradicted: for some say that he came from the heavens, others that he had a body such as ours, so that through the likeness of the body he might also redeem our bodies from sins and give us the hope of resurrection. He rose from the dead, and this is a sign that is contradicted: in what way he rose, whether he himself and such as he had died, or rather rose in a body of better substance; and there is endless dispute, some saying: he showed to Thomas the mark of the nails in his hands, others arguing from the opposite side: if he had the same body, how did he "enter through closed doors and stand"? You see, therefore, how by various arguments even the question of his resurrection is stirred up, and how it is "a sign that is contradicted". I think that this too, which was foretold by the mouth of the prophets, is a sign that is contradicted; for there are many heretics who assert that he was not at all foretold by the prophets. And what need is there for me to pursue many things? Everything that the account relates concerning him is a sign that is contradicted — not that those who believe in him contradict it (for we indeed know that all things which are written are true), but because among unbelievers everything that is written concerning him is a sign that is contradicted.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What does this mean which he says: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel"? To this I have found something similar written in the Gospel according to John: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind". Therefore, just as he came for judgment, that "those who do not see" of the nations "might see", and those who saw before, of Israel, "might be made blind", so he came "for the fall and rising of many". For at the coming of the Lord the Savior, those who had stood before fell down, and those who had fallen rose up. This is one interpretation of that which was said: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel". But there is also something deeper to be understood against those especially who bark against the Creator, and, gathering together from here and there out of the Old Testament testimonies which they do not understand, "deceive the hearts of the simple". For they say: behold, the God of the Law and the Prophets, see what sort he is. "I", he says, "will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal, and there is none who can deliver out of my hands". They hear: "I will kill", and they do not hear: "I will make alive"; they hear: "I will strike", and they disdain to hear: "and I will heal". On occasions of this kind they slander the Creator. Therefore, before I interpret what sense there is in: "I will kill and make alive, I will strike and heal", I will set against them a testimony of the Gospel and will say against the heretics — for there are countless heresies which receive the Gospel according to Luke —: If the Creator is bloodthirsty and only a judge and cruel because he says: "I will kill and make alive, I will strike and heal", it is most manifest that Jesus too is his son; for the same things are written of him: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel", not "for the rising" only, but also "for the fall". If it is evil to kill, let it be evil also to come "for the fall". What will they answer? Will they either withdraw from his worship, or will they seek some interpretation and flee to figurative readings, so that his coming "for the fall" may sound of kindness rather than of severity? And how will it be just, when something of this sort is found in the Gospel, to flee to allegories and new understandings, but when it is found in the Old Testament, at once to accuse and to accept no explanation, however probable it may be? But even this which follows: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind", however much they seek to expound it, they will not be able to fulfill. But I, who desire to be of the Church and to be named and to bear a name not from any heresiarch, but from the appellation of Christ, and to have a name that is blessed upon the earth, and long to be and to be called a Christian both in work and in thought, seek an equal principle both in the old and in the new law. God speaks: "I will kill"; I am glad that God kills. For when the old man is in me and I still live as a man, I long that God may kill in me the old man and make me alive from the dead. For, he says, "the first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly". According to this sense that also is understood: "for judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may be made blind". We all have in ourselves both sight and blindness. Adam both saw and did not see. Eve too, before her eyes were opened, is described as having seen: "the woman saw", it says, "the tree, that it was good for eating and most delightful to the eyes for seeing: and taking of the fruit of the tree she ate, and gave to her husband, and they ate". Therefore they were not blind, but saw. Then it follows: "and their eyes were opened". Therefore they had been blind and did not see, whose eyes were afterward opened; but those who had seen well before, after they transgressed the commandment of the Lord, began to see badly, and afterward, as the offense crept in, they lost the sight of obedience. Thus I understand also that which God says: "Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" There is an eye of the body, with which we behold these earthly things, an eye according to the sense of the flesh, of which the Scripture says: "walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of the flesh". To this we have another, contrary and better, that savors of divine things; and because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might be made blind. According to this sense, then, is that also to be understood which we now have in hand: "behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel". I have something in me that stands badly and raises itself up in the pride of sin: let this fall, let this be pulled down; and if it falls, that which had before fallen down will, rising, stand. My "inner man" once lay struck down, and the outer stood erect. Before I believed in Jesus, the good in me lay down, the evil stood.
