After he came, then what was evil in me fell down, and that was fulfilled: "always carrying about the dying of Jesus in the body", and that: "put to death your members upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, luxury, idolatry, sorceries", and the rest. The fall of all these has been made useful. And of this fall it is said: "Wherever the corpse shall be, there the eagles will be gathered". For a corpse (cadaver) has received its name from falling (a casu). Good is this fall, to which Jesus first comes, and he cannot bring about the rising unless the fall has gone before. Let him come first to destroy what was evil in me, so that, when that is destroyed and put to death, there may rise up in me and be made alive that which is good, so that in it may follow the kingdom of heaven: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the evil thoughts of men were revealed, that He Who died for us might slay them; for while they were hidden, it was impossible to utterly destroy them. Hence also when we have sinned we ought to say, Mine iniquity have I not hid. (Ps. 32:5.) For if we make known our sins not only to God, but to whoever can heal our wounds, our sins will be blotted out.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then Simeon says: "and a sword shall pierce through your own soul". What is this sword, which pierced not only through the hearts of others, but even through the heart of Mary? It is plainly written that in the time of the passion all the apostles were scandalized, the Lord himself also saying: "you shall all be scandalized in me this night". Therefore they were all scandalized to such a degree that even Peter, the chief of the apostles, denied him three times. What are we to think — that, while the apostles were scandalized, the mother of the Lord was immune from scandal? If she suffered no scandal at the passion of the Lord, then Jesus did not die for her sins. But if "all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified by his grace and redeemed", then surely Mary too was scandalized at that time. And this is what Simeon now prophesies, saying: "and your own soul" — you who know that you gave birth as a virgin without a man, you who heard from Gabriel: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" — "the sword" of unbelief "shall pierce through", and you will be struck by the blade of doubt, and your thoughts will tear you in different directions, when you see him, whom you had heard to be the Son of God and knew to have been begotten without the seed of a man, crucified and dying and subjected to human torments and at the last tearfully complaining and saying: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me". "And" therefore "a sword shall pierce through your soul, that the thoughts out of many hearts may be revealed". There were evil thoughts in men, which were for this reason revealed, that, being brought out into the open, they might be destroyed and slain, and cease to be, being dead, and that he who died for us might slay them. For as long as the thoughts were hidden and not brought out into the open, it was impossible for them to be utterly slain. Hence we too, if we have sinned, ought to say: "I have made my sin known to you, and my iniquity I have not hidden. I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord". For if we do this and reveal our sins not only to God but also to those who are able to heal our wounds and sins, our sins will be blotted out by him who says: "behold, I will blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For the Holy Spirit dwelt not by chance in her. For the highest blessing, if any can possess it, is the grace of virginity, but if this cannot be, and it chance to a woman to lose her husband, let her remain a widow, which indeed not only after the death of her husband, but even while he is living, she ought to have in her mind, that supposing it should not happen, her will and determination might be crowned by the Lord, and her words should be, "This I vow, and promise, that if a certain condition of this life be mine, (which yet I wish not,) I will do nothing else but remain inviolate and a widow." Most justly then was this holy woman thought worthy to receive the gift of prophecy, because by long chastity and long fastings she had ascended to this height of virtue, as it follows, Who departed not from the temple with fastings and prayers, &c.

From which it is plain that she possessed a multitude of other virtues; and mark how she resembles Simeon in his goodness, for they were both in the temple together, and both counted worthy of prophetic grace, as it follows, And she coming in at this very instant, gave thanks to the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After the prophecy of Simeon, because it was necessary that women too should be saved, there came a prophetess, a woman, of whom it is written: "and there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser". How beautiful the order! The woman does not come before the man, but first comes Simeon, who took up the infant and held him in his arms, then the woman, whose words indeed are not set down, but it is said generally that "she confessed to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem". And rightly did the holy woman deserve to receive the spirit of prophecy, because by long chastity and long fastings she had ascended to this height. See, women, the testimony of Anna, and imitate it! If it should ever happen to you that you lose your husbands, consider what is written of her: "she lived seven years from her virginity with a husband" and the rest; for this reason she was a "prophetess"; for the Holy Spirit did not dwell in her at random and by chance. It is good and best, if any woman is able to possess the grace of virginity; but if she has not been able to do this, and it has befallen her to lose her husband, let her remain a widow. And this she ought to have in mind not only after the death of her husband, but even while he lives, so that, even if her own will and resolve do not come to pass, she may be crowned by the Lord and may say: this I vow and promise, that if anything human, which I do not wish for, should befall me, I will do nothing else than remain undefiled and a widow. But now second and third and fourth marriages — to say nothing of more — are found in the Church, and we are not unaware that such a union will cast us out of the kingdom of God. For just as not only fornication but also second marriages exclude a man from ecclesiastical dignities — for neither a bishop nor a presbyter nor a deacon nor a widow can be twice-married — so perhaps the twice-married man will also be cast out from the assembly of the "firstborn and undefiled", the "Church, which has no spot or wrinkle"; not that he is sent into the eternal fire, but that he has no part in the kingdom of God. I recall that, when I was interpreting that which is written to the Corinthians: "to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all who call upon him", I said that there is a distinction between the "church" and those "who call upon" the name of the Lord. For I think that the man of one marriage and the virgin and he who perseveres in chastity belong to the church of God, but that he who is twice-married, although he may have had a good manner of life and abound in the other virtues, nevertheless does not belong to the "church" and to that number which "has no wrinkle or spot, or any such thing", but belongs to a second rank and to those "who call upon" the name of the Lord, and who are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ, yet are by no means crowned by him: to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 17

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But because Anna's words were nothing remarkable, and of no great note respecting Christ, the Gospel does not give the particulars of what she said, and perhaps for this reason one may suppose that Simeon anticipated her, since he indeed bore the character of the law, (for his name signifies obedience,) but she the character of grace, (which her name is by interpretation,) and Christ came between them. Therefore He let Simeon depart dying with the law, but Anna he sustains living beyond through grace.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: My Lord Jesus was born, and his parents went up to Jerusalem to fulfill the things that had been commanded in the law, and to offer for him "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". Simeon held him in his arms, as was read a little while ago, and prophesied concerning him the things that the account relates. And after everything was completed according to custom, the parents returned. In what year was Jesus at that time? He was assuredly still a little child, and yet he "grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom" and grace; he had not yet completed the forty days of purification, he had not yet come to Nazareth, and already he was receiving all wisdom. Scripture could have said: "he grew and became strong, and received the Spirit"; but because "he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant", as soon as the sacrifice was offered for his purification, that which he had emptied out he filled up again — not that his body was thereupon made greater, but that something more sacred might be shown, as Scripture reports: "but the child grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom". Let us inquire whether anywhere else it is written of a little child: "he grew and became strong", so that by comparing many passages we may be able to understand what more is said in the case of our Lord. We read concerning John: "but the child grew and became strong", and yet there is not added: "and was filled with wisdom", but rather: "he became strong in spirit". But here, concerning the Lord, it says: "he grew and became strong and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him". All these things were said of a child who had not yet completed twelve years.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since some who seem to believe the holy Scriptures deny the divinity of the Savior, as though for the glory of the almighty God, it seems just to me that they should be taught from the authority of those very Scriptures that something divine came into a human body, and not only into a human body, but also into a human soul. Yet, if we attend carefully to the meaning of the Scriptures, that soul had something more than the rest of human souls. For every human soul, before it comes to virtue, is defiled by vices. But the soul of Jesus was never stained with the filth of sin. Indeed, before he reached the twelfth year of his age, the Holy Spirit writes concerning him in the Gospel of Luke: "But the boy grew and was strengthened and was filled with wisdom". This human nature does not admit, that one should be filled with wisdom before twelve years. It is one thing to have a part of wisdom, another to be filled with wisdom. Let us not doubt, therefore, that something divine appeared in the flesh of Jesus, and something beyond not only man, but beyond every rational creature as well. And "he grew", it says. For "he had humbled himself, taking the form of a servant", and by the same power by which "he had humbled himself", he grows. He had appeared weak, because he had taken up a weak body, and for that reason he is again strengthened. The Son of God "had emptied himself", and therefore he is again filled with wisdom. "And the grace of God was upon him". Not when he came to adolescence, not when he was teaching openly, but while he was still a little child, he had the grace of God; and just as all things in him had been marvelous, so also his childhood was marvelous, that the wisdom of God might be fulfilled.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But we must not wonder that they are called His parents, seeing the one from her childbirth, the other from his knowledge of it, deserved the names of father and mother.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And so his parents went according to custom to Jerusalem to the solemn day of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old". Observe carefully, that before he was twelve years old, he was being filled with the wisdom of God and with the other things that are written of him.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But as when the Jews plotted against Him He escaped from the midst of them, and was not seen; so now it seems that the Child Jesus remained, and His parents knew not where He was. As it follows, And not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking for him. (John 10:29.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when he was twelve years old, he remained behind in Jerusalem. His parents, not knowing this, seek him anxiously and do not find him.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When therefore, as we have said, he was twelve years old, and the days of the solemnity had been completed according to custom, and his parents were returning, "the boy remained in Jerusalem and his parents did not know it". And here understand something more sublime than human nature undergoes. For he did not simply "remain" while his parents were ignorant of where he was; but just as it is written in the Gospel of John, when the Jews were lying in wait for him and he slipped away out of their midst and did not appear, so also now I think that the boy remained in Jerusalem and that his parents were ignorant of where he had remained. Nor let us wonder that they are called parents, of whom the one merited the name because of the childbirth, the other because of his service to the mother and the father.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And when they sought him, they did not find him "among their kinsfolk". For human kinship could not contain the Son of God. They did not find him "among their acquaintances", because the divine power was greater than mortal acquaintance and knowledge.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He is not found as soon as sought for, for Jesus was not among His kinsfolk and relations, among those who are joined to Him in the flesh, nor in the company of the multitude can He be found. Learn where those who seek Him find Him, not every where, but in the temple. And do thou then seek Jesus in the temple of God. Seek Him in the Church, and seek Him among the masters who are in the temple. For if thou wilt so seek Him, thou shalt find Him. They found Him not among His kinsfolk, for human relations could not comprehend the Son of God; not among His acquaintance, for He passes far beyond all human knowledge and understanding. Where then do they find Him? In the temple! If at any time thou seek the Son of God, seek Him first in the temple, thither go up, and verily shalt thou find Christ, the Word, and the Wisdom, (i. e. the Son of God.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: They seek "among their kinsfolk", they seek "in the company", they seek "among their acquaintances", and in all these they do not find him. Jesus, then, is sought by his parents, by the father who had been his nurse and companion when he went down to Egypt, and yet he is not found immediately when he is sought. For Jesus is not found among relatives and kinsmen of the flesh, not among those who are joined to him bodily. In the company of many my Jesus cannot be found.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Learn where those seeking him find him, so that you too, seeking with Joseph and Mary, may find him. And seeking him, it says, "they found him in the temple". Not anywhere in some other place, but "in the temple", and not simply "in the temple", but "in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them". You too, therefore, seek Jesus "in the temple" of God, seek him in the Church, seek him among the masters who are "in the temple" and do not go out from it; for if you seek in this way, you will find him. Moreover, if anyone says that he is a master and does not have Jesus, that man is a master in name only, and therefore Jesus, the word of God and wisdom, cannot be found with him. He was found, it says, "in the midst of the teachers". Just as it is written in another place concerning the prophets, so also now understand "in the midst of the teachers". "If", it says, "anything is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first keep silence". They find him "sitting in the midst of the teachers", and not only "sitting", but also "questioning and hearing them". And now too Jesus is present; he questions us and hears us speaking.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Where, then, do they find him? "In the temple"; for there the Son of God is found. If ever you too shall seek the Son of God, seek first the temple, hasten thither, there you will find Christ, the Word and the wisdom, that is, the Son of God. But because he was a little one, he is found "in the midst of the teachers", sanctifying and instructing them. Because he was a little one, he is found "in the midst" not teaching them, but "questioning", and this in accordance with the duty of his age, that he might teach us what befits children, however wise and learned they be, namely that they should rather hear their masters than desire to teach, and should not vaunt themselves with vain display. He was questioning, I say, the masters, not that he might learn something, but that in questioning he might instruct. For from one fountain of teaching flows both to question and to answer wisely; and it belongs to the same knowledge to know what you should ask and what you should answer. It was fitting that the Savior should first become a master of learned questioning, that afterward he might respond to questions according to the reason and word of God: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Because moreover He was the Son of God, He is found in the midst of the doctors, enlightening and instructing them. But because He was a little child, He is found among them not teaching but asking questions, as it is said, Sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions. And this He did as a duty of reverence, that He might set us an example of the proper behaviour of children, though they be wise and learned, rather to hear their masters than teach them, and not to vaunt themselves with empty boasting. But He asked not that He might learn, but that asking He might instruct. For from the same source of learning is derived both the power of asking and answering wisely, as it follows, All who heard him were astonished at his wisdom.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And all", it says, "were amazed". At what were they "amazed"? Not at his questions, although these too were marvelous, but "at his answers". For it is one thing to ask, another to answer. He was questioning the teachers, and because at times they could not answer, he himself answered them concerning the things about which he had asked. But that an answer signifies not the alternation of conversing but teaching in the holy scriptures, let the divine law teach you. "Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice". That answer was concerning the matters about which the Lord was instructing the ignorant Moses. Sometimes Jesus asks, sometimes he answers, and as we said above, although his questioning is marvelous, nevertheless his answering is far more marvelous.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The holy Virgin knew that He was not the Son of Joseph, and yet calls her husband His father according to the belief of the Jews, who thought that He was conceived in the common way. Now to speak generally we may say, that the Holy Spirit honoured Joseph by the name of father, because he brought up the Child Jesus; but more technically, that it might not seem superfluous in St. Luke, bringing down the genealogy from David to Joseph. But why sought they Him sorrowing? Was it that he might have perished or been lost? It could not be. For what should cause them to dread the loss of Him whom they knew to be the Lord? But as whenever you read the Scriptures you search out their meaning with pains, not that you suppose them to have erred or to contain anything incorrect, but that the truth which they have inherent in them you are anxious to find out; so they sought Jesus, lest perchance leaving them he should have returned to heaven, thither to descend when He would. He then who seeks Jesus must go about it not carelessly and idly, as many seek Him who never find Him, but with labour and sorrow.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore, that we too may hear him and that he may set before us questions which he himself may resolve, let us beseech him and seek him with the utmost labor and sorrow, and then we shall be able to find him whom we seek. For it is not written in vain: "I and your father have been seeking you with sorrow". He who seeks Jesus must seek not negligently, not carelessly, not in passing, as some seek and therefore cannot find him. But let us say: "with sorrow we seek you".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There follows: "sorrowing we were seeking you". I do not think that they sorrowed for this reason, because they supposed the boy had strayed or perished; nor could it happen that Mary, who knew that she had conceived of the Holy Spirit, who had heard both the angel speaking and the shepherds hastening and Simeon prophesying, should fear that she might lose the boy through his wandering off. Remove this opinion especially from Joseph, to whom it had been commanded by the angel that he should take the boy and go to Egypt, who had heard: "do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit". It could never come to pass that he should dread as lost the infant whom he had known to be divine. The sorrow and the seeking of the parents sounds like something other than the simple reader understands. Just as you, if ever you read the Scriptures, seek in them the meaning with a certain sorrow and torment—not that you should judge the Scriptures to have erred or to contain something amiss, but because they hold within a word and reason of truth, and you are unable to find what is true: so also they were seeking Jesus, lest perhaps he had withdrawn from them, lest, leaving them, he had migrated to other things and—what I think more likely—lest he had returned to the heavens, intending, when it should please him, to descend again. "Sorrowing", therefore, they were seeking the Son of God.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 19

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And when we have said this, he will answer our laboring soul that seeks him with sorrow, and will say: "Do you not know that I must be in my Father's house?". Where are the heretics, where are the impious and the mad, who assert that the law and the prophets do not belong to the Father of Jesus Christ? Surely Jesus was "in the temple" that was built by Solomon, and he confesses that that temple belongs to his Father, whom he revealed to us, whose Son he said he was. Let them answer, how one God is good and another just. Since, therefore, the Savior is the Son of the Creator, let us together praise the Father and the Son, whose is the law, whose also is the temple: to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Mary and Joseph were seeking Jesus "among their kinsfolk" and did not find him; they were seeking him "in the company" and could not find him. They sought him "in the temple", and not simply "in the temple", but with the teachers, and "in the midst of the instructors" they find him. Wherever the teachers may be, there "in the midst of the teachers" Jesus is found, if only the teacher sits "in the temple" and never departs from it. Jesus profited his own teachers, and those whom he seemed to be questioning he taught, speaking "in their midst", and in a certain way he stirred them up to seek out the things they did not know, and to investigate the things which, up to that point, they were unable to know—whether they knew them or were ignorant of them. Jesus, then, is found "in the midst of the teachers", and once found he says to those who sought him: "Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" First, understanding this simply, let us arm ourselves against the impious heretics who say that the Creator is not the Father of Christ Jesus, nor the God of the Law and the prophets. Behold, the Father of Christ is asserted to be the God of the temple. Let the Valentinians blush when they hear Jesus saying: "I must be in my Father's house". Let all the heretics blush who receive the Gospel according to Luke and yet despise the things that are written in it. Let these things, as I said, be understood in the simpler sense. But since it is added: "they, however, did not understand the saying", let us more diligently sift out the meaning of the Scripture.

Were they so foolish and senseless that they did not know what he was saying—whether this, which he says, "I must be in my Father's house", signified "in the temple", or whether it signifies something else more profound, and something that edifies the hearers more? Each one of us, if he is good and perfect, is a possession of God the Father. Generally, therefore, concerning all, the Savior taught that he ought not to be anywhere except among those who are the Father's. If any one of you belongs to God the Father, he has Jesus in his midst. Let us indeed believe the one who says: "I must be in my Father's house". And I suspect that this is the more rational and living and true temple of God, rather than that one which was built typologically by an earthly work. Hence, as he was in that temple typologically, so also typologically he withdrew from it. For he "went out of the temple" that was earthly, saying: "Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate", and leaving that house he came to the possession of God the Father—the churches scattered throughout the whole world—and says: "I must be in my Father's house". Then, therefore, "they did not understand the word which he spoke to them".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or they knew not whether when He said about my Father's business, He referred to the temple, or something higher and more edifying; for every one of us who doeth good, is the seat of God the Father; but whoso is the seat of God the Father, has Christ in the midst of him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Or they knew not whether when He said about my Father's business, He referred to the temple, or something higher and more edifying; for every one of us who doeth good, is the seat of God the Father; but whoso is the seat of God the Father, has Christ in the midst of him.

Jesus frequently went down with His disciples, for He is not always dwelling on the mount, for they who were troubled with various diseases were not able to ascend the mount. For this reason now also He went down to them who were below. It follows: And he was subject to them, &c.

Let us then also ourselves be subject to our parents. But if our fathers are not, let us be subject to those who are our fathers. Jesus the Son of God is subject to Joseph and Mary. But I must be subject to the Bishop who has been constituted my father. It seems that Joseph knew that Jesus was greater than he, and therefore in awe moderated his authority. But let every one see, that oftentimes he who is subject is the greater. Which if they who are higher in dignity understand, they will not be clated with pride, knowing that their superior is subject to them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And at the same time attend to this: that, as long as he was in the possession of his Father, he was above. And because Joseph and Mary did not yet have full faith, for that reason they could not remain above with him, but he is said to have come down with them. Frequently Jesus comes down with his disciples, nor is he always dwelling on the mountain, nor without end does he hold to sublime things. On the mountain he is with Peter, with James, with John, and again in another place with the rest of the disciples. Further, because those who labored under various sicknesses were not able to ascend the mountain, therefore he "came down and came" to those who were below. Now also it is written: "he came down with them and came to Nazareth and was subject to them". Let us learn, children, to be subject to our parents: the greater is subject to the lesser. He, because he saw that Joseph was greater in age, therefore honored him with the honor due to a parent, giving to all sons an example, that they should be subject to their fathers and, if they have no fathers, that they should be subject to those who are of a father's age. Why do I speak of parents and children? If Jesus the Son of God is subject to Joseph and Mary, shall I not be subject to the bishop, who has been appointed by God as a father to me? Shall I not be subject to the presbyter, who by the Lord's condescension has been set over me? I think that Joseph understood that Jesus, who was subject to him, was greater than he; and knowing that the greater one was subject, he tempered his authority with awe. Let each one, then, see that often an inferior is set over better people, and it sometimes happens that the one who is subject is better than the one who seems to be set over him. When one who is higher in dignity understands this, he will not be lifted up with pride because he is greater, but he will know that a better one is subject to him, just as Jesus too was subject to Joseph. Then it follows: "But Mary kept all these words in her heart". She surmised something more than about a man; hence also she "kept all his words in her heart", not as the words of a boy who was twelve years old, but of him who had been conceived of the Holy Spirit, whom she saw "advancing in wisdom and grace with God and men".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Jesus "advanced in wisdom" and appeared wiser through each successive age. Was he not wise, that he should become wiser? Or was it that, since he had "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant", he was taking up again what he had laid down, and being filled again with the virtues which, a little before, upon assuming a body, he had seemed to relinquish? He "advanced", therefore, not only "in wisdom", but also "in age". There is also an advancement of age. Two ages are spoken of in the Scriptures: one of the body, which is not in our power but in the law of nature; the other of the soul, which properly lies within us, and according to which, if we will, we daily grow and come to its summit, "so that we may be no longer little children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine", but, ceasing to be "little children", may begin to be "men" and may say: "when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belonged to a little child". Of this age, as I said, the advancement, which is the increase of the soul, is in our power. But if this testimony is not enough, let us take yet another example from Paul: "until we all attain", he says, "to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of the body of Christ". It is in us, therefore, that we should "attain to the measure of the age of the body of Christ"; and, if it is in us, let us strive with all effort to lay aside the little child and to destroy him and to come to the remaining ages, so that we too may be able to hear: "but you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age"—a spiritual old age, surely, which is truly a good old age, growing gray and coming through to the very end in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 20

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Sin makes a man small and slight, virtue renders him eminent and great. For just as sickness of the body makes a man's body meager and slight, but health makes it flourishing and strong, so understand that sickness of sin makes the soul too lowly and small, but the health of the inner man and the works of virtue make it great and eminent, and the more it grows in virtues, the more it renders the greatness of itself extensive. Thus do I understand that which is written of Jesus: that "he advanced in wisdom and in stature and in grace with God and men". For who among men is there who does not "advance in stature" in boyhood, that this should be written of Jesus as though it were something remarkable? To you I say this, who hear in a bodily way that Jesus "advanced in stature". Understand therefore that "he advanced in the stature" of the soul, and his soul became great because of the great and enormous works which he did. Indeed the Apostle too, knowing that this stature is to be understood of the inner man, writes thus: "until we all meet in the perfect man, in the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ". For to grow according to the body and to become great is not in our power. For the body takes the material of its quantity from its generative origin, so as to become either great or slight; but the soul has in us the causes and the freedom of choice, so as to be either great or small.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the word of prophecy, spoken to the Jews alone, the Jewish kingdom only is mentioned, as, The vision of Esaias, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. (Is. 1:1.) But in the Gospel which was to be proclaimed to the whole world, the empire of Tiberius Cæsar is mentioned, who seemed the lord of the whole world. But if the Gentiles only were to be saved, it were sufficient to make mention only of Tiberius, but because the Jews also must believe, the Jewish kingdom therefore, or Tetrarchies, are also introduced, as it follows, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judæa, and Herod tetrarch, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When the prophetic word was sent to the Jews alone, Jewish kings were set at the heading. For example: "The vision which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw against Judea and against Jerusalem, in the reign of Uzziah and Jotham and Ahaz and Hezekiah"; nor do I see anyone else, apart from the kings of Judea, designated in Isaiah's time. In certain of the prophets we read also the kings of Israel, as in that place: "and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel". But when the mystery of the Gospel was to be proclaimed and the Gospel was to be spread throughout the whole world, whose herald John was in the wilderness, and the empire of Tiberius ruled the world, then "in the fifteenth year" of him "the word of the Lord" is described as having "come to John". And if salvation had had to be announced only to those who were about to believe from among the nations, and Israel had had to be wholly excluded, it would have sufficed to say: "In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea". But because from Judea also and from Galilee many were about to believe, therefore these kingdoms too are set at the heading, and it is said: "Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 21

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Of old "the word of God came to Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, who was of the priests" in the time of this or that king of Judah; now "the word of God comes to John, the son of Zechariah", which never came to the prophets "in the desert". But because "the children" of the desolate one "were to be more" than of "her who has a husband", therefore "the word of God came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert". And at the same time consider that it has more reason in it, if the desert is understood mystically and not according to the simple letter. For he who preaches "in the desert" acts to no purpose in crying out there where no one hears him speaking. The forerunner of Christ, therefore, and "the voice of one crying in the desert", preaches "in the desert" of the soul that does not have peace. And not only then, but also in the present, first "the burning and shining lamp" comes and "preaches the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins"; then "the true light" follows after, when "the lamp" itself says: "he must increase, but I must decrease". The word of God comes "in the desert".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 21

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Jordan is the same as descending, for there descends from God a river of healing water. But what parts would John be traversing but the country lying about Jordan, that the penitent sinner might soon arrive at the flowing stream, humbling himself to receive the baptism of repentance. For it is added, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And "he came into all the country round about the Jordan". For what other places ought the Baptist to have gone around, except those neighboring the Jordan, so that whoever wished to do penance might be at hand for the washing of water? Moreover, "Jordan" is interpreted "descending". And the river "descending" and running with a great rush is God our Savior, the Lord, into whom we are baptized with true water, with saving water. Baptism is preached also "for the remission of sins": Come, catechumens, do penance, that you may obtain baptism "for the remission" of sins. He receives baptism "for the remission of sins" who ceases to sin. For if anyone comes to the washing while sinning, no remission of sins is made for him. Therefore I beseech you, do not come to baptism without caution and careful circumspection, but first show "fruits worthy of repentance"! Spend some time in good conduct, keep yourselves clean from all filth and vices, and then remission of sins will be made for you, when you yourselves also have begun to despise your own sins. Forgive your offenses, and they will be forgiven you.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 21

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, a way must be prepared in our heart for the Lord, for the heart of man is large and spacious if it has become clean. For imagine not that in the size of the body, but in the virtue of the understanding, consists that greatness which must receive the knowledge of the truth. Prepare then in thy heart by good conversation a way for the Lord, and by perfect works pursue the path of life, that so the word of God may have free course in thee.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But this very thing, which is now set down from the old instrument, we read written in the prophet Isaiah. For there it is said: "The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight". The Lord wishes to find ways in you—he who, that he may be able to enter into your souls and make his journey, prepare for him the path of which it is said: "make his paths straight". "The voice of one crying in the desert". "The voice" cries: "prepare the way"; for first "the voice" reaches the ears, then after the voice—rather, together with the voice—the word penetrates the hearing. According to this sense Christ was announced by John. Let us see, therefore, what "the voice" announces concerning the word. "Prepare", it says, "the way for the Lord". What "way for the Lord" are we to prepare? Surely not a bodily one? Or can the word of God travel by such a road? Or is the way to be prepared for the Lord within, and straight and even paths to be laid out in our heart? This is the way by which the word of God enters, which consists in the capacity of the human heart. Great is the heart of man, and spacious and capacious, if only it be clean. Do you wish to know its greatness and breadth? See how great a magnitude of divine perceptions it can contain. It itself says: "he gave me true knowledge of the things that are: to know the constitution of the world and the operations of the elements, the beginning and the end and the middle of the ages, the changes of the seasons and the transitions of the months, the circuits of the years and the positions of the stars, the natures of living creatures and the ragings of beasts, the violences of spirits and the thoughts of men, the diversities of trees and the power of roots". You see that the heart of man is not small, which can contain so much. And understand its greatness not in the quantity of the body, but in the strength of perception, which can contain so great a knowledge of the truth. But that I may also lead the simpler folk by everyday examples to believe that the heart of man is great, let us look at what follows. Whatever cities we have passed through, we have them in our mind, and the qualities and situations of the streets and the walls and the buildings are turning over in our heart. The road that we have entered upon we retain in the picture and description of memory; the sea that we have sailed we embrace in silent thought. It is no small thing, as I have said, the heart of man, which can contain so much. But if it is no small thing, containing so much, consequently in it the way of the Lord is prepared and a straight path is made, so that the word of God and wisdom may walk in it. Prepare the way for the Lord through good conduct, and by outstanding works wear smooth the path, so that the word of God may walk in you without any stumbling and may grant you the knowledge of his mysteries and of his coming: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 21

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For when Jesus had come and sent His Spirit, every valley was filled with good works, and the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which if thou hast, thou wilt not only cease to become a valley, but will begin also to be a mountain of God.

Or you may understand the mountains and hills to be the hostile powers, which have been overthrown by the coming of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see what things are foretold at the coming of Christ, among which first it is written concerning John: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord, make straight his paths". And what follows pertains properly to the Lord the Savior. For "every valley" was not "filled" by John, but by the Lord the Savior. Let each one consider himself, what he was before he believed, and then he will observe that he was a lowly valley, a headlong valley plunged into the depths. But when the Lord Jesus came and sent the Holy Spirit as his vicar, "every valley" was "filled". And it was "filled" with good works and with the fruits of the Holy Spirit. Love does not permit a valley to remain in you, for, if you have peace and patience and goodness, not only will you cease to be a "valley", but you will even begin to be a "mountain" of God. We see this happening and being fulfilled daily among the Gentiles: "every valley shall be filled", as also concerning the people of Israel, who has been brought down from on high: "every mountain and hill shall be brought low". That people was once a "mountain" and a "hill", which has been brought down and destroyed. "By their transgression salvation has been given to the Gentiles, to provoke them to emulation". But if you should also say that the hostile powers, which were raised up against mortals, are the mountains and hills that have been brought down, you will not err. For in order that valleys of this kind may be filled, the hostile powers, the mountains and hills, must be brought low. But let us also contemplate whether this too, which was prophesied at the coming of Christ, has been fulfilled. For there follows: "and all the crooked shall be made straight". Each one of us was crooked—if indeed he was, and does not continue so to this very day—and through the coming of Christ, which has taken place unto our soul, whatever things were "crooked" have been "made straight". For what does it profit you, if Christ once came in the flesh, unless he has also come to your soul? Let us pray that his coming may be made to us daily, and that we may be able to say: "But I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me". For if Christ lives in Paul and does not live in me, what will it profit me? But when he has come also to me and I have had enjoyment of him, just as Paul had enjoyment of him, then I too shall speak like Paul: "I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me". Let us therefore consider also the other things that are foretold at the coming of Christ. Nothing was rougher than you: look at your former impulses, look at your anger and your other vices—if indeed they have ceased to be what they were—and you will understand that nothing was rougher than you and, to speak more pointedly, that nothing was more uneven. Your manner of life was uneven, and your speech, and your works were uneven. Therefore my Lord Jesus came and leveled your roughnesses and turned whatever was disordered "into level ways", so that there might be made in you a journeying without stumbling, and light and most pure, and that God the Father might walk in you, and that Christ the Lord might make his dwelling with you and say: "I and my Father will come and make our dwelling with him".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There follows: "and all flesh shall see the salvation of God". You were once "flesh", and you who were once "flesh"—nay, to speak more wondrously, while you are still in the flesh—you see "the salvation of God". But what it may mean, that it is said "all flesh", in that none is excepted who does not see "the salvation of God", I leave to be understood by those who know how to search out the mysteries and veins of the Scriptures.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: No one that remains in his old state, and forsakes not his old habits and practices, can rightly come to be baptized; whoever then wishes to be baptized, let him go forth. Hence are those words significantly spoken, And he said unto the multitude that went forth to be baptized of him. To the multitudes then who are going forth to the laver of baptism, He speaks the following words, for if they had already gone forth, He would not have said, O generation of vipers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But this too must be attended to, that John speaks "to the peoples going out" to baptism. If anyone wishes to be baptized, let him go out; for one remaining in his former state and not leaving his ways and his custom by no means comes rightly to baptism. And that you may understand what it is to go out to baptism, receive the testimony and hearken to the words in which God speaks to Abraham: "go out from your land" and the rest. And so, as the crowds were going out to the washing—not having gone out, but only striving to go out—John speaks the things that follow. For if they had already gone out, he would never have said to them: "brood of vipers". Whatever things, therefore, he speaks to them, he speaks also to you, O catechumens, male and female, who are preparing to come to baptism. Consider whether perhaps it may be said also to you: "brood of vipers"; for if you too have some likeness to the vipers of sense and to the invisible serpents, to you too it will be said: "brood of vipers". But also that which follows, unless you have driven out the wickedness and the venom of serpents from your heart, will be said to you: "who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?" Great wrath hangs over this age; the whole world is to suffer the wrath of God. So great a vastness of heaven and breadth of earth and choirs of stars, the splendor of the sun and the nocturnal comforts of the moon, the "wrath" of God will overthrow; for all these things shall pass away because of the sins of men. And formerly, indeed, the "wrath" of God came upon one earth only, "because all flesh had abandoned its way upon the earth"; but now the "wrath" of God is to come both upon heaven and upon earth: "the heavens shall pass away, but you shall remain"—it is said to God—"and all shall grow old like a garment". See of what kind and how great the "wrath" is, which is about to consume the whole world and will punish those who are worthy of punishment, and will find material in which to exercise itself. Each one of us, from that which he has done, has prepared material for wrath: "for according to your hardness and impenitent heart you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God", it is said to the Romans.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then there follows: "Who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance". And to you, who come to baptism, it is said: "bring forth fruits worthy of repentance". Do you wish to know what are the fruits worthy of repentance? "Love is the fruit of the spirit, joy is the fruit of the spirit, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, self-control" and the rest of this kind. If we have all these things, we have brought forth "fruits worthy of repentance". Again it is said to those who came to John's baptism: "and do not begin to say within yourselves: we have Abraham as father; for I say to you, that God is able from these stones to raise up sons of Abraham". John, the last of the prophets, prophesies the casting out of the former people and the calling of the Gentiles. For to those who gloried in Abraham he says: "and do not begin to say within yourselves: we have Abraham as father". And again he speaks concerning the Gentiles: "for I say to you, that God is able from these stones to raise up sons of Abraham". From what stones? He was certainly not pointing to irrational and bodily stones, but to insensible men, once hard, who, because they worshiped stones or wood, had that fulfilled in them which was sung in the psalm concerning such men: "let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them". Truly those who make idols and trust in them are like their gods: they have been turned, without sense and without any reason, into stones and wood. For although they see so great an order of created things, their beauty, their function, so great a beauty of the world, they are unwilling to understand the creator from the created things, nor do they consider that there is some providence over so great a dispensation, some governor; but they are blind, seeing the world only with those eyes with which irrational beasts of burden and wild animals see. For they do not perceive that there is present, in these things which they see governed by reason, some reason. These things are said because John had said: "God is able from these stones to raise up sons of Abraham". Let us therefore also beseech God that, even if we were at some time stones, we may be turned into "sons of Abraham" in place of those sons who have been cast out and who have lost the promise and the adoption by their own fault. I will yet set down one testimony concerning stones, since indeed in the canticle of Exodus it is written: "let them be turned into stones, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this your people pass over, whom you have possessed". And so God is asked that for a little while the Gentiles be turned into stones—for the Greek word sounds this more pointedly, "ἀπολιθούντωσαν" (let them be petrified)—"until the people" of the Jews "pass over". There is no doubt that, after those have passed over, the Gentiles will cease to be stony and, in place of a hard heart, will receive in Christ a human and rational nature: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If it were impossible to be rid of these serpents, the serpents residing in the soul on account of its wickedness, then the Savior (or John) would not have said: "Bring forth then fruits worthy of repentance!" Having turned, you will no longer be serpents, broods of vipers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the completion of all things had been then already begun, and the end of time close at hand, I should have no question but that the prophecy was given, because at that time it was to be fulfilled. But now that many ages have elapsed since the Spirit spoke this, I think it was prophesied to the people of Israel, because their cutting off was approaching. For to those that went out to him that they should be baptized, he gave this warning among others.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
John at that time was already speaking: "Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees". And indeed, if the consummation were already pressing in and the end of the times were at hand, no question would arise for me. For I would say that what he says—"Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees"—and that other saying—"Every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire"—was prophesied for this reason, because it was being fulfilled at that time. But since so many ages have flowed by since then, and such innumerable years have passed from that time to the present day, we must inquire how the Holy Spirit says in the prophet: "Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees". I think it is prophesied to the people of Israel, that their cutting-down is near. For "to those" who "were going out" to him, "to be baptized", he was saying, among other things: "Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance", and, as if to the Jews, he was saying: "Do not begin to say within yourselves: We have Abraham for our father. For I tell you that God is able to raise up sons of Abraham from these stones". Therefore this, which he says—"Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees"—he speaks to the Jews.

With this sense there agrees also that saying of the Apostle, that the branches were broken off and cut down by this axe of unbelief, so that it might cut away from the tree not the root, but those things which had sprouted from the root, in order that the branches of the wild olive might be grafted into the root of the original tree. "Every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire". For it has this end, that it be consumed by burning.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 23

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Three classes of men are introduced as enquiring of John concerning their salvation, one which the Scripture calls the multitude, another to which it gives the name of Publicans, and a third which is noticed by the appellation of soldiers.

But this place admits of a deeper meaning, for as we ought not to serve two masters, so neither to have two coats, lest one should be the clothing of the old man, the other of the new, but we ought to cast off the old man, and give to him who is naked. For one man has one coat, another has none at all, the strength therefore of the two is exactly contrary, and as it has been written that we should cast all our crimes to the bottom of the sea, so ought we to throw from us our vices and errors, and lay them upon him who has been the cause of them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Then three orders are introduced of those inquiring of John concerning their salvation: one, which Scripture called "the peoples going out to the baptism"; another, which it names "tax collectors"; a third, which is reckoned under the appellation of "soldiers". "The crowds asked him, saying: What shall we do? And he answering said to them: He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none, and he who has food, let him do likewise"—which indeed I do not know whether it is fitting to be commanded to the crowds. For it befits the apostles rather than the common people that he who has two tunics should give one to him who has none. And that you may know that this befits the apostles rather than the peoples, hear what is said by the Savior to them: "Do not take two tunics on the way". And so the double garment with which each one is clothed, and the command that he give the other "to him who has none", sounds forth another understanding. For the Savior wishes that, just as we ought not to "serve two masters", so neither should we have two tunics nor be wrapped in a double garment, lest there be one garment of the old man and another of the new. On the contrary, he desires that "we strip off the old man and put on the new". Thus far the exposition is easy. But further it is asked how, according to this interpretation, we are bidden to give a garment "to him who has none".

Who then is that one who does not have even a single garment upon his flesh, who is naked, who is covered by no clothing at all? Nor indeed do I say this in order that liberality and mercy toward the poor and hyperbolic clemency should not be commanded, so that we should cover even the naked with a second tunic. But I say this, that this passage admits also a deeper understanding, and that we ought to give a tunic to him who has none at all.

Who then is this one who has no tunic? Surely he who utterly does not have God. We ought therefore to strip ourselves and give to him who is naked. One has God, another has him not at all—that contrary power, namely. And just as it is written that "we should cast our sins into the depth of the sea", so we ought to throw off from ourselves our vices and sins and cast them upon him who was for us the cause of them. "And he who has food", he says, "let him do likewise". He who has food, let him give to him who has none, so that he may bestow upon him not only clothing, but also that which he may eat.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 23

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Now the tax collectors also came to be baptized by him". This, even according to the simple understanding, may teach the tax collectors to seek "nothing more" than what is commanded in the law; for those who exact more transgress not the commandment of John, but of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in John. But I do not know whether, according to the ἀναγωγήν (the anagogical or higher sense), the discourse signifies something else more excellent, and whether we ought to bring forth things so mystical in such an audience, especially among those who do not look into the marrow of the Scriptures, but delight only in the surface. It is indeed dangerous, yet it must be touched upon summarily and briefly. When we have departed from the world and this our life has been changed, there will be certain ones sitting at the boundaries of the world, most diligently searching, as if by the office of tax collectors, lest they find anything of their own in us. It seems to me that "the prince of this world" is like a tax collector, whence it is written of him: "The prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing". That also which we read in the Apostle: "Render to all their debts; to whom tribute, tribute; to whom custom, custom; to whom honor, honor; owe nothing to anyone, except that you love one another"—is to be understood in a sacred sense. Wherefore let us consider to how great dangers we are subject, lest perchance, when we do not have that which we may render for the custom, we ourselves be dragged off for the debt, as is wont to happen also among the tribute-payers of the world, when someone for a debt is himself shut up to serve the state. Very many of us are to be held by tax collectors of this sort—whom that holy man Jacob did not greatly dread, nor fear that anything from the tax collectors' tributes should be found in him. Whence Laban spoke boldly to that tax collector: "Recognize, if anything of your goods is with me". Concerning which Scripture gives testimony, saying: "And Laban did not recognize anything with Jacob". Therefore our Savior, and the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets, teaches not only men, but also angels and invisible powers. Why do I speak of the Savior? The prophets themselves too and the apostles preach all that they proclaim not only to men, but also to angels. That you may know this to be true, he says: "Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak", and: "In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you", and: "Praise the Lord, you heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord", and: "Let the angels praise him", and: "In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul". You will find in many places, and especially in the Psalms, that discourse is directed also to the angels, since power is given to man—to him, that is, who has the Holy Spirit—to address even the angels. Of these I will set down one example, that we may know that the angels too are instructed by human voices. It is written in the Apocalypse of John: "To the angel of the church of the Ephesians write: I have something against you". And again: "To the angel of the church of Pergamum write: I have something against you". Certainly it is a man who writes to the angels and commands them something. I do not doubt that angels are present also in our assembly, not only generally to the whole church, but even individually, concerning whom the Savior says: "Their angels always behold the face of my Father, who is in heaven". A twofold church is present here, one of men, the other of angels. If we say anything according to reason and according to the will of the Scriptures, the angels rejoice and pray with us. And because the angels are present in the church—in that church, at least, which merits it and is Christ's—therefore it is commanded to women when praying that they have "a veil upon the head because of the angels". What angels? Surely those who assist the saints and rejoice in the church, whom indeed we do not see, because our eyes are darkened by the filth of sins, but the apostles of Jesus see them, to whom he says: "Amen, amen I say to you, you shall see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man". But if I had this grace, that I might see as the apostles saw and behold as Paul beheld, I would now discern the multitude of angels which Elisha saw, and which Gehazi, who had stood with him, did not see. Gehazi was in fear lest he be captured by the enemies, seeing Elisha alone. But Elisha, as a prophet of the Lord, prays and says: "O Lord, open the eyes of this boy, that he may see, for there are many more with us than with them". And immediately, at the prayers of the holy man, he beheld the angels which Gehazi previously did not see. We have said these things for this reason, to show that the tax collectors are taught by John—not only those who serve the tributes of the state, but also those who were coming to repentance and were tax collectors other than the bodily ones, just as there were also other soldiers who were going out to the baptism of repentance. For not only John and the prophets came, but the Savior himself also came to preach saving repentance to men and to angels and to the other powers, so that "in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father": to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 23

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It was meet that more deference should be paid to John than to other men, for he lived such as no other man. Wherefore indeed most rightly did they regard him with affection, only they kept not within due bounds; hence it is said, But while the people were expecting whether he were the Christ.

But love is dangerous when it is uncontrolled. For he who loves any one ought to consider the nature and causes of loving, and not to love more than the object deserves. For if he pass the due measure and bounds of love, both he who loves, and he who is loved, will be in sin.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Even love has its danger, if it exceed due measure. For whoever loves someone ought to consider the nature and the reasons for loving, and not to love him more than he deserves. For if love should overstep its measure and limit, both the one who loves and the one who is loved will be in sin. That this may become clearer, let us set forth an example. The people marveled at John and loved him, and it was truly a wonder deserving that more honor be paid to him than to the rest of men, since he had lived otherwise than all mortals. We are none of us content with simple food, but we take delight in a variety of dishes; a single kind of wine does not suffice us to drink, and we purchase wines of various flavors; but John always fed on "locusts", always on "wild honey", and was content with simple and meager food, lest his body should grow fat with richer viands and be weighed down with dainty banquets. For our bodies are of such a nature that they are burdened by superfluous food, and when the body has been burdened, the soul too is weighed down, which, being diffused throughout the whole body, lies subject to its passions. Wherefore it is rightly enjoined upon those who are able to observe it: "It is good not to eat flesh nor to drink wine, nor anything by which your brother is made to stumble". The life of John, therefore, was wonderful and much different from the manner of life of other men. He had no purse, no servant, not even a cheap hut. He dwelt in the desert, not only up to "the day of his showing forth to Israel", but also at that time when he preached repentance to the people, he was in the wilderness of Judea and was watered by plain water, so that in his drink also he was different from the rest. We who dwell in cities, who are in the midst of peoples, seek finer garments and foods and dwellings; but he, who dwelt in the wilderness—see with what clothing he was clad: "from camels' hair" he had made himself a tunic, and he was girded with "a leather belt". All things, therefore, in him were new, and because of the unlikeness of his life all who saw him marveled at him, and, marveling, most zealously honored him, above all because he baptized the penitent "unto the remission of sins". For which reasons they indeed loved him most justly, but they did not keep due measure in their love: for they were thinking, "lest perhaps he himself were the Christ". Guarding against such disordered and irrational love, the apostle Paul spoke of himself: "But I fear lest anyone should think of me above that which he sees or hears from me; and lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me", and so on. Fearing this, lest he himself also fall into it, he was unwilling to disclose about himself all that he knew, lest anyone should suppose him to be more than he perceived, and, exceeding the measure of honor, should say what had been said of John, namely that "he himself was the Christ". This indeed some have said even of Dositheus, the heresiarch of the Samaritans, and others also of Judas the Galilean. In short, certain men rushed into such audacity of love that they invented certain new and unheard-of monstrosities concerning Paul. For some say that what is written, "to sit at the right hand of the Savior and at the left", is said of Paul and of Marcion—that Paul sits "at the right hand", and Marcion sits "at the left". Others, moreover, reading, "I will send you an advocate, the Spirit of truth", are unwilling to understand a third person distinct from the Father and the Son, and a divine and sublime nature, but rather the apostle Paul. Do not all these seem to you to have loved more than is fitting, and, while they marvel at the excellence of each one, to have lost the measure of love? This indeed we too suffer in the church; for very many, while they love us more than we deserve, boast these things and speak, praising our sermons and doctrine in a way that our conscience does not accept. Others, on the contrary, slandering our treatises, accuse us of holding views which we know we have never held. But neither these, who love more, nor those, who hate, hold to the rule of truth, and the ones lie through love, the others through hatred. Whence it is fitting to put reins upon love also, and to permit it only so much liberty of roaming as will not let it plunge over precipices. It is written in Ecclesiastes: "Be not overly just, nor think things greater than yourself, lest perhaps you be struck senseless". Following this example, I can say something similar: do not love a man "with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength"; do not love an angel "with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole strength", but keep this precept, according to the word of the Savior, for God alone. For "you shall love", he says, "the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength". Let someone answer me and say: The Savior commanded, "You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength, and your neighbor as yourself". I wish to love Christ also: teach me, then, how I am to love him. For if I love him "with my whole heart and with my whole soul and with my whole strength", I act against the precept, in that I would so love another besides the one God. But if I love him less than the almighty Father, I fear lest I be found impious and profane toward the "firstborn of all creation". Teach me and show me the reasoning, how, walking midway between the two, I ought to love Christ. Do you wish to know with what love Christ is to be loved? Listen briefly! Love the Lord your God in Christ, and do not think that you can have a different love toward the Father and toward the Son. Love God and Christ together; love the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, "with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength". But if anyone inquires and says: prove from the scriptures what you assert, let him hear the apostle Paul, who had a reasonable love, saying: "For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord and Savior": to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 25

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And as John was waiting by the river Jordan for those who came to his baptism, and some he drove away, saying, Generation of vipers, but those who confessed their sins he received, so shall the Lord Jesus stand in the fiery stream with the flaming sword, that whoever after the close of this life desires to pass over to Paradise and needs purification, He may baptize him with this laver, and pass him over to paradise, but whoso has not the seal of the former baptisms, him He shall not baptize with the laver of fire.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The people received John, who was lesser than Christ, supposing and pondering "whether perhaps he himself were the Christ"; but him who came as "greater" than John they did not receive. Do you wish to know the reason? Learn it: John's baptism was visible, Christ's baptism was invisible. "For I", he says, "baptize you with water; but he who comes after me is greater than I, and he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire". When does Jesus baptize "with the Holy Spirit", and again, when does he baptize "with fire"? Does he baptize both "with the Spirit and with fire" at one and the same time, or at a distinct and different time? "But you", he says, "shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence". The apostles were baptized "with the Holy Spirit" after his ascension into the heavens; but that they were baptized "with fire", Scripture does not record. But just as John, beside the river Jordan, awaited those coming to the baptism, and drove others away, saying: "brood of vipers" and the rest, while those who confessed their vices and sins he received, so the Lord Jesus Christ will stand in the river of fire beside the "flaming sword", so that whoever, after the departure from this life, desires to pass over to paradise and has need of cleansing, he may baptize with that stream and send across to the things longed for; but him who does not have the sign of the earlier baptisms he will not baptize with the fiery washing. For it is fitting that one first be baptized "with water and the Spirit", so that, when he comes to the fiery river, he may show that he has kept both the washings of water and of the Spirit, and then may deserve to receive also the baptism of fire in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 24

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, because without the wind the wheat and chaff cannot be separated, therefore He has the fan in His hand, which shows some to be chaff, some wheat; for when you were as the light chaff; (i. e. unbelieving,) temptation showed you to be what you knew not; but when you shall bravely endure temptation, the temptation will not make you faithful and enduring, but it will bring to light the virtue which was hid in you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "God is a spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth". Our God too "is a consuming fire". God, therefore, is called by two names: both "spirit" and "fire": spirit for the righteous, fire for sinners. But the angels also are called spirits and fire: "he who makes", it says, "his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire"; to the holy ones they are spirits, but to those who deserve punishments they supply fire and burning. According to which sense our Lord and Savior too, since he is "spirit", "came to send fire upon the earth"; "spirit" according to that which is written: "but when you have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away", and: "the Lord is a spirit". But "he came to send fire" not upon heaven, but "upon the earth", as he himself shows when he says: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it already blaze?" For if "you have turned to the Lord", who is "spirit", Christ will be "spirit" to you and "he did not come to send fire upon the earth". But if you are not turned to him, but have earth and its fruits, "he came to send fire upon" your "earth". Something like this is also written concerning God: "a fire is kindled in my fury", not as far as heaven, but "as far as hell beneath", and "it shall devour" not heaven, but "the earth and its produce". To what end have I recalled these things? Because the baptism too, with which Jesus baptizes, is "in the Holy Spirit" and "in fire". I remember the things I spoke recently, nor has the earlier explanation escaped me, but I wish to bring in something new as well. If you are holy, you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit; if a sinner, you will be plunged into fire; and one and the same baptism will be turned, for the unworthy and for sinners, into condemnation and fire, but to those who are holy and turn to the Lord with their whole faith, the grace and salvation of the Holy Spirit is to be granted. He, therefore, who is said to baptize "in the Holy Spirit and in fire", has "a winnowing fork in his hand and he will cleanse his threshing floor; and he will gather his wheat into the granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire". I wish to find the reason why our Lord has a "winnowing fork", and by what wind blowing the light chaff is snatched hither and thither, while the heavy wheat is carried down into one place; for neither can the wheat and the chaff be separated without wind. I consider that temptations are to be understood in place of the wind, which out of the mingled heap of believers show some to be chaff, others to be wheat. For when your soul has been overcome by some temptation, the temptation does not turn you into chaff, but, since you were chaff — namely light and unbelieving — the temptation reveals you to be what you were hiding. On the contrary, however, when you bravely endure trials, the temptation does not make you faithful and patient, but it brings out into the open the virtue of patience and fortitude which was in you, but was hidden. "For do you think", says the Lord, "that I spoke to you otherwise than that you might appear righteous?" And elsewhere: "I afflicted you and beset you with want, that the things which were in your heart might be made manifest". In this manner too the storm does not make a building stand firm upon the sand, but, if you wish to build, upon "the rock"; and when the storm has arisen, that which is founded "upon the rock" it will not overthrow, but that which sways "upon the sand" it proves at once to have been not well founded. Wherefore, before the storm arises, before the blasts of the winds rise up, before the rivers swell, while all things are still silent, let us turn all our zeal to the foundations of our buildings, let us build our house with the varied and firm stones of the precepts of God, so that, when persecution rages and a dreadful whirlwind rises up against Christians, we may show that we have a building "upon the rock", Christ Jesus. But if anyone — far be it from us — should deny him, let that one know that he did not deny Christ at that time when he seemed to have denied, but that he had the seeds and the roots of denying already long before, and that then was recognized what he had, and it was brought out into the open. Let us therefore pray to the Lord that we may be a firm building, which no storm may overturn, "founded upon the rock", our Lord Jesus Christ: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 26

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
John having announced the coming of Christ, was preaching the baptism of the Holy Spirit, and the other things which the Gospel history has handed down to us. But besides these he is declared to have announced others in the following words, And many other things in his exhortation preached he unto the people.

And as in the Gospel according to St. John it is related of Christ that He spoke many other things, so also in this place we must understand Luke to say the same of John the Baptist, since certain things are announced by John too great to be entrusted to writing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who teaches the word of the Gospel proclaims not one thing but very many.
