For this is what Scripture signifies when it says: "now with many other exhortations also he was proclaiming good news". And so John was preaching to the people "other" things as well, which are not written down; but the things that are written—consider how many they were. He proclaimed Christ, he pointed him out, he preached the baptism of the Holy Spirit; he taught the tax collectors salvation, the soldiers discipline, that the threshing floor is to be cleansed, that the trees are to be cut down, and the rest that the narrative of the Gospel relates. Therefore, apart from these things that are written, he is shown to have proclaimed still other things that are not written, in that it is said: "now with many other exhortations also he was proclaiming good news to the people". And just as in the Gospel according to John it is reported concerning Christ that he spoke many other things also, "which are not written in this book", "which, if they were written, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written": so also in the present passage understand that Luke perhaps, since certain things greater than ought to be committed to letters were being proclaimed by John, was unwilling to state them by name, but only indicated that they had been spoken, and therefore said: "now with many other exhortations also he was proclaiming good news to the people".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 27

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But we marvel at John, because among them that are born of women there was not a greater than he, for by his good deeds he had been exalted to so high a fame for virtue, that by many he was supposed to be Christ. But what is much more marvellous he feared not Herod, nor dreaded death, as it follows, But Herod the tetrarch being reproved by him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us marvel at John, and indeed from the very things that follow, most of all because "among those born of women there was none greater than John the Baptist", and because he rightly rose to so great a reputation by his virtue that he was thought by very many to be "the Christ". But this is far more marvelous: Herod the tetrarch held royal power and could have killed him whenever he wished; and although he had done an unjust deed and one contrary to the law of Moses, in taking his brother's wife, who had a daughter by her former husband, John did not fear him, did not show partiality, did not consider, as I have said, the royal power, did not dread destruction—for he knew, even if he were not a prophet, that when provoked Herod could kill him—so then, though he knew all these things, with prophetic liberty he rebuked Herod and denounced the incestuous marriage.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 27

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And on that account, shut up "in prison", he was anxious not about death, not about the uncertain judgment of the judge, but in his chains was thinking about Christ, whom he had proclaimed. And because he himself could not go to him, he sends his disciples to inquire: "Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?" Take note that he taught "even in prison". For whence had he disciples even in that place, and for what reason did they persevere there, unless because even in prison he was performing the office of a master and was instructing them with divine discourses? And among these, when a question had arisen concerning Jesus, he sends some of his disciples and asks: "Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?" The disciples return and report to their master what the Savior had commanded to be reported: armed with his words, John dies confidently for the battle and is gladly beheaded, confirmed by the very voice of the Lord that he whom he believed was truly the Son of God. So much concerning John and his liberty, and concerning the madness of Herod, who upon many crimes added this one also, that he first shut John up in prison and afterward beheaded him.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 27

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But because the Lord was baptized and the heavens were opened and "the Holy Spirit descended" upon him and a voice thundered from the heavens saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased", it must be said that at the baptism of Jesus heaven was unbarred, and that the heavens were opened for the dispensation of the remission of sins—not of him "who had done no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth"—but for the whole world.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 27

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And that the Holy Spirit descended so that, after the Lord "had ascended on high leading captivity captive", he might bestow on us the Spirit who had come to him; which Spirit indeed he also gave at the time of his resurrection, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone's sins, they will be forgiven him; if you retain anyone's, they will be retained". Now "the Holy Spirit descended upon" the Savior "in the form of a dove", a bird that is gentle, innocent, and simple. Whence it is also commanded to us that we should imitate the innocence of doves. Such is the Holy Spirit—clean and winged and rising to the heights. Wherefore in prayer we say: "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall fly and be at rest?"—that is: who will give me the wings of the Holy Spirit? And in another place the prophetic word promises: "If you sleep in the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts of its back in the greenness of gold". For if we take our rest "in the midst of the lots" of the Old and New Testament, there will be given to us "the wings of a dove covered with silver", that is, the words of God, and "its hinder parts" radiant with the gleam and "greenness" of gold, so that our understanding may be filled with the perceptions of the Holy Spirit—that is, so that our speech and mind may be filled with his coming, and that we may neither say anything nor understand anything except what he has suggested, and that all sanctification, both in heart and in words and in deed, may come from the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 27

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But you too, who hear these things, if you attend to the holy Scriptures in your leisure, will find very many deeds of great matters contained under the number thirty or fifty. At thirty years of age Joseph is brought out of prison and receives the sovereignty of all Egypt, that by divine foresight he might drive off the ruin of the impending famine. Jesus is related to be of thirty years when He came to the baptism and "saw the heavens divided and the Spirit of God coming upon Himself in the likeness of a dove"; where also the mystery of the Trinity first began to be disclosed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Having related our Lord's baptism, he next enters upon the generation of the Lord, not bringing it down from the higher to the lower, but beginning with Christ, he carries it up to God Himself. Hence he says, And Jesus Himself began. For when He was baptized, and had Himself undergone the mystery of the second birth, then He is said to have begun, that thou also mightest destroy this first birth and be born in the second.

The Lord descending into the world took upon Him the person of all sinners, and was willing to be born of the stock of Solomon, (as Matthew relates,) whose sins have been written down, and of the rest, many of whom did evil in the sight of God. But when He ascended, and is described as being born a second time in baptism, (as Luke relates,) He is not born through Salomon, but Nathan, who reproves the father for the death of Uriah, and the birth of Solomon.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Our Lord and Savior, who was far better than Melchizedek, whose lineage Scripture has not disclosed, is now described as having been born according to the order of the fathers; and although his divinity is not subject to any human beginning, for your sake, who were born in the flesh, he willed to be born. And yet the order of his birth is not narrated in the same way by the evangelists, a matter which has greatly troubled some people. For Matthew, beginning to weave the sequence of that birth from Abraham, arrives at the point of saying: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was in this way", and he describes not the one who was baptized, but the one who came into the world; whereas Luke, in setting forth his birth, does not lead down from higher to lower, but, when he had first spoken of him as baptized, ascends all the way to God himself. Nor are the persons the same in his genealogy when he is said to descend and when he is said to ascend. For the one who makes him descend from the heavens introduces women too, and not just any women, but sinful ones, and women whom Scripture had censured; but the one who narrates him as baptized makes mention of no woman. In Matthew, therefore, as we have said, there is named Tamar, who by deceit lay with her father-in-law, and Ruth the Moabite, not of the stock of Israel, and Rahab, whose origin I cannot know, and the wife of Uriah, who violated her husband's bed. For because our Lord and Savior had come for this purpose, that he might take up the sins of men, and God "made him who had done no sin to be sin for us", therefore, descending into the world, he assumed the person of sinful and vicious men, and willed to be born of the line of Solomon, whose sins are recorded, and of Rehoboam, whose transgressions are related, and of the rest, many of whom did "evil in the sight of the Lord". But when he ascends from the washing and is described as born a second time, he is born not through Solomon, but through Nathan, who rebuked his father over the death of Uriah and the birth of Solomon. But in Matthew the term "begetting" is always added; here, however, it is entirely passed over in silence. For there it is written: "Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers, Judah begot Perez and Zerah of Tamar", and right up to the end "begot" is always attached. But in Luke, where Jesus ascends from the washing, he is called "son", "as was supposed, of Joseph"; and in so long a series of names, except for the fact that he "was supposed to be the son of Joseph", the term "begetting" is nowhere written down. In Matthew it is not written: "he was beginning"; but here, because he was about to ascend from baptism, "he was beginning" is read, Scripture relating: "and this same Jesus was beginning". For when he was baptized and took up the mystery of the second birth, so that you too might destroy your former nativity and be born in the second regeneration, then he is said "to have begun". And just as the people of the Jews, when they were in Egypt, did not have a beginning of months, but when they had gone out of Egypt, then it is said to them: "this month, the beginning of months, shall be the first for you among the months of the year", so he who is not yet baptized is not narrated "to have begun". For let us not suppose that it was added in vain to that which is said, "this same was Jesus", what follows: "beginning". But this also, which he says, "about thirty years old", must be considered. "Joseph was thirty years old" when he was released from his chains and, having interpreted the dream of Pharaoh, was made ruler of Egypt, and in the time of plenty gathered wheat, so that in the time of famine he might have what he could distribute. I think that the thirty years of Joseph went before, as a type of the thirty years of the Savior. For this Joseph gathered not such wheat as that Joseph in Egypt, but true and heavenly wheat, so that, the wheat having been gathered in the time of plenty, he might have what he could distribute when famine had been sent into Egypt, "not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God". And so he gathers from the prophets, from the law, from the apostles the words of abundance, so that when now no more books are written, nor is any new instrument composed, nor are apostles sent, then he may distribute those things which had been brought together by Jesus into the storehouses of the apostles — that is, into their souls and the souls of all the saints — and may nourish Egypt, imperiled by famine, and especially his brothers, of whom it is written: "I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the church I will sing to you". Other men too have words of patience and words of justice and the words of the remaining virtues; this is the wheat which Joseph distributed to the Egyptians. But the grain which he gives to his brothers, that is, to his disciples, is another kind, from the land of Goshen, from that land which looks toward the east: the wheat of the Gospel, the wheat of the apostles. From this wheat we ought to make loaves, yet in such a way that they are not mixed with "the old leaven", and that we may have new bread milled from the wheat and flour of the Scriptures in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 28

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When therefore you read that Jesus was full of the Holy Spirit, and it is written in the Acts concerning the Apostles, that they were filled with the Holy Spirit, you must not suppose that the Apostles were equal to the Saviour. For as if you should say, These vessels are full of wine or oil, you would not thereby affirm them to be equally full, so Jesus and Paul were full of the Holy Spirit, but Paul's vessel was far less than that of Jesus, and yet each was filled according to its own measure. Having then received baptism, the Saviour, being full of the Holy Spirit, which came upon Him from heaven in the form of a dove, was led by the Spirit, because, as many as are led by the Spirit, they are the sons of God, (Rom. 8:14.) but He was above all, especially the Son of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When you read in the Gospel: "But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned", and in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written of them that they were "filled" with "the Holy Spirit", take care not to suppose that the apostles were equal to the Savior; rather, understand that Jesus and the apostles and any other of the saints are full of the Holy Spirit according to the measure of their own vessel. Just as, for example, if you wish to say: these vessels are full of wine or oil, you do not thereby indicate that they are full in equal measure — since one can hold a sextarius, another an urn, another an amphora — in the same way both Jesus and Paul were full of the Holy Spirit; but the vessel of Paul was much smaller than the vessel of Jesus, and yet each was full according to its own measure. And so, having received baptism, the Savior, "full of the Holy Spirit", which had come upon him from the heavens "in the form of a dove", "was led by the Spirit". For since "as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God", and he beyond all others was properly the Son of God, therefore he too had to be led by the Holy Spirit.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 29

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But Jesus is tempted by the devil forty days, and what the temptations were we know not. They were perhaps omitted, as being greater than could be committed to writing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For it is written: "And he was led into the desert by the Spirit for forty days and was tempted by the devil". For forty days Jesus is tempted, and what the temptations were, we do not know; and these were perhaps passed over for the reason that they were too great to be entrusted to writing. And if it is right to say it thus: just as "the world could not contain all the books", if the things which Jesus taught and did had been written down, so the world could not bear the temptations of the forty days, by which the Lord was tempted by the devil, if Scripture had recorded them. It suffices for us to know only this much: that "he was for forty days in the desert and was tempted by the devil and ate nothing in those days"; for he was mortifying the sense of the flesh by continual and unbroken fasting.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 29

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
When a father is asked by his son for bread, he does not give him a stone for bread, but the devil like a crafty and deceitful foe gives stones for bread.

I suppose also that even now at this very time the devil shows a stone to men that he may tempt them to speak, saying to them, Command this stone to be made bread. If thou seest the heretics devouring their lying doctrines as if they were bread, know that their teaching is a stone which the devil shows them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And when the days were completed, he hungered. And the devil said to him: If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread". "Tell", he says, "this stone". Which stone? Surely the one the devil was pointing out, the one he wants to be made bread. What sort of temptation is this, that when a son asks his father for bread and the father does not give him a stone, this adversary, crafty and deceitful, should give a stone in place of bread? Is this the whole of what the devil wanted — that a stone should become bread, and that men should feed not on bread but on a stone, which the devil had pointed out in place of bread? I think that even to this day the devil shows a stone and urges each person to say: "tell this stone to become bread". By every temptation with which men were to be tempted, the Lord was tempted first, according to his assumption of the flesh. And he is tempted for this reason, that we too, when he conquers, may conquer. What I say perhaps becomes obscure, unless it is made clearer by an example. If you see heretics eating the lie of their own doctrines in place of bread, know that their teaching is a stone which the devil points out. But do not suppose that he has only one stone; he has many stones, from which he is introduced speaking in Matthew: "tell these stones to become loaves". Marcion spoke, and the devil's stone became bread for him. Valentinus spoke, and another stone was turned into bread for him. Basilides too had bread of this kind, and so did the rest of the heretics. Hence we must anxiously take care, lest perhaps, while eating the devil's stone, we suppose that we are feeding on the bread of God. Otherwise, what temptation was there in a stone becoming bread and being eaten by the Savior? For let us imagine that, at the devil's suggestion, the Lord had turned a stone into bread, and had eaten what he himself had made by his own power, and had satisfied his hunger: what sort of temptation is this, what victory over the devil, if these things were written down in a plain sense? But these things, as we have said, when their reason is discerned, both show that there would have been a temptation, if they had been done, and that the victory came about because they were spurned.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 29

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And at the same time it is shown that this bread, which comes from a stone, is not the word of God which feeds man, of which it is written: "man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word which shall proceed through the mouth of God shall man live". I answer you, O crafty and wicked one, who do not fear to tempt me: there is another bread, that of the word of God, which gives life to man. And at the same time let us see that these things are spoken not by the Son of God, but by the man whom the Son of God deigned to assume; for he answers as though concerning a man and says: "It is written: man shall not live by bread alone", from which it is manifest that it was not God, but man, who was tempted. Sifting the sense of the Scripture diligently, I think I find the reason why John did not describe the temptation of the Lord, but only Matthew, Luke, and Mark. For John, because he had made his beginning from God, saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word", and could not weave the order of the divine generation, but had only expressed that he was from God and with God, added: "And the Word was made flesh". Furthermore, since God cannot be tempted — and it was of God that his discourse concerned — therefore he does not bring in that one being tempted by the devil. But because "the book of the generation of Jesus Christ" is narrated in Matthew's Gospel concerning that man who had been born of Mary, and in Luke his generation is described, and in Mark it is a man who is tempted, therefore his corresponding answer is reported: "man shall not live by bread alone". If, then, the Son of God, being God, was made man for you and is tempted, you, who are man by nature, ought not to be indignant if perhaps you are tempted. But if, when tempted, you have imitated that man who was tempted for you, and have conquered every temptation, you will have hope together with him who then was a man, but now has ceased to be a man. For he who was once a man, after he was tempted and "the devil departed from him until a time" of death, "rising from the dead dies no more". Every man is subject to death; therefore this one, who in no way dies, is now no longer a man, but is God. But if he is God who was once a man, and you must become like him — when "we shall be like him and shall see him as he is" — it will be necessary that you too become God in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 29

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Both the Son of God and the Antichrist have a zeal for reigning. But the Antichrist desires to reign in order to kill those whom he has subjected to himself; Christ reigns for this purpose, that he may save. And each one of us, if he is faithful, is ruled by Christ through the word, wisdom, justice, truth. But if we are lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God, we are ruled by sin, concerning which the Apostle speaks: "let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body". Two kings, therefore, hasten in rivalry to reign: the king of sin over sinners, the devil; the king of justice over the just, Christ. And the devil, knowing that Christ had come for this purpose, to take away his kingdom, and that those who were under him should begin to be under Christ, "showed him all the kingdoms of the world" and of the men of this age—how some are ruled by fornication, others by avarice, how these are carried off by the breeze of popular favor, those are captivated by the allurements of beauty. Nor indeed is it to be thought that, in showing him the kingdoms of the world, he pointed out, for example, the kingdom of the Persians and of the Indians, but rather "he showed him all the kingdoms of the world"—that is, his own kingdom, how he reigned in the world—so that, urging him to do what he wished, he might begin to have even Christ subject to him. Do you wish, he says, to reign over all these?
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 30

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He showed the innumerable multitudes of men who were held under his dominion. And in truth, if we are willing simply to confess our misery and unhappiness, the devil is king of almost the whole world; whence too he is called "the prince of this age" by the Savior. What he says, therefore, is this: Do you see these men who are under my kingdom?—and "he showed him in a moment of time", that is, in the present course of the ages, which, in comparison with eternity, holds the place of a point. For the Savior had no need that the affairs of this age should be displayed to him for any length of time: as soon as he turned the keen edge of his eyes to contemplate, he beheld both the sins that reign and those who are ruled by vices, and the very "prince of the age", the devil, exulting and rejoicing to his own ruin, because he held so many under his dominion.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 30

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Or, to view the whole in another light. Two kings are earnestly contending for a kingdom; The king of sin who reigneth over sinners, that is, the devil; The king of righteousness who ruleth the righteous, that is, Christ. The devil, knowing that Christ had come to take away his kingdom, shows Him all the kingdoms of the world; not the kingdoms of the Persians and of the Medes, but his own kingdom whereby he reigned in the world, whereby some are under the dominion of fornication, others of covetousness. And he shows Him them in a moment of time, that is, in the present course of time, which is but a moment in comparison of eternity. For the Saviour needed not to be shown for any longer time the affairs of this world, but as soon as He turned His eyes to look, He beheld sins reigning, and men made slaves to vice. The devil therefore says unto Him, Camest Thou to contend with me for dominion? Worship me, and behold I give Thee the kingdom I hold. Now the Lord would indeed reign, but being Righteousness itself, would reign without sin; and would have all nations subject to Him, that they might obey the truth, but would not so reign over others as that He Himself should be subject to the devil. Hence it follows, And Jesus answering said unto him, It is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God.

Or else, All these, he says, I would have subject to me, that they might worship the Lord God, and serve Him alone. But dost thou wish sin to begin from Me, which I came hither to destroy?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The devil therefore says to the Lord: You have come for this, to fight against me and to take from my dominion those whom I now hold subject. I do not wish you to contend, I do not wish you to strive, lest you have any trouble in the struggle. There is one thing that I beg: "falling down, adore me", and receive all the kingdom that I hold. But our Lord and Savior does indeed wish to reign and to have all the nations subject to himself, that they may serve justice, truth, and the other virtues; yet he wishes to reign as justice itself, so that he may reign without sin, so that he may do nothing unseemly, and he does not wish to be crowned without labor by being subject to the devil, nor so to reign over the rest that he himself should be ruled by the devil. Whence he speaks to him: "it is written: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve". All these, he says, I wish for this reason to be subject to me, that they may "adore the Lord God and serve him alone"; this is the desire of my kingdom. But you wish sin to begin from me—sin which I have come here to dissolve, and which I desire to take away from the rest as well. Know and understand that I abide in what I have said, that the Lord God alone should be adored, and that I will bring all these under my power and subject them to my kingdom. To whom we too rejoice to be subject, and let us beseech God that he may put to death "the sin reigning in" our "body" and that Christ Jesus alone may reign in us: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 30

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He followed evidently as a wrestler, gladly setting out to meet the temptation, and saying, as it were, Lead me where you will, and you will find me the stronger in every thing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Search the Scriptures, so that even in those things which are thought to be simple you may discover mysteries that are by no means small. Let us search the beginning of the Gospel reading which we have heard today, and let what was hidden come forth into the open. "He brought," it says, that is, the devil brought Jesus "into Jerusalem." This is incredible, that the devil should lead the Son of God and that he should follow. Yet he clearly followed, like an athlete going of his own accord to the contest. He did not dread the tempter, nor was he afraid of the snares of the craftiest of enemies, and in a certain manner he was saying: lead where you wish, tempt as you please, of my own accord I give myself over to be tempted, I endure whatever you may suggest, I offer myself in whatever you may try: you will find me stronger in all things. "He brought him therefore into Jerusalem, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: if you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here." He brought him up to the top, to the summit of the temple, and urges him to throw himself down from there.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 31

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Whence knowest thou, Satan, that those things are written? Hast thou read the Prophets, or the oracles of God? Thou hast read them indeed, but not that thyself mightest be the better for the reading, but that from the mere letter thou mightest slay them who are friends to the letter. (2 Cor. 3:6.) Thou knowest that if thou wert to speak from His other books, thou wouldest not deceive.

But mark how wily he is even in this testimony. For he would fain throw a slur upon the glory of the Saviour, as though He needed the assistance of angels, and would stumble were He not supported by their hands. But this was said not of Christ, but of the saints generally; He needs not the aid of angels, Who is greater than angels. But let this teach thee, Satan, that the angels would stumble did not God sustain them; and thou stumblest, because thou refusest to believe in Jesus Christ the Son of God. But why art thou silent as to what follows, Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk, (Ps. 91:13.) except that thou art the basilisk, thou art the dragon and the lion?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And at the same time consider how the devil tempts. He does not dare to tempt from any other source than from the divine books, and taking a testimony from the Psalms he says: "If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down. For it is written: that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone." Whence do you know, O devil, that these things are written? Have you perhaps read the prophets or come to know the divine utterances? Though you be silent, I will answer for you. You have read, not that you yourself might become better from the reading of the holy things, but that from the bare letter you might slay those who are friends of the letter. You know that, if you should wish to speak to him from other volumes, you will not deceive, nor will your assertions be able to have any authority. Thus Marcion reads the Scriptures like the devil, thus Basilides, thus Valentinus, so that with the devil they might say to the Savior: "It is written, that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone." Whenever you hear testimonies drawn from the Scriptures, see that you do not at once give assent to the one speaking, but consider the man—of what life, of what opinion, of what will he is—lest perhaps he feign himself to be holy, which he is not, and, infected with the poisons of heresy, lie hidden as a wolf under the sheep's skin, lest perhaps the devil speak in him from the Scriptures. But just as the devil, according to the occasion of the times, speaks from the Scriptures, so, on the contrary, Paul, for the benefit of those who hear, takes a testimony not only from the Scriptures but even from secular books, and says: "The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies," and again from another: "for we are also his offspring," and likewise from the comic poet: "evil conversations corrupt good morals." But neither, if the devil has spoken from the Scriptures, will he be able by this occasion to deceive me, nor, if Paul has taken some example from Gentile writings, will he deter me from his own discourse. For Paul takes up words even from those things which are outside, in order to sanctify them. Let us see, then, what the devil speaks to the Lord from the Scriptures: "For it is written, that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone." See how, even in the testimonies themselves, he is shifty. For he wishes to diminish the glory of the Savior, as though he needed the help of the angels, being about to dash his foot unless he were lifted up by their hands. He takes up a testimony and interprets of Christ that which was written not of Christ, but of the saints generally. For freely and with all confidence I contradict the devil, that this cannot be understood of the person of Christ. For he does not need the help of the angels, who is greater than the angels and has obtained by inheritance a name better than they. To none of the angels did God ever say: "You are my Son, this day have I begotten you." To none of them did he speak as to a son, "he who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire," but to his own proper Son, of whom he speaks innumerable things in the prophets. He does not need, I say, the help of the angels, the Son of God. Nay rather, learn, O devil, that, unless Jesus should help the angels, they dash their own foot. And if any of the angels has seemed to dash his foot—of whom it was read a little while ago: "that we shall judge angels"—he dashes it for this reason, that he did not stretch out his hand to Jesus, so that, being grasped by him, he might not dash it. For when anyone, trusting in his own strength, does not call upon the protection of Jesus, he dashes his foot and falls. And you too, O devil, fell for this reason "like lightning from heaven," because you were unwilling to believe in Jesus Christ the Son of God. But that you may know that you have interpreted wrongly, and that what follows is to be understood not of Christ but of the saints, listen. "From ruin and the noonday demon" God delivers not Jesus Christ, but the saints. Read the ninetieth Psalm, whose beginning is: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven," and you will find that these things befit rather a just man than the Son of God: "a thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you; nevertheless with your eyes you shall behold, and you shall look upon the requital of sinners," and the rest, interpreting it of the person of the just. But even thus, perversely taking up the testimonies so as to assert that the things which were said of the just are to be understood of the Savior, the devil is silent and passes over the little verses which are written against himself. For when he had said: "he has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone," he was silent about that which follows: "you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample down the lion and the dragon." Why are you silent about these things, O devil, unless because you are the "basilisk," you are the little king of all serpents, having more harmful poisons than the rest, who slay someone the moment you see him? You know too that there is another opposing power, an associate of yours, which is called the "asp" and is made subject to the just man, and for that reason you keep silent about all these things. You are the "dragon," you are the "lion," of whom it is written: "you shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample down the lion and the dragon." But though you be silent, we who read the Scriptures more rightly know that we have the power of trampling upon you and that this dominion has been given to us—for I speak not only in the Old Testament, as is now sung in the Psalm, but also in the New, the Savior saying: "behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you." Let us take up arms, strengthened by so great a power, and let us do all things, so that through our manner of life we may trample down the lion and the dragon. Furthermore, that you may know how "the lion is trampled down" and "the dragon crushed," read Paul's epistle, in which he asserts that the Son of God is trampled upon by the sinner. As therefore he who is a sinner tramples upon the Son of God, so on the contrary he who is just "tramples upon the lion and the dragon," and tramples down "all the power of the enemy" in the name of Jesus Christ: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 31

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And when the devil deceitfully proposed this and, under the show of glory, was striving after something else, the Savior said: "It is written: you shall not tempt the Lord your God."
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 31

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But John, who had commenced his Gospel from God, saying, In the beginning was the Word, did not describe the temptation of the Lord, because God can not be tempted, of whom he wrote. But because in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke the human generations are given, and in Mark it is man who is tempted, therefore Matthew, Luke, and Mark have described the temptation of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But John, who had commenced his Gospel from God, saying, In the beginning was the Word, did not describe the temptation of the Lord, because God can not be tempted, of whom he wrote. But because in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke the human generations are given, and in Mark it is man who is tempted, therefore Matthew, Luke, and Mark have described the temptation of the Lord.

The Lord having overcome the tempter, power was added to Him, i. e. as far as regards the manifestation of it. Hence it is said, And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: First indeed: "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the desert for forty days". When he was being tempted by the devil, and because he was still to contend against him, once and again "Spirit" is set down without any addition. But when he had overcome by his fighting the three temptations which Scripture records, see what is placed concerning the Spirit pointedly and carefully. "Jesus", it says, "returned in the power of the Spirit". "Power" is added, because he had trampled upon the dragon and had conquered the tempter in close combat. "Jesus" therefore "returned in the power of the Spirit into the land of Galilee, and the report went out concerning him through all the surrounding region."
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But you must not think that they only were happy, and that you are deprived of Christ's teaching. For now also throughout the world He teaches through His instruments, and is now more glorified by all men, than at that time when those only in one province were gathered together.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And he himself taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all. When you read: "he taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all", beware lest you judge those men alone blessed and think yourself deprived of the teaching. If the things that are written are true, not only then in the assemblies of the Jews, but also today in this assembly the Lord speaks: and not only in this one, but also in another gathering and in the whole world Jesus teaches, seeking instruments through which he may teach. Pray that he may find me too composed and fit for singing! For just as almighty God seeks prophets at that time when mortals have need of prophecy, and finds, for example, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, so Jesus seeks instruments through which he may teach his word, or instruct the peoples in the synagogues, and "be glorified by all". Now Jesus is "glorified by all" more than at that time, when he was known only in a single province.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then "he came into Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and having entered according to his custom into the synagogue on the sabbath day, he stood up to read; and the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him; and unrolling the book he found the place where it was written: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; wherefore he has anointed me". Not by chance did he unroll the book and find the chapter prophesying about himself as the reading, but this too was of the providence of God. For just as it is written: "A sparrow does not fall into the snare without the will of the Father", and because "the hairs of the head" of the apostles "are all numbered", so perhaps this also — that the book of Isaiah especially was found, and the reading not another, but this one, which spoke the mystery of Christ: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; wherefore he has anointed me" — for it is Christ who recounts these things — is not to be thought to have happened as it pleased and by chance, but by the providence and disposition of God.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He opens not the book by chance, and finds a chapter containing a prophecy of Himself, but by the providence of God. Hence it follows, And when he had opened the book, he found the place, &c. (Is. 61:1.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
By the poor He means the Gentile nations, for they were poor, possessing nothing at all, having neither God, nor Law, nor Prophets, nor justice, and the other virtues.

For what had been so shattered and dashed about as man, who was set at liberty by Jesus and healed?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us therefore contemplate what those things are which he spoke in the prophet and afterward sounds forth about himself in the synagogue. "He sent me", it says, "to evangelize the poor". The "poor" signifies the nations; for these were "poor", possessing nothing at all, not God, not the law, not the prophets, not justice and the remaining virtues. For which cause God sent him to announce to the poor: "to preach release to the captives". Captives we were, whom for so many years Satan had bound, holding us captive and subject to himself. Jesus came "to preach release to the captives and to the blind, that they might see"; for indeed by the word and preaching of his teaching the blind see. Let the preaching therefore be understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (in common), not only over the captives, but also over the blind. "To send forth the broken into liberty". What was ever so broken and crushed as man, who was released and healed by Jesus?
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But all these things were mentioned first, in order that after the recovery of sight from blindness, after deliverance from captivity, after being healed of divers wounds, we might come to the acceptable year of the Lord. As it follows, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Some say that, according to the simple meaning of the word, the Saviour preached the Gospel throughout Judæa in one year, and that this is what is meant by preaching the acceptable year of the Lord. Or, the acceptable year of the Lord is the whole time of the Church, during which while present in the body, it is absent from the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "To preach the acceptable year of the Lord". According to the simple understanding they say that the Savior preached the Gospel in Judea for one year, and that this is what is said: "to preach the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution", unless perhaps the divine word signifies something of a mystery in the preaching of the year of the Lord. For there are to be other days, not such as we now discern in the world, and other months, and a different order of the Kalends. Just therefore as those are other, so also the year of the Lord to come is pleasing. But all these things have been foretold, that after sight from blindness, after liberty from chains, after health from diverse wounds, we may come to the "acceptable year of the Lord".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And now also if we will, our eyes can look upon the Saviour. For when you direct your whole heart to wisdom, truth, and the contemplation of the only-begotten Son of God, your eyes behold Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when Jesus had read these things, rolling up "the book he gave it to the minister and sat down, and the eyes of all in the synagogue were attending upon him". And now, if you will, in this synagogue and gathering your eyes can attend upon the Savior. For when you have directed the principal gaze of your heart to wisdom and truth and to contemplating the Only-begotten of God, your eyes behold Jesus. Blessed congregation, of which Scripture testifies that "the eyes of all were attending upon him"! How I would wish that this gathering should have a like testimony, that the eyes of all — both of catechumens and of the faithful, both of women and of men and of infants — not the eyes of the body, but of the soul, should look upon Jesus! For when you shall have looked back to him, from his light and his gaze your faces will be brighter, and you will be able to say: "the light of your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord": to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 32

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As far as Luke's account is concerned, Jesus had not yet stayed in Capernaum, nor is he described as having done any sign there — indeed, in a place where he had not been. But before he came to Capernaum, it is signified that he had been in his own homeland, that is, in Nazareth, and he speaks to his fellow citizens: "You will surely say to me this parable: Physician, heal yourself. Whatever we have heard done in Capernaum, do here also in your own homeland". From this I think that something of a mystery lies hidden in the present passage, and that Nazareth went before as a type of the Jews, Capernaum as a type of the Gentiles. And so Jesus, knowing that he would have no honor in his own homeland — neither he himself, nor the prophets, nor the apostles — was unwilling to preach there, but preached among the Gentiles, lest it be said to him by the men of his own homeland: "You will surely say to me this parable: Physician, heal yourself". For there will be a time when the people of the Jews will say: "Whatever we have heard done in Capernaum" — the signs and portents among the Gentiles — "do also among us in your own homeland"; what you have shown to the whole world, show to us also; preach your word to your people Israel, that at least, "when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel may be saved".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 33

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As far as Luke's narrative is concerned, our Lord is not yet said to have worked any miracle in Capernaum. For before He came to Capernaum, He is said to have lived at Nazareth. I cannot but think therefore that in these words, "whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum," there lies a mystery concealed, and that Nazareth is a type of the Jews, Capernaum of the Gentiles. For the time will come when the people of Israel shall say, "The things which thou hast shown to the whole world, show also to us." Preach thy word to the people of Israel, that then at least, when the fulness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel may be saved. Our Saviour seems to me to have well answered, No prophet is accepted in his own country, but rather according to the type than the letter; though neither was Jeremiah accepted in Anathoth his country, nor the rest of the Prophets. But it seems rather to be meant that we should say, that the people of the circumcision were the countrymen of all the Prophets. And the Gentiles indeed accepted the prophecy of Jesus Christ, esteeming Moses and the Prophets who preached of Christ, far higher than they who would not from these receive Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For this reason it seems to me that the Savior answered the Nazarenes who questioned him consequently and in due order: "no prophet is accepted in his own homeland". And I think that what is said is more true according to the sacred meaning than according to the letter. Granted that Jeremiah too was not accepted in Anathoth his homeland, and Isaiah, whatever his homeland was, and the rest of the prophets; but it seems to me better to understand it thus, that we should say the homeland of all the prophets was the people of the circumcision, and that this people did not receive the prophets and their prophecies, whereas the nations, which had been far from the prophets and had no knowledge of them, received the prophecy of Jesus Christ. "No prophet" therefore "is accepted in his own homeland", that is, among the people of the Jews. But we, who were strangers to the covenant and foreigners to the promises, have received the prophets with our whole heart, and we "have Moses and the prophets" preaching about Christ more than they do, who, from the fact that they did not receive Jesus, did not receive either those who announced concerning him.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 33

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For when a famine came upon the people of Israel, i. e. of hearing the word of God, a prophet came to a widow, of whom it is said, For the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband; (Isa. 54:1, Gal. 4:27.) and when he had come, he multiplies her bread and her nourishment.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Hence to what he had said — "no prophet is accepted in his own homeland" — he adds another thing also: "for in truth I say to you, that there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when heaven was shut up for three years and six months". What he says is this: Elijah was a prophet and was among the people of the Jews; but when he was about to do something wonderful, although there were many widows in Israel, he left them and came "to the widow in Sarepta of Sidon", to a Gentile woman, unfolding a figure of a thing to come — that, when the people of Israel was seized "not with hunger for bread nor with thirst for water, but with hunger for hearing the word of God", he came to the widow, of whom the prophet also bears witness, saying: "many are the children of the deserted woman, more than of her who has a husband", and, when he had come, he multiplies her bread and her food. You were the widow in Sarepta of Sidon, from whose borders "the Canaanite woman comes forth" and desires that her daughter be healed and, on account of her faith, deserved to receive what she asked. "There were therefore many widows among the people of Israel, but to none of them was Elijah sent, except to the widow woman in Sarepta".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 33

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He cites also another similar example, adding, And there were many lepers in Israel at the time of Eliseus the Prophet, and none of them were cleansed but Naaman the Syrian, who indeed was not of Israel.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But he speaks also another thing pertaining to the same sense: "there were many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed, except Naaman the Syrian", who assuredly was not of Israel. Consider how up to the present day there are many lepers in "Israel according to the flesh"; see, on the contrary, those drenched with the squalor of leprosy being cleansed by the spiritual Elisha, our Lord and Savior, through the sacrament of baptism, and it being said to you: "rise and go into the Jordan and wash, and your flesh will be restored to you". Naaman rose and went, and having washed he fulfilled the mystery of baptism, "and his flesh became like the flesh of a child". Of what child? Of him who has been born in Christ Jesus "in the washing of regeneration": to whom is glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 33

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Here Luke speaks figuratively, as of a command given to a sensible being, saying, that the fever was commanded, and neglected not the work of Him who commanded it. Hence it follows: And she arose, and ministered unto them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It was ordered about sun-set, that is, when the day was gone, that they should bring them out, either because during the day they were employed about other things, or because they thought that it was not lawful to heal on the sabbath. But He healed them, as it follows, But he laid his hands upon every one of them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The phrase "lift up your eyes" occurs in many places in Scripture. By this expression, the divine Word admonishes us to exalt and lift up our thoughts. It invites us to elevate the insight that lies below in a rather sickly condition and is stooped and completely incapable of looking up. For instance, it is written in Isaiah, "Lift up your eyes on high and see. Who has made all these things known?"The Savior too, when he is about to deliver the Beatitudes, lifts up his eyes to the disciples and says "blessed" are such and such.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 13.274-77

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I beg you to remember in your entire present contest the great reward laid up in heaven for those who are persecuted and reviled for righteousness' sake. Be glad and leap for joy on account of the Son of man, just as the apostles once rejoiced when they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for his name.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: [Scripture] says that man was made in the image of God; and in him are manifestly to be discovered traces of the divine image, not by any appearance of the bodily frame, which is corruptible, but by mental wisdom, by justice, moderation, virtue, wisdom, discipline; in fine, by the whole band of virtues, which are innate in the essence of God, and which may enter into man by diligence and imitation of God; as the Lord also intimates in the Gospel, when He says, "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful; " and, "Be ye perfect, even as your Father also is perfect." From which it is clearly shown that all these virtues are perpetually in God, and that they can never approach to or depart from Him, whereas by men they are acquired only slowly, and one by one.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The good tree" is the Holy Spirit. The "bad tree" is the devil and his underlings. The person who has the Holy Spirit manifests the fruits of the Spirit, which the apostle describes when he says, "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control." The one who has the opposing power brings forth briars and thistles, the passions of dishonor.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, there came to him a woman having an alabaster jar of precious ointment and poured it upon his head as he reclined. But when his disciples saw it, they were indignant, and so forth (26:6—13).

Many indeed suppose that the four evangelists have given an account of one and the same woman, because they wrote something of this kind about a woman and all alike named an alabaster jar of ointment; but John, instead of the alabaster jar, put "a pound of ointment." But also what is said, this could have been sold and given to the poor, was said by Matthew and Mark and John; and that Christ declared that ointment to have been poured out for his burial, these too expounded; and that it happened in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, these three wrote; but John indeed said Bethany, where "they made him a supper and Martha was serving and Lazarus was one of those reclining, and Mary took a pound of ointment of pure precious nard" and so forth, from which it appears that they made a supper for him. But Luke, although he did not put Simon as a leper, nevertheless said that he was a Pharisee, who had asked Jesus "to eat with him," just as the Lord himself testifies concerning his name, saying to him there: "Simon, Simon, I have something to say to you." There seems, therefore, to be much similarity and a certain kinship concerning the woman among the four evangelists.

Yet I will say to those who think that it was one woman about whom all the evangelists wrote: Do you suppose that this woman who poured upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment, as Matthew and Mark expounded, is the same one who also "anointed his feet with myrrh," as Luke and John expounded? But it is not possible that the evangelists, in expounding about the same woman — since they were "perfected in the same understanding and in the same spirit and in the same judgment," they who were to minister the salvation of the churches — should have said things contrary to one another. But if anyone thinks that she was the one who anointed the Lord's feet with ointment in Luke and John, let him tell us whether Mary here was the very one who in Luke is written to have been "a sinner in the city," who "learning that he had reclined in the house of the Pharisee brought an alabaster jar of ointment and standing behind at his feet weeping began to wash his feet with her tears." For it is not credible that Mary whom "Jesus loved," the sister of Martha "who had chosen the better part," should be said to have been "a sinner in the city." And do you suppose that the woman who according to Matthew and Mark poured upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment is not written to have been a sinner, whereas the one who according to Luke is reported as "a sinner" did not dare to come to the head of Christ but "washed his feet with her tears" as though scarcely even worthy of his very feet, from sadness working "repentance unto stable salvation"? And the one who is in Luke weeps and sheds many tears, so as to wash the "feet" of Jesus "with her tears," whereas the one who in John is Mary is introduced neither as a sinner nor as weeping. Perhaps then someone will say that there were four women about whom the evangelists wrote; but I rather agree that there were three: one indeed about whom Matthew and Mark wrote, making no difference in their exposition in that chapter; another about whom Luke wrote; and yet another about whom John wrote, since she differs from the other women not only in the things which are written about the ointment, but because "Jesus loved" Mary and Martha — although she too is reported to have been in Bethany, just as also the woman about whom Matthew and Mark expound. There is a third difference. For Matthew indeed and Mark expound that this happened in the house of Simon the leper; but John says that "Jesus six days before the Passover came into Bethany, where Lazarus was whom Jesus had raised, and they made him a supper" — not Simon, but Mary and Martha, perhaps also Lazarus, "and Martha was serving, but Lazarus was one of those reclining." Furthermore, according to John, "six days before the Passover he came into Bethany," when also Mary and Martha "made him a supper"; but here, when also, as he reclined in the house of Simon the leper, there came to him a woman, "after two days it was to be the Passover," as was said above. It remains that someone may say: If Matthew and Mark wrote about one woman, but John about another, and Luke indeed about a third, how is it that the disciples, once rebuked by Christ in the case of one woman (as being wrongly indignant about the woman's deed), did not correct themselves, so as not to be indignant over another woman doing likewise? Therefore let him know that in Matthew and Mark the disciples are indignant out of a good intention, but in John Judas alone out of a desire to steal, whereas in Luke no one murmurs. From these things, then, and others which you yourself will be able to observe, it is certain that either the evangelists say things contrary to one another, so that some of them even lie, or (if it is impious to believe this) it is necessary to say that the evangelists did not all write about the same woman, but either about three or about four. But someone a little bolder will say: Perhaps according to the history there was some one woman who did something of this kind — suppose too a second (if you wish) and a third — yet the evangelists' chief purpose was directed toward the mysteries, and they were not much concerned to narrate according to the truth of the history, but to expound the mysteries of things which arose out of the history. For which reason they also wove in certain discourses fitting and consonant with the understandings of the mysteries.

But concerning these things, which are expounded among the four evangelists on account of the women or of the one woman (as many suppose), we have treated more carefully in expounding the Gospel according to John — those things which seemed to us, since they were similar and kindred yet as it were contrary and divergent. But now let us touch on them briefly. Reasonably, then, Luke, when he spoke of the sinful woman, introduced her weeping more abundantly, so as even to wash the feet of Jesus, and indeed not pouring on the ointment but only anointing, and not the head but the feet. But that woman, who was not accused as a sinner, did not anoint but poured out, and not upon the feet, but upon the head. But if anyone should also treat of the things written about Mary the sister of Lazarus, who likewise "anointed" the Lord's "feet," let him note for himself what is written there, that the whole "house was filled with the odor of the ointment"; which is not written of her who was said to be "a sinner," but neither about the woman of whom Matthew and Mark wrote, who was not said to have been "a sinner," is anything of this kind written, that the whole "house was filled with the odor of the ointment."

Perhaps then through the differences of these women the differences of the faithful are demonstrated, of whom some indeed pour upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment, but others anoint not the head, but the feet, while others do not pour on abundantly, but only anoint; and of those anointing, some indeed anoint with such ointment that the whole house is filled with the odor of his very divinity, while others anoint not with such indeed, yet with one likewise acceptable to Christ, since they too anoint his feet with ointment — feet which the Pharisee did not anoint even with "oil." And it was fitting that these things be done in Bethany, which is interpreted HOUSE OF OBEDIENCE, and by this woman who poured out the ointment upon the head of the Lord, not accused as "a sinner in the city," and by Mary, at whose house, when a banquet was made for Jesus, she came to him and anointed. But that the house of obedience should be understood as the Church, no one doubts. But she who in Luke was called "a sinner" was not yet worthy to be in Bethany, although she was doing penance for her sins. For she still had the less, so that afterward she might be found made in the house of obedience (as now perfected) and be called neither "a sinner" nor "weeping" and washing the Lord's "feet," but herself too pouring the ointment upon his head. But Simon too is a mystery of OBEDIENCE, since so it is interpreted, but the obedience of the letter, not of the spirit: for which reason Simon, lifted up from the letter of the law through Jesus to the spiritual law, was no longer Simon only, but was made also Peter, and in place of the Jewish edifice was held worthy of the edifice of the Church to be founded upon the rock. Jesus therefore came to be in the house of Simon indeed, of one OBEDIENT, yet a leper and still having need of cleansing from Jesus. But it was not mentioned in Luke concerning Simon that he was also a leper; I judge that he himself was a debtor of fifty denarii and had already received remission of them, because he had loved little; yet loving somewhat, "he asked him to eat with him." But there came a woman (not a sinner) according to Matthew and Mark, having an alabaster jar of precious ointment. And consider how carefully among these, who did not report a sinner, her ointment is praised as precious. But in Luke, who expounded the sinful woman, the ointment is simply named, neither precious nor "of pure nard," such that "the house" might be filled "from the odor" of it; for she could not yet have ointments of this kind, but this was a great thing, that she could anoint the Lord's feet even with "ointment." But of this woman the ointment is reported as precious, for it was not fitting that what was poured out upon the head of the Savior should be not precious.

And over the ointment indeed of the sinful woman, anointing the Lord's feet and not pouring out, neither were the disciples indignant nor did they grieve, nor did Judas say: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" But over the woman in Matthew and Mark the disciples were indignant and grieved at the loss of the ointment which was running down from his head to the rest of his body. For even if that ointment could have been sold for a great price and given to the poor, nevertheless this ought not to have been done, because it was fitting that it be poured upon the head of Christ with a holy and seemly pouring. But those who strive to understand these things according to the simple text, let them say what beauty the ointment poured upon the head of Jesus praiseworthily had according to the text, that it should be poured upon the head of such and so great a master. That ointment therefore was not worthy of the poor nor fitting (as regards its own honor) that it be divided among many, but that, remaining whole, it should be poured upon the head of Jesus only. For which reason Jesus also receives the woman who had done this, and says to the indignant disciples: "Let her be, and do not be troublesome to her, for she has worked a good work in me." And to such a degree is the praise of a good work of this kind effective, that it exhorts all of us to fill the Lord's head with fragrant and rich works, so that of us too it may be said that we have done a good work upon his head; for we always indeed have (as long as we remain in this life) the poor with us and having need of care from those who have advanced in the word and have been made rich in the wisdom of God, but they cannot suffice to have always, by days and nights, with them the Son of God, the Word of God and the Wisdom and all things, whatever our Lord the Savior is.

See also what he says: she has worked a good work in me, since he did not say concerning the sinful woman anointing his feet that "she did a good work in me." But if it is also necessary to discuss what he says, she has done it to prepare me for burial, you will compare with it what is said: "we were buried together with Christ through baptism, and we rose again together with him." Consider furthermore that concerning the woman according to Luke it is not said, amen I say to you: wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she did shall be told in memory of her, but concerning the woman according to Matthew and Mark this is written. For it was just, not concerning her who had anointed the feet, but concerning this one who had poured the ointment upon the head of Jesus, that it should be said, wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she did shall be told in memory of her. If, then, we wish that of us too it may be said what we do to Jesus, pouring the precious ointment upon his head, let us advance from the anointing of his feet to pouring the precious ointment upon his head.

But what oil is and what ointment, and what ointment is that which serves for anointing the body of Christ and what for the head, is difficult indeed to explain. Nevertheless we shall attempt to show that which seems to us, knowing most certainly that oil everywhere in the scriptures is understood either as a work of mercy (by which the lamp of the word, being nourished, shines brightly) or as doctrine (by whose constant hearing the word of faith which is kindled in us is nourished and shines more brightly). Just as, then, generally everything with which one is anointed is called oil, but of oil one kind is ointment another kind is not ointment, likewise of ointment one kind is a middling ointment, another precious: so every just act is called a good work, but of a good work one kind is what we do for the sake of men or according to men, and another what is for the sake of God and according to God. Likewise this very thing, which we do for the sake of God, one kind is what serves the use of men, and another what does not serve the use of men but only the glory of God. For instance, someone does good to a man, moved by natural justice, not for the sake of God (as sometimes the Gentiles too did and as many men do), that work is common oil of no great odor, and yet it too is acceptable to God; as Daniel signifies, saying to Nebuchadnezzar, who did not know God: hear my counsel, O king, and redeem your sins with almsgivings. Something of this kind Peter too says in Clement, that the good works which are done by unbelievers in this world profit them, but not also in that world for the attaining of eternal life; and fittingly, because they too do not do them for the sake of God, but for the sake of human nature itself. But those who do them for the sake of God, that is, the faithful, it profits them not only in this world, but also in that, and rather in that.

But what the faithful do for the sake of God, this is the ointment of good odor. But this very work of the faithful for the sake of God, which is ointment, one kind is done for the benefit of men — for instance almsgivings, visitations of the sick, receptions of strangers, humility, meekness, forbearance, and other things of this kind which profit men. He who does these things toward Christians anoints the Lord's feet with ointment, because they are the Lord's feet, with which he always walks. This the penitent are especially wont to do for the remission of their sins, and that is the work which is called ointment, fragrant indeed, but not the highest. But he who is zealous for chastity, perseveres in fastings and prayers, has patience in adversities like Job, in temptations does not fear to confess the truth of God (all which things profit other men nothing, but serve only the glory of God), this is the ointment which anoints both the head of the Lord, Christ, and from there runs through the whole body of Christ, that is, through the whole Church; and this is the ointment exceedingly precious from whose odor the whole house is filled, that is, the Church of Christ; and this is the work proper not to the penitent, but to the perfect saints. Or certainly: the doctrine which is necessary to men, through which are nourished souls poor in spiritual goods or perhaps also weak in sins, this is the middling ointment with which the Lord's feet are anointed; but the knowledge of the true faith which pertains to God alone is the precious ointment with which is anointed the head of Christ, God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The officer does not have the power to be able to remit to me even a "farthing" and the smallest portion; there is one who can remit to debtors who have nothing wherewith to pay. "There approached him", he says, "one who owed five hundred denarii, and another fifty; and since they had nothing wherewith to pay, he forgave them both". He who forgave was the master; but this one, who is the officer, is not the master, but is appointed by the master to exact the debts. You were not worthy that five hundred or fifty denarii should be forgiven you, nor did you deserve to hear: "your offenses are forgiven you".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is that first one, by which we are baptized "unto the remission of sins". The second remission is in the suffering of martyrdom. The third is that which is given through almsgiving; for the Savior says: "but nevertheless give the things that you have, and behold, all things are clean to you". The fourth remission of sins comes to us through this, that we too remit sins to our brothers; for thus the Lord and Savior himself says that: "if you remit to your brothers from the heart their sins, your Father too will remit to you your sins. But if you do not remit to your brothers from the heart, neither will your Father remit to you", and just as he taught us to say in the prayer: "remit to us our debts, as we too remit to our debtors". The fifth remission of sins is when "someone turns a sinner from the error of his way". For thus the divine Scripture says that "he who causes a sinner to be turned from the error of his way saves a soul from death, and covers a multitude of sins". A sixth remission too comes about through the abundance of love, as the Lord himself also says: "Amen, I say to you, her many sins are remitted to her, because she loved much", and the Apostle says: "because love covers a multitude of sins". There is still a seventh also, though hard and laborious — the remission of sins through penance, when the sinner washes "his bed with tears" and his "tears" become to him "bread day and night", when he is not ashamed to make known his sin to the priest of the Lord and to seek the remedy, according to him who says: "I said: I will declare against myself my injustice to the Lord, and you remitted the impiety of my heart".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And therefore it is significantly said, When much people were gathered together, and were come to him out of every city. For not many but few there are who walk the strait road, and find the way which leadeth to life. Hence Matthew says, that He taught without the house by parables, but within the house explained the parable to His disciples. (Matt. 13:36.)

(in Prov. 1.) Now a parable is a narration of an action as done, yet not done according to the letter, though it might have been, representing certain things by means of others which are given in the parable. An enigma is a continued story of things which are spoken of as done, and yet have not been done, nor are possible to be done, but contains a concealed meaning, as that which is mentioned in the Book of Judges, that the trees went forth to anoint a king over them. (Judges 9:8.) But it was not literally a fact as is said, A sower went out to sow, like those facts related in history, yet it might have been so.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if we indeed hear "the word" and from the hearing "immediately" our earth produces grass, and this grass, before it comes to maturity or to fruit, "withers," our earth will be called "rocky." But if the things that are said rest on deeper roots in our heart, so that they both "bear fruit" of works and have in themselves the seeds of future ones, then truly the earth of each one of us bears fruit according to its power, one "a hundredfold," another "sixtyfold," another "thirtyfold." But we have thought it necessary to give this warning also, that our fruit nowhere have "tares," that is, nowhere have "darnel," so that it may not be "along the way," but may be sown in the very way, in that which says: "I am the way," so that "the birds of heaven" may not eat our fruits nor our vineyard.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For he who "went out to sow" "sows the word" over every place, but hear the Lord himself saying what the seed of God is wont to suffer: "some," he says, "fell by the wayside, and the birds of heaven come and snatch it away." Which, interpreting in what follows, he himself says: "but those who were sown by the wayside are they who hear the word of God and receive it with joy; but the devil comes and takes away from their heart what was sown." So therefore these too now come to the seed of God and wish to "take it away from the heart of those in whom it was sown," because they find them placed in the valleys and pursuing all that is lowest. For they belong to those who receive the word of God humbly and unworthily and, so to speak, with a Jewish understanding, and therefore the demons are able to "snatch it away from their heart." But he who ascends from the humility of the letter to the heights of the spirit, and, fleeing carnal understanding, pursues among the loftier things those which are of the Spirit of God — from him neither the Midianites nor the Amalekites can snatch anything.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But he who would adapt his lantern to the more perfect disciples of Christ, must persuade us by those things which were spoken of John, for he was a burning and a shining light. (John 5:35.) It becomes not him then who lights the light of reason in his soul to hide it under a bed where men sleep, nor under any vessel, for he who does this provides not for those who enter the house for whom the candle is prepared, but they must set it upon a candlestick, that is, the whole Church.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Scripture does not say this about a tangible lamp but about a comprehensible one. One does not "light" the lamp and conceal it "with a vessel" or put it "under a bed, but on the lamp stand" within himself. The vessels of the house are the powers of the soul. The bed is the body. "Those who go in" are those who hear the teacher.…He calls the holy church a "lamp stand." By its proclamation, the Word of God gives light to all who are in this world and illuminates those in the house with the rays of the truth, filling the minds of all with divine knowledge.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The outer man has a sense of touch; and the inner man has it too. With such a touch the woman with the flow of blood touched the edge of Jesus' garment. She truly touched Him, as follows from His question: "Who touched me?" Yet a moment before, Peter says: "The crowd presses upon You, and You say, who touched Me?" He imagines that the one who touched did so fleshly, not spiritually. Those who surrounded Jesus did not touch Him, since they did not touch Him with faith. Only the woman, who had a kind of touch-by-grace, touched Jesus, and through it was healed. And after she touched Him, power went out from Jesus at her touch-by-grace. Therefore He says: "Who touched me? For I felt power going out from me."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do you wish me to show you "what" is "the soul which touched the unclean thing" and was made unclean, and again touched the clean thing and was made clean? She "who suffered an issue of blood and spent all her substance on physicians and could gain nothing" was brought down to this through the uncleanness of sin. For she had touched sin, and for that reason had received the "scourge" of the flesh. But after, full of faith, "she touched the fringe of Jesus, the flow of her blood stood still", and suddenly she was made clean who before had lived unclean for so long a time. And just as, when she had touched the Lord and Savior, he himself said: "who touched me?
