For I felt power go out from me" — that power, without doubt, which had healed the woman and made her clean — so it is to be understood that, if anyone touches sin, there goes out from that very sin a certain malignant power, which makes him who has touched it unclean; and this is truly to have touched the unclean thing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the same cure which the woman obtained by touching Him, our Saviour confirmed by His word; as it follows, And he said unto her, Thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, that is, Be released from thy scourge. And indeed He first heals her soul by faith, then truly her body.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Matt. tom. 12.) A man also denies himself when by a sufficient alteration of manners or a good conversation he changes a life of habitual wickedness. He who has long lived in lasciviousness, abandons his lustful self when he becomes chaste, and in like manner a forsaking of any crimes is a denial of one's self.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (ut sup.) He assigns the cause of this when He adds, For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; that is, whosoever will according to the present life keep his own soul fixed on things of sense, the same shall lose it, never reaching to the bounds of happiness. But on the other hand He adds, but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake, shall save it. That is, whosoever forsakes the things of sense looking upon truth, and exposes himself to death, as it were losing his life for Christ, shall the rather save it. If then it is a blessed thing to save our life, (with regard to that safety which is in God,) there must be also a certain good surrender of life which is made by looking upon Christ. It seems also to me from resemblance to that denying of one's self which has been before spoken of, that it becomes us to lose a certain sinful life of ours, to take up that which is saved by virtue.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do you wish to see that Moses is always with Jesus, that is, the law with the gospels? Let the gospel teach you that, when Jesus "had been transfigured" into glory, also "Moses and Elijah appeared" together with him in glory, so that you may know that the law and the prophets and the gospels always come into one and remain in one glory. Finally Peter too, when he wished to make "three tabernacles" for them, is marked for his lack of skill, as one "who knew not what he said". For to the law and the prophets and the gospel there is not three tabernacles, but one, which is the church of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Matt. tom. 12.) Now His disciples being unable to bear this, fell down, humbled under the mighty hand of God, greatly afraid since they knew what was said to Moses, No man shall see my face, and lice. Hence it follows, And they feared as they entered into the cloud.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (ubi sup.) Now Jesus wishes not those things which relate to His glory to be spoken of before His passion. Hence it follows, And they kept it close. For men would have been offended, especially the multitude, if they saw Him crucified Who had been so glorified.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Matt. tom. 13.) But it is not clearly expressed by whom He is to be delivered, for one says, that He is to be delivered up by Judas, another by the devil; but Paul says, that God the Father delivered Him up for us all; (Rom. 8:32.) but Judas, as he delivered Him up for money, did it traitorously, the Father for His mercies' sake.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For these things and things like these ought especially to be held in mind by those who put "their hand", that is, their action, "to the plow" of teaching the doctrine of Christ, so that, knowing to whom woe is laid up (not on account of anything else except that they do not teach), they may not turn "back" after they have once put "their hand to the plow" that plows the souls of men, so that after this they may also receive the seeds of the word.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But you also yourself, O hearer, be the farmer of your own soul; use this plow which Shamgar uses. But when "you have put your hand to the plow", do not "look back" — that is, after "you have taken up your cross and followed Christ", after you have renounced the world and the things which are in the world, do not "look back", do not seek again those things which "for the sake of Christ you had counted as dung", because, if you always keep your "hand upon this plow", so that you may confidently say: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world", then, as you say these things, "there shall fall at your right hand ten thousand, and at your left hand a thousand, but unto you they shall not come near".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Likewise also the twelve were reckoned by two and two, as Matthew shows in his enumeration of them. (Matt. 10:2.) For that two should be joined in service, seems from the word of God to be an ancient custom. For God led Israel out of Egypt by the hands of Moses and Aaron. Joshua and Caleb also, united together, appeased the people who had been provoked by the twelve spies. (Numb. 13, 14. Ex. 12.) Hence it is said, A brother assisted by a brother is as a fortified city. (Prov. 18:19. Vulg.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By wiping off the dust of their feet against them, they in some sort say, The dust of your sins shall deservedly come upon you. And mark that the cities which receive not the Apostles and sound doctrine have streets, according to Matthew, Broad is the way which leadeth to destruction. (Matt. 7:13.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For a feeling of deficiency is the preparation for coming perfection. For whoever by the presence of the apparent good perceives not that he is destitute of the true good, is deprived of the true good.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (non occ.) He wishes to reveal as the Word, not without the exercise of reason; and as Justice, who knoweth rightly both the times for revealing, and the measures of revelation; but He reveals by removing the opposing veil from the heart, (2 Cor. 3:15) and the darkness which He has made His secret place. (Ps. 18:11.) But since upon this men who are of another opinion think to build up their impious doctrine, that in truth the Father of Jesus was sent down to the ancient saints, we must tell them that the words, To whomsoever the Son will reveal him, not only refer to the future time, after our Saviour uttered this, but also to the past time. But if they will not take this word reveal for what is past, they must be told, that it is not the same thing to know and to believe. To one is given by the Spirit the word of knowledge; to another faith by the same Spirit. (1 Cor. 12:8, 9.) There were then those who believed, but did not know.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Cant. 1:2.) But why does he say that many prophets desired, and not all? Because it is said of Abraham, That he saw the day of Christ and was glad, (John 8:56.) which sight not many, but few attained to; but there were other prophets and just men not so great as to reach to Abraham's vision, and the experience of the Apostles, who, He says, saw not, but desired to see.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Although there are many precepts in the law, the Savior set down in the Gospel only these, which by a kind of summary would lead the obedient to eternal life. For he has regard to that which the doctor of the law had asked him, saying: "Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?" — the reading which according to Luke has today been recited to you. He answered: "What is written in the law? how do you read? You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength, and with your whole mind; and your neighbor as yourself". And then he said: "You have answered well; do this, and you shall live". There is no doubt that it is everlasting life about which both the doctor of the law had inquired and the Savior's discourse had treated. And at the same time we are plainly taught that it is commanded in the law that we should love God. In Deuteronomy he says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God", and: "You shall love the Lord your God with your whole mind" and the rest, and "your neighbor as yourself". And the Savior bore witness concerning these things, saying: "On these two commandments the whole law hangs, and the prophets".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From these words it is undoubtingly gathered, that the life which is preached according to God the Creator of the world, and the Scriptures given by Him, is life everlasting. For the Lord Himself bears testimony to the passage from Deuteronomy, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God; (Deut. 6:5.) and from Leviticus, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. (Lev. 19:18.) But these things were spoken against the followers of Valentinus, Basil, and Marcion. For what else did he wish us to do in seeking eternal life, but what is contained in the Law and the Prophets?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when the doctor of the law "wished to justify himself" and to show that no one was neighbor to him, and said: "Who is my neighbor?", the Lord introduced a parable whose beginning is: "A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho", and the rest.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Although these things are said reasonably and beautifully, it is nevertheless not to be supposed that they pertain to every man. For not every man "goes down from Jerusalem to Jericho", nor do all on that account tarry in the present age, even though he who "was sent because of the lost sheep" — "of the house of Israel" — came. The man, therefore, who "went down from Jerusalem to Jericho", because he himself willed to go down, for that reason "fell among robbers". But the robbers are none other than those of whom the Savior says: "all who came before me were thieves and robbers". Yet he fell not among thieves, but among "robbers" much more wicked than thieves, who, when he was going down "from Jerusalem" and had fallen among them, "stripped him and laid blows upon him". What are the blows, what the wounds, by which the man was wounded? Vices and sins. Then, because the robbers who had stripped him and wounded him do not sit by the naked man, but, blows having again been laid on, abandon him, for this reason it is written: "stripping him and laying on wounds, they departed and left him" not dead, but "half-dead".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: A certain one of the elders, wishing to interpret the parable, used to say that the man who went down is Adam, Jerusalem paradise, Jericho the world, the robbers the hostile powers, the priest the law, the Levite the prophets, the Samaritan Christ, the wounds disobedience, the beast the body of the Lord, the pandochium — that is, the inn, which receives all who wish to enter — he interpreted to be the Church. Further, the two denarii are to be understood as the Father and the Son, and the innkeeper as the president of the Church, to whom its stewardship has been entrusted. And as for the fact that the Samaritan promises he will return, he figured this according to the Savior's second coming.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And it came to pass that on the same road there went down first a "priest", then a "Levite", who had perhaps done certain good things to other men, yet not to this one who had gone down "from Jerusalem to Jericho". For the "priest" saw him — the law, I think — the "Levite" saw him — the prophetic word, as I suppose — and when they had seen him, they passed by and left him.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For providence was keeping the half-dead man for him who was stronger than the law and the prophets, namely the Samaritan, which is interpreted "guardian". This is he who "neither slumbers nor sleeps, keeping Israel". On behalf of the half-dead man this Samaritan set out, not going down "from Jerusalem to Jericho" as the priest and the Levite went down; or if he did go down, he went down for this reason, that he might save and guard the one about to die — the Samaritan to whom the Jews said: "You are a Samaritan and have a demon", and who, when he had denied that he had a demon, would not deny that he was a "Samaritan"; for he knew that he was a "guardian". And so when he had come to the half-dead man and had seen him wallowing in his own blood, he took pity and approached him, that he might become his neighbor.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He "bound up the wounds, poured in oil mixed with wine", and did not say what is read in the prophet: "there is no salve to lay on, nor oil, nor bandages". This is the "Samaritan" of whose care and aid all who are ill have need — of whose aid especially that man had need who, going down "from Jerusalem", "had fallen among robbers" and, wounded by them, had been left half-alive. And that you may know that it was according to the providence of God that this Samaritan went down, so that he might heal him who "had fallen among robbers", you will be plainly taught from this: that he had bandages with him, oil with him, wine with him — which indeed I think the Samaritan carried with him not on account of this one half-dead man alone, but also on account of others who for various causes had been wounded and were in need of bandages and oil and wine. He had "oil", of which it is written: "that he may make the face cheerful with oil" — without doubt the face of him who had been healed. He heals with "oil", that the swellings of the wounds might be soothed, but also cleanses the wounds with "wine", mixing in something of sharpness, and him who had been wounded he "set upon his own beast", that is, upon his own body, in accordance with the fact that he deigned to take up manhood. This Samaritan "bears our sins" and grieves for us, bears the half-dead man, brings him into the "pandochium", that is, into the Church, which receives all and denies its aid to none, to which Jesus calls all, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you". And after he had brought him in, he does not at once withdraw, but for one day he perseveres in the inn with the half-dead man and tends his wounds not only in the day but also in the night, bestowing upon him the remainder of his care and diligence.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or the two pence seem to me to be the knowledge of the sacrament, in what manner the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, which is given as a reward by the Angel to the Church that she may take more diligent care of the man entrusted to her whom in the shortness of the time He Himself had also cured. And it is promised that whatever she should spend on the cure of the half dead man, should be restored to her again, And whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again I will repay thee.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And when he wished to set out in the morning, from his tested silver, from his tested money, he "takes out two denarii" and pays the innkeeper — without doubt the angel of the Church — whom he charges to tend him carefully and to bring him through to health, the one whom, because of the shortness of time, he himself also had tended. The "two denarii" seem to me to be the knowledge of the Father and the Son and the understanding of the mystery — how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father — which is given as a kind of wage to the angel, that he may more diligently tend the man commended to him; and it is promised to him that whatever of his own he shall have spent for the healing of the half-dead man is to be repaid forthwith.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And he teaches that he who was going down was neighbor to no one except to him who was willing to keep the precepts and to prepare himself, so as to be neighbor to every man who is in need of aid. For this is what is set down at the end after the parable: "Which of these three seems to you to be neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?" For neither the priest nor the Levite was his neighbor, but, as the doctor of the law himself also answered, "he who did mercy" was his neighbor. Whence it is also said by the Savior: "Go, and you also do likewise".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Truly this "guardian" of souls is nearer than the law and the prophets — he "who did mercy to him who had fallen among robbers" — and he appeared as his "neighbor" not so much by word as by deed. Since, therefore, it is possible, according to that which is said: "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ", for us to imitate Christ and to have mercy on those who "have fallen among robbers", to approach them, to bind up their wounds, to pour in oil and wine, to set them upon our own beast and to bear their burdens — for this reason the Son of God, exhorting us to such things, speaks not so much to the doctor of the law as to us all also: "Go, and you also do likewise". And if we shall do likewise, we shall attain eternal life in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 34

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The name of which village Luke indeed here omits, but John mentions, calling it Bethany. (John 11.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And that he might point out the kind of teaching, the disciple proceeds, as John also taught his disciples. Of whom in truth thou hast told us, that among them that are born of women there had arisen none greater than he. And because thou hast commanded us to seek things that are great and eternal, whence shall we arrive at the knowledge of these but from Thee, our God and Saviour?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I think that one of Jesus' disciples was conscious in himself of human weakness, which falls short of knowing how we ought to pray.… Are we then to conclude that a man who was brought up in the instruction of the law, who heard the words of the prophets and did not fail to attend the synagogue, did not know how to pray until he saw the Lord praying "in a certain place"? It would certainly be foolish to say this. The disciple prayed according to the customs of the Jews, but he saw that he needed better knowledge about the subject of prayer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or, because the name of God is given by idolaters, and those who are in error, to idols and creatures, it has not as yet been so made holy, as to be separated from those things from which it ought to be. He teaches us therefore to pray that the name of God may be appropriated to the only true God; to whom alone belongs what follows, Thy kingdom come, to the end that may be put down all the rule, authority, and power, and kingdom of the world, together with sin which reigns in our mortal bodies.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Perhaps we should … pray … only to the God and Father of all, to whom even our Savior himself prayed, as we have explained, and to whom he taught us to pray. When he heard "teach us to pray," he did not teach us to pray to himself but to the Father by saying "Our Father in heaven and so forth." …When the saints give thanks to God in their prayers, they acknowledge through Christ Jesus the favors he has done. If it is true that one who is scrupulous about prayer should not pray to someone else who prays but rather to the Father whom our Lord Jesus taught us to address in prayers, it is especially true that no prayer should be addressed to the Father without him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Luke says, "Forgive us our sins," since sins are associated with our debts if we have not paid them. He says the same thing as Matthew but does not seem to leave room for the person who wishes to forgive debtors only if they repent. He says that our Savior has given the law that we should add to our prayer, "For we ourselves forgive every one who is indebted to us." Surely we all have authority to forgive sins against ourselves. This is clear from "as we forgive our debtors" and from "for we ourselves forgive every one who is indebted to us." The person inspired by Jesus and known by his fruits, as the apostles were, has received the Holy Spirit. He has become spiritual by being led by the Spirit to do everything by reason as a child of God. This person forgives whatever God forgives and retains sins that cannot be healed, serving God as the prophets by not speaking his own words but those of the divine will. He also serves God who alone has authority to forgive.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do you wish us to bring forth for you examples of a similar mystery from the gospels too? Let us recall the words of the Lord, where he says that "at midnight" a certain man came to his friend, knocking at his door, and said: "friend, lend me three loaves, since a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him". In which, to touch briefly upon it, the night is this time of life, and the three loaves are: one which is cooked "in the oven", another "in the frying-pan", the third "on the gridiron".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But some one may seek to know, how it comes that they who pray are not heard? To which we must answer, that whose sets about seeking in the right way, omitting none of those things which avail to the obtaining of our requests, shall really receive what he has prayed to be given him. But if a man turns away from the object of a right petition, and asks not as it becomes him, he does not ask. And therefore it is, that when he does not receive, as is here promised, there is no falsehood. For so also when a master says, "Whoever will come to me, he shall receive the gift of instruction;" we understand it to imply a person going in real earnest to a master, that he may zealously and diligently devote himself to his teaching. Hence too James says, Ye ask and receive not, because ye ask amiss, (James 4:3.) namely, for the sake of vain pleasures. But some one will say, Nay, when men ask to obtain divine knowledge, and to recover their virtue they do not obtain? To which we must answer, that they sought not to receive the good things for themselves, but that thereby they might reap praise.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who believes that the mouth of Jesus cannot lie would hesitate a moment to be persuaded to pray, when he says, "Ask, and it will be given you … for everyone who asks, receives." When we ask for the living bread, the good Father certainly gives him (and not the stone that his adversary wishes to give to Jesus and his disciples for food) to those who have received the Spirit of sonship from the Father. The Father gives a good gift, raining it down from heaven for those who ask him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Consider then this, if the bread be not indeed the food of the soul in knowledge, without which it can not be saved, as, for example, the well planned rule of a just life. But the fish is the love of instruction, as to know the constitution of the world, and the effects of the elements, and whatever else besides wisdom treats of. Therefore God does not in the place of bread offer a stone, which the devil wished Christ to eat, nor in the place of a fish does He give a serpent, which the Ethiopians eat who are unworthy to eat fishes. Nor generally in the place of what is nourishing does he give what is not eatable and injurious, which relates to the scorpion and egg.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For see what is written: "When" it says "an unclean spirit has gone out from a man, it goes through dry places, seeking rest, and finds none. And then it says: I will return into my house, whence I came out. And if, coming, it finds it empty, swept, and adorned, it goes and brings with it seven other spirits worse than itself, and entering into that house it dwells therein. And the last state of that man shall be worse than the first". If we heed these things, how can we give even in a small matter a place to negligence? For an unclean spirit dwelt in us before we believed, before we came to Christ, when still, as I said above, our soul was fornicating away from God and was with its lovers, the demons. But after she said: "I will return to my former husband" and came to Christ, who from the beginning "created her according to his own image", the adulterous spirit necessarily gave place when it saw the lawful husband. We have been received, then, by Christ, and our house has been "cleansed" from former sins and "adorned" with the ornaments of the sacraments of the faithful, which those who have been initiated know. But this house does not at once merit to have Christ as its inhabitant, unless its life and conduct be so holy, so pure and undefiled, that it may merit to be a "temple of God". For it must be no longer a house, but a temple, in which God may dwell. If, then, it neglect the grace received and entangle itself in worldly affairs, straightway that unclean spirit returns and claims for itself the empty house. And, that it may not be able to be expelled again, it brings "with it seven other spirits worse", and "the last state of a man of this kind becomes worse than the first", because it had been more tolerable for a soul that once played the harlot not to have returned to its former husband than, having returned after the confession of the husband, to become an adulteress again.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That is, to those who are of Israel, whom he saw possessing nothing divine in them, but desolate, and vacant for him to take up his abode there; and so it follows, And when he came, he findeth it swept and garnished.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For He gives the name of the eye especially to our understanding, but the whole soul, although not corporeal, He metaphorically calls the body. For the whole soul is enlightened by the understanding.

For the understanding from its very beginning desires only singleness, containing no dissimulation, or guile, or division in itself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That is, If thy material body, when the light of a candle shines upon it, is made full of light, so that not one of thy members is any longer in darkness; much more when thou sinnest not, shall thy whole spiritual body be so full of light, that its brightness may be compared to the shining of a candle, while the light which was in the body, and which used to be darkness, is directed whithersoever the understanding may command.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Next let us see whether, beyond those we have spoken of, it is possible to see also others who shut and open the kingdom of heaven. For those who have been counted worthy and fit to expound the Gospel, and who show themselves such that they can truly say "Do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?", open the kingdom of heaven before men, when they demonstrate, with all clarity and proof, the loftiness of the divine words — words which were not spoken about earthly things but about heaven and about the mind of the Lord, who came to men — so that, so far as it lies in them, they would lead "Gentiles and barbarians, wise and unwise" to the piety of Christ. But those who, through their unteachableness and unrighteousness, with much rashness gave themselves over to the profession of teaching before they had learned and come to know the truth, and who therefore, in imitation of vain Jewish fables, hand down the bodily narratives of the Scriptures and not their spiritual sense or intention, and who moreover disparage those "who have risen with Christ and seek the things that are above" in the Scriptures "and not upon the earth," nor reckon that the truth set forth in the Scriptures lies in earthly things: these, so far as it lies in them, shut the kingdom of heaven before men, shutting it by their unrighteousness and drawing to themselves those who were able — by hearing the more divine and greater teaching and the loftiness of the truth — to enter into the kingdom of heaven through the heavenly doctrines and through the deeds befitting them. To this exposition it is fitting what Luke writes: "Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves have not entered in, and you have hindered those who were entering." For those who accuse the allegorical exposition and want to teach that the divine Scripture is plain and has nothing more than the text shows, and who do not admit any more divine sense concerning circumcision or the Passover or the unleavened bread or foods and drinks or the feasts or the new moons or the sabbaths, and do not accept that the Jews then served "in the display and shadow of things to come" — these indeed are lawyers, yet they have taken away "the key of knowledge," so far as their teaching goes, that is, taking away every way of the law for understanding its ordinances; and therefore neither did they themselves enter in nor, so far as it lay in them, did they permit others to enter.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He either then says this concerning that time when God shall judge the secrets of men, or He says it because however much a man may endeavour to hide the good deeds of another by discredit, good of its own nature cannot be concealed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Notice that this commandment is not given to Jesus' servants but to his friends. "Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do." The One to fear is he "who can destroy both soul and body in hell." He alone, "after he has killed," has "power to throw into hell." He throws into hell those who fear those who kill the body and do not fear "him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into hell." We may suppose that no matter who else has the hair of his head numbered, the verse is obviously true of those who are cut off for Jesus. We will confess the Son of God before people and not before gods, that he who is confessed may confess us in turn before God and his Father, and confess in heaven the one who confessed him on earth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Literally, hereby is signified the quickness of the Divine foresight, which reaches even to the least things. But mystically, the five sparrows justly represent the spiritual senses, which have perception of high and heavenly things: beholding God, hearing the Divine voice, tasting of the bread of life, smelling the perfume of Christ's anointing, handling the Word of Life. And these being sold for two farthings, that is, being lightly esteemed by those who count as perishing whatever is of the Spirit, are not forgotten before God. But God is said to be forgetful of some because of their iniquities.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For He will be girded about His loins with righteousness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And when someone is in this state, it is possible that, even if he does not have the strength of the sun, yet he may be illumined by some slight brightness of the word which is a "lamp", while still indeed remaining amid evils, yet already having a purpose of better things and a watchfulness, so that his purpose, looking toward better things, may not be broken in upon. For, as we read in the Shepherd, no one quickly tastes full vessels, for they are not easily changed; but the half-full ones, because they are readily believed to be changed, are frequently tasted.

And see whether you can draw to such an understanding that which is written elsewhere: "but let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be you like men awaiting their lord, when he shall return"; since he who is not yet in the light and in the day of the virtues, but already offers himself to the teaching that illumines his soul, so far as is possible, is in the first place girded. And turning himself away from the outpouring of malice, he uses not yet, as it were, the clear daylight of virtue, but the lamp by which it is possible for even one who is in malice to be illumined. This one, therefore, whose lamp is thus lit, is one awaiting his lord, God the Word,

that returning he may come to him who meanwhile has had within himself the lamp and has illumined his whole mind, evidently as it were a sun. And each one according to his own progress kindles his lamp either less or more from the light of knowledge, and pours oil into it through meditation, and watching in it against sinful works, hoping through abstinence of this kind and meditation to receive even the lord into himself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And so the thief too comes at a certain watch and hour of the night and digs through the house of him whom he shall have found not keeping watch nor having a lamp lit. And upon some indeed he comes in the evening, but upon others at midnight, and upon some even at cockcrow, and there are also those upon whom he comes in the morning. And the master too comes at a certain watch and hour of the night, and perhaps the master comes to that man to whom the thief, in coming, could do nothing — namely, not being permitted to dig through the house of the one keeping watch and having a lamp lit. But to him who has his house dug through the master does not come, especially if anyone has learned what was said: "let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be yourselves like men awaiting their master", and, despising the things that were said, has given "sleep to his eyes and drowsiness to his eyelids". But to make clear the sense of this passage which has come upon us, let us use such an example: in the time of temptations or of calamities of whatever kind the thief is especially wont to come, wishing to dig through the house of the soul; but when the thief comes, the one who bears the mishaps and endures all things for the love of God, having suffered nothing from him, will straightway see the master coming to him. But whoever shall have had his house dug through by the thief in the time of his calamity will, as unworthy of the coming of his master to him, not be worthy to look upon him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And Paul, having learned from the words of the Saviour, "Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom the lord will set over his household, to give the measure of grain in due season to his fellow-servants", says, But what is further sought in stewards is that a man be found faithful. For neither does knowing suffice, nor ought the one who has come to know to speak at random, but, understanding the "giving of the measure of grain in due season" to his fellow-servants, he must see which of the fellow-servants ought to receive a greater "measure of grain" of the mysteries of God or a lesser one, and when; for if he administers the stewardship well and blamelessly, what promise has he? "Over all" he says "his possessions the master of the house will set him". But if Paul is afraid and says these things concerning himself and concerning Cephas and Apollos, how much more must the stewards among us fear, that they may be found faithful stewards.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: According to which sense our Lord and Savior too, since he is "spirit", "came to send fire upon the earth"; "spirit" according to that which is written: "but when you have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away", and: "the Lord is a spirit". But "he came to send fire" not upon heaven, but "upon the earth", as he himself shows when he says: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it already blaze?" For if "you have turned to the Lord", who is "spirit", Christ will be "spirit" to you and "he did not come to send fire upon the earth". But if you are not turned to him, but have earth and its fruits, "he came to send fire upon" your "earth".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 26

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For our "proof" extends not only as far as blows, but reaches even to the shedding of blood, because Christ also, whom we follow, poured out His blood for our redemption, that from it we might come forth washed in our own blood. For the baptism of blood alone is what renders us purer than the baptism of water rendered us. And this I do not presume of myself, but Scripture reports it, the Lord saying to His disciples: "I have a baptism to be baptized with, which you know not. And how am I pressed until it be accomplished?" You see, then, that He named the shedding of His blood a "baptism." And if in saying these things I give no offense, I fear that this baptism may be more eminent than that baptism which is handed on through water. For of that one, once received, very few are so blessed as to have been able to keep it unstained even to the end of life; but whoever has been baptized with this baptism can sin no more thereafter. And if it is not rash to venture anything in such matters, we may say that through that baptism past sins are purged, but through this one even future sins are done away. There sins are forgiven, here they are shut out.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But had it not been implanted in our nature to judge what is right, our Lord would never have said this.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Unless the power of judging what is just were implanted in us by nature, the Savior would never say: "But why do you not also judge of yourselves what is just?" But lest we wander too far afield in proving this statement — especially since much more difficult matters are appended to this chapter — let it suffice to have merely touched upon this.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: or rather let us spread the sails of our souls toward God and beg for the coming of his word, that it may interpret the parable of which it is written: "When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen I say to you: you will not come out from there until you pay back the very last mite". I see four persons set down: the adversary, the ruler, the judge, the officer. And because the evangelist Matthew seems to have said something similar in that he says: "Be well-disposed toward your adversary while you are on the way with him", I ask whether the meaning is the same or whether there is some kinship, since with Matthew one person is omitted and another is changed. Omitted is the "ruler", and in place of "officer" a "servant" is inserted, while "adversary" and "judge" are alike set down by both. So then we go "with our adversary to the ruler", and it is necessary for us, while we are still "on the way", to labor mightily so that we may be freed from him. From whom? For the word is ambiguous and can be referred both to the ruler and to the adversary: "lest perhaps he hand you over" — whether the adversary or the ruler — "to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer"; and: "you will not come out from there until you pay back the very last mite", for which Matthew says: "until you pay back the last farthing". The word "last" both retained, but they seemed to differ in that the one set down "farthing", the other "mite". There are certain more hidden matters I must touch upon, so that we may understand that the adversary is one thing, and the other three persons — that is, the ruler, the judge, the officer — are another. We read — if indeed anyone is pleased to accept a writing of this kind — of the angels of justice and of iniquity contending over the salvation and destruction of Abraham, while each band wishes to claim him for its own company. But if this displeases anyone, let him pass over to the volume that is inscribed with the title of the Shepherd, and he will find that two angels attend all men: an evil one, who exhorts to perverse things, and a good one, who persuades to whatever is best. It is written elsewhere too that a double set of angels stand by a man, whether toward the good side or toward the bad. Of the good ones also the Savior makes mention, saying: "Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven". At the same time inquire whether the angels of the little ones in the Church "always see the face of the Father", and whether the angels of others do not have the liberty to gaze upon the face of the Father. For it is not to be hoped that the angels of all men always see "the face of the Father who is in heaven". If I belong to the Church, however least I may be, my angel has the liberty and the confidence always to see "the face of the Father who is in heaven". But if I am on the outside and not of that Church "which has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing", and by the very fact am proved to be a stranger to such a congregation, my angel does not have the confidence to look upon "the face of the Father who is in heaven". For which reason the angels are anxious on behalf of the good, knowing that, if they govern us well and lead us through to salvation, they themselves also have the confidence to see "the face of the Father". For just as, if by their care and diligence salvation is procured for men, they gaze always upon "the face of the Father", so, if through their negligence a man has fallen, they are not unaware that it is a matter of their own peril as well. And just as a good bishop and an excellent steward of the Church knows that it is to his own merit and virtue if the sheep of the flock entrusted to him have been kept safe, so understand it also of the angels. It is a disgrace to an angel if the man entrusted to him has sinned, just as, on the contrary, it is a glory to an angel if the one entrusted to him — even the least in the Church — has made progress. For they will see, not sometimes, but "always the face of the Father who is in heaven", while others do not always see it. For according to the merit of those whose angels they are, the angels will contemplate the face of God either always or never, or little or more. The clear knowledge of this matter God knows, and also if anyone — though rarely — has been found whom Christ has instructed. Let us see, then, first, who the "adversary" is with whom we make our journey. The "adversary" is always with us: unhappy and wretched are we! As often as we sin, our adversary exults, knowing that he has the opportunity, before the ruler of this age who had sent him, of exulting and glorying, because the adversary — for example, of this or that man — has made him subject to the ruler of this age through such and so many sins, through this or that offense. But it sometimes happens that, if someone has been equipped with the armor of God and has covered himself on every side, the "adversary" indeed tries to inflict a wound, but does not have the opportunity to strike. The "adversary" always walks with us, never deserts us, seeks an occasion for his snares, whether he can in some way subvert us and cast an evil thought into the governing part of our heart. "When you go to the ruler". Who then is this ruler? "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and the Lord's portion became his people Jacob, the cord of his inheritance Israel". Therefore from the beginning the earth was divided among the rulers, that is, the angels. For Daniel more plainly testifies that those whom Moses had named "angels" are "rulers", saying: "the ruler of the kingdom of the Persians" and "the ruler of the kingdom of the Greeks" and "Michael your ruler"; and so there are rulers of the nations. And each one of us has an adversary clinging to him, whose work it is to lead us to the ruler and to say: O ruler — for example, of the kingdom of the Persians — this man, who was under you, I have kept for you as he was; none of the remaining rulers was able to lead him over to himself, not even that one who boasted that he had come for this purpose, to snatch men from all the inheritances of the Persians or the Greeks and of all the nations and make them subject to the inheritance of God. Christ our Lord conquered all the rulers and, passing beyond their boundaries, carried over the captive peoples to himself for salvation. And you were of the portion of some ruler: Jesus came and snatched you from the perverse power and offered you to God the Father. Our "adversary", then, walks along, leading us "to" his "ruler". Hence I, believing that all the words of the Scriptures have their reason, do not think it was in vain that "judge" among the Greeks is set down with the article, which is a marker of singularity, while "ruler" is written simply, without the article. "When", he says, "you go with your adversary". He says pointedly: "your". For not all are the adversaries of all, but individuals have their own individual adversaries, who everywhere follow them and are their companions. "When you go with your adversary to a ruler". He did not set down "ruler" with the article, lest it should seem to point to a definite one, but without the article, to show that it is one out of many, which is better understood among the Greeks. For each one of us does not have his own proper ruler; but if someone is an Egyptian, he has the ruler of Egypt; he who is a Syrian is under the ruler of the Syrians; and each one is under the ruler of his own nation — if indeed it is enough for me to have advanced this far and not to pass from this discussion to another and greater one, so as to make mention that the other nations too exist. Whence it is said: "behold Israel according to the flesh". It belongs to a prudent man to have begun to speak; though this very thing is rash, to have begun a discourse on such a matter among the people. He who wishes, he says, to lead you to his ruler and to carry you over from another ruler — "when you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him". Unless you "labor with all zeal to be freed" while you are still traveling the road, before you enter in to the ruler, before the ruler hands you over — prepared by the adversary — to the judge, afterward you will strive in vain. "Make" therefore "an effort to be freed" from your adversary, or from the ruler to whom the adversary drags you. "Make an effort" to have wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and then it will be fulfilled: "behold, the man and his works before his own face". Unless you "make an effort", you will not be able to break the compact of the adversary, whose "friendship is enmity against God". "When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort". Something lies hidden in this place, and it is secret: "on the way make an effort". The Savior says: "I am the way and the truth and the life". If you "make an effort" to be freed from the adversary, be on the way; and when you have stood in him who says: "I am the way", it is not enough to have stood, but "make an effort to be freed" from the adversary. For unless you "make an effort" to "be freed" from the adversary, hear what things follow you. "He drags you to the judge" — the adversary or the ruler, when he has received you from the adversary, "drags you to the judge". How elegant is the word "drags", that it may show them, as it were, drawing back and unwilling, dragged to condemnation and compelled to go! For what murderer proceeds to the judge with a quickened step? Who, rejoicing, hastens to go to his own condemnation, and is not dragged unwilling and resisting? For he knows that he is going for this, to receive the sentence of death. "Lest perhaps he drag you to the judge". Who, do you suppose, is this "judge"? I know no other judge than our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is also said elsewhere: "he will set the sheep on the right, but the goats on the left", and again: "whoever confesses me, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Or else, He here introduces four characters, the adversary, the magistrate, the officer, and the judge. But with Matthew the character of the magistrate is left out, and instead of the officer a servant is introduced. They differ also in that the one has written a farthing, the other a mite, but each has called it the last. Now we say that all men have present with them two angels, a bad one who encourages them to wicked deeds, a good one who persuades all that is best. Now the former, our adversary whenever we sin rejoices, knowing that he has an occasion for exultations and boasting with the prince of the world, who sent him. But in the Greek, "the adversary" is written with the article, to signify that he is one out of many, seeing that each individual is under the ruler of his nation. Give diligence then that you may be delivered from your adversary, or from the ruler to whom the adversary drags you, by having wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance. But if you have given diligence, let it be in Him who says, I am the life, (John 14:6.) otherwise the adversary will hale thee to the judge. Now he says, hale, to point out that they are forced unwillingly to condemnation. But I know no other judge but our Lord Jesus Christ who delivers to the officer. Each of us have our own officers; the officers exercise rule over us, if we owe any thing. If I paid every man every thing, I come to the officers and answer with a fearless heart, "I owe them nothing." But if I am a debtor, the officer will cast me into prison, nor will he suffer me to go out from thence until I have paid every debt. For the officer has no power to let me off even a farthing. He who forgave one debtor five hundred pence and another fifty, (Luke 7:41.) was the Lord, but the exactor is not the master, but one appointed by the master to demand the debts. But the last mite he calls slight and small, for our sins are either heavy or slight. Happy then is he who sinneth not, and next in happiness he who has sinned slightly. Even among slight sins there is diversity, otherwise he would not say until he has paid the last mite. For if he owes a little, he shall not come out till he pays the last mite. But he who has been guilty of a great debt, will have endless ages for his payment.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "He drags you to the judge, and the judge hands you over to the officer". Each one of us, through each single sin, sustains a loss, and according to the quality and account of the offense the magnitude of the loss is reckoned. I ought to bring forward some testimony from the Scriptures concerning loss and a fine of money. One man sustains a loss of five hundred denarii and owes them; another is condemned in fifty denarii; which sum is remitted to both by the creditor. Further, another, as the Scripture says: "one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents", is condemned in a debt of ten thousand talents. And what need is there for me to pursue more? Each one, according to the quality and quantity of his sin, receives a different sentence of fine. If it is little that you sin, you will be struck with the loss of a "mite", as Luke writes, or, as Matthew, of a "farthing". Nevertheless, it is also necessary to pay this very thing in which you have become a debtor; for you will not come out of the prison unless you have paid off even the very least things. But he who is faithful is struck by no loss, but is daily enriched; for the whole world of riches is his; the unbeliever, however, has not even an obol. One is condemned in a denarius, another in a mina, another in a talent. There is an examiner of this business, who knows the measures of all sins and says: This offense is condemned in a talent, that sin merits a fine of this kind. For it is written: "but when he had begun to make a reckoning". A "reckoning" must be computed for all of us. There is no other time for making the reckoning than the time of judgment, when it will be clearly known what has been entrusted to us and what gain or what loss we have made, which of us received a mina, which one talent, which two, which five. What need is there to repeat more, when it is enough to have said this in general, that we shall render an account and, if we are found to be debtors, be dragged to the judge and handed over by the judge to the officer? As individuals we have our own officers, but the whole multitude is handed over to several, according to that which is written in Isaiah: "my people, your officers plunder you, and those who are powerful lord it over you" — the officers lord it over us, if we owe anything. But if we have confidence and with free brow say: I have kept the precept that commands: "render to all their debts, to whom tribute, tribute, to whom fear, fear, to whom custom, custom, to whom honor, honor" — if I have rendered all things to all, I come to the officer and with untroubled mind answer: I owe you nothing. The officer comes to demand back — I resist him; for I know that, if I owe nothing, he has no power over me. But if I am a debtor, my "officer will cast" me "into prison", in that order which was foretold. For the "adversary" leads me to the ruler, the ruler to the judge, the judge will hand me over to the officer, the officer "will cast me into prison". What is the law of that prison? I do not go out from it, nor does the officer allow me to go out, unless I have paid off the whole debt. The officer does not have the power to be able to remit to me even a "farthing" and the smallest portion; there is one who can remit to debtors who have nothing wherewith to pay. "There approached him", he says, "one who owed five hundred denarii, and another fifty; and since they had nothing wherewith to pay, he forgave them both". He who forgave was the master; but this one, who is the officer, is not the master, but is appointed by the master to exact the debts. You were not worthy that five hundred or fifty denarii should be forgiven you, nor did you deserve to hear: "your offenses are forgiven you": you are cast into prison, and there you are exacted through labor and works, or through penalties and torments, and you will not come out from there unless you have paid back the "farthing" or the "very last mite", which in Greek can be called "the fine thing". Our sins are either gross — for it is written: "the heart of this people has grown fat" — or, in comparison with greater ones, fine and subtle. Blessed, therefore, is he first who does not sin; secondly, that in comparison one should have at least a fine sin. And even among these fine and subtle sins there is a diversity of sins. For unless among a fine and subtle sin there were another still subtler, it would never be said: "you will not come out from there until you pay back the last farthing". Just as, if he were speaking of money, the "very last mite" — the mite, which is a denarius or a coin or an obol or a stater —; but what if we owe a great sum of money, like that man who is written to have owed ten thousand talents; for how long a time we shall be shut up in prison until we pay back the debt — I cannot openly declare. For if he who owes little does not come out unless he pays off the "least farthing", surely he who has become liable for so great a debt will have countless ages numbered to him for paying back the debt. Wherefore "let us make an effort to be freed from the adversary" while we are on the way, and let us be joined to the Lord Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

author: Origen of Alexandria
Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Let us inquire into what is written in Luke, the Lord saying: "because it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem." If, then, "it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem," that is, be killed, you will ask whether after the destruction of Jerusalem there is now no prophet, lest perhaps the one who is killed "outside Jerusalem" should, being a prophet, prove the word of Christ false. But if the scriptures compel us — on account of Agabus and the daughters of Philip the evangelist (not on account of the false prophets of Phrygia) — let us inquire whether perhaps every righteous person is in Jerusalem and not "outside Jerusalem," since "it cannot be" that the one who is outside Jerusalem be afflicted with sufferings for the sake of the word.

But that Jerusalem which is free from the servitude of sin, which is above in its manner of life, "which is our mother," does not kill the prophets nor stone those who are sent to her. It is another matter that, after the likeness of that Jerusalem which killed and stoned the prophets, frequently there are certain persons set up in this Jerusalem, unskilled and not fearing God, who (as far as in them lies) kill and stone, with words uttered without judgment, men advanced in word and in life — men who indeed do not abandon the canon of the churches, but on account of the profundity of their doctrines are held suspect by those who are accustomed to say certain novel things and do not attend to the "sound word" of our Lord Jesus Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But mystically, he who shuns vain-glory calls to a spiritual banquet the poor, that is, the ignorant, that he may enrich them; the weak, that is, those with offended consciences, that he may heal them; the lame, that is, those who have wandered from reason, that he may make their paths straight; the blind, that is, those who discern not the truth, that they may behold the true light. But it is said, They cannot recompense thee, i. e. they know not how to return an answer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: They who have bought a piece of ground and reject or refuse the supper, are they who have taken other doctrines of divinity, but have despised the word which they possessed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who has bought five yoke of oxen is he who neglects his intellectual nature, and follows the things of sense, therefore he cannot comprehend a spiritual nature.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He who has married a wife is he who is joined to the flesh, a lover of pleasure rather than of God. (1 Tim. 3:4.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This journey, then, must be made by those who follow God; but there is also a tower on this journey. What is that tower? That one, surely, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: "which of you, wishing to build a tower, will not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has the means to complete it?" This, then, is the tower, the steep and lofty seat of the virtues.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: People of God are truly the salt of the earth. They preserve the order of the world. Society is held together as long as the salt is uncorrupted. If the salt lost its savor, it is neither suitable for the land or the manure pile. It will be thrown out and trampled underfoot. "He that has ears, let him hear" the meaning of these words. When God gives to the tempter permission to persecute us, then we suffer persecution. When God wishes us to be free from suffering even in the middle of a world that hates us, we enjoy a wonderful peace. We trust in the protection of him who said, "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For of this matter there is also that image which is spoken of in the Gospel concerning "the steward of iniquity," who says to each debtor: "Take your bond, and sitting down write eighty," and the rest that is reported. You see, then, that it is said to each: "Take your bond." Whence it is established that the letters of sin are ours; but the letters of righteousness God writes. For thus says the Apostle: "For you are an epistle inscribed not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone, but on the fleshly tablets of the heart." You have, then, within you the letters of God and the letters of the Holy Spirit. But if you offend, you yourself write for yourself the handwriting of sin. But see that, once you have come to the cross of Christ and to the grace of baptism, your handwriting has been fastened to the cross and blotted out in the font of baptism. Do not write again the things that have been blotted out, nor restore the things that have been abolished; keep in you only the letters of God, let only the writing of the Holy Spirit remain in you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
(in Prov. 1:1.) But because the Gentiles say that wisdom is a virtue, and define it to be the experience of what is good, evil, and indifferent, or the knowledge of what is and what is not to be done, we must consider whether this word signifies many things, or one. For it is said that God by wisdom prepared the heavens. (Prov. 3:19.) Now it is plain that wisdom is good, because the Lord by wisdom prepared the heavens. It is said also in Genesis, according to the LXX, that the serpent was the wisest animal, wherein He makes wisdom not a virtue, but evil-minded cunning. And it is in this sense that the Lord commended the steward that he had done wisely, that is, cunningly and evilly. And perhaps the word commended was spoken not in the sense of real commendation, but in a lower sense; as when we speak of a man being commended in slight and indifferent matters, and in a certain measure clashings and sharpness of wit are admired, by which the power of the mind is drawn out.

The children of this world also are not called wiser but more prudent than the children of light, and this not absolutely and simply, but in their generation. For it follows, For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us come also to the Gospels, if we find anything said in them concerning tabernacles, so that through the judgment of the Lord what we seek may be beyond doubt. We find, then, that the Savior himself, Jesus Christ, mentions not one tabernacle, but many, and not temporal, but eternal, when he says: "Make yourselves friends of the mammon, that, when it shall fail, they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles". Thou hast heard the Lord declaring the tabernacles to be eternal; hear now also the Apostle saying: "desiring to be clothed over with our tabernacle, which is from heaven". Is not the way now opened to thee from all these things, whereby, the earth being forsaken, following the prophetic and apostolic sense and — what is greatest of all — following the word of Christ with the whole mind and whole sense, thou mayest ascend to heaven and there seek the magnificence of the eternal tabernacle, whose figure is shadowed forth through Moses on the earth?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But perhaps some Jewish man of those who dare to oppose the teaching of our Saviour will say, that when Jesus said, "Whosoever shall put away his own wife, saving for the cause of fornication, makes her an adulteress," [Matthew 5:32] He also gave permission to put away a wife like as well as Moses did, who was said by Him to have given laws for the hardness of heart of the people, and will hold that the saying, "Because he found in her an unseemly thing," [Deuteronomy 24:1] is to be reckoned as the same as fornication on account of which with good cause a wife could be cast away from her husband. But to him it must be said that, if she who committed adultery was according to the law to be stoned, clearly it is not in this sense that the unseemly thing is to be understood. For it is not necessary for adultery or any such great indecency to write a bill of divorcement and give it into the hands of the wife; but indeed perhaps Moses called every sin an unseemly thing, on the discovery of which by the husband in the wife, as not finding favour in the eyes of her husband, the bill of divorcement is written, and the wife is sent away from the house of her husband; "but from the beginning it has not been so." [Matthew 19:8] After this our Saviour says, not at all permitting the dissolution of marriages for any other sin than fornication alone, when detected in the wife, "Whosoever shall put away his own wife, saving for the cause of fornication, makes her an adulteress." [Matthew 5:32] But it might be a subject for inquiry if on this account He hinders any one putting away a wife, unless she be caught in fornication, for any other reason, as for example for poisoning, or for the destruction during the absence of her husband from home of an infant born to them, or for any form of murder whatsoever. And further, if she were found despoiling and pillaging the house of her husband, though she was not guilty of fornication, one might ask if he would with reason cast away such an one, seeing that the Saviour forbids any one to put away his own wife saving for the cause of fornication. In either case there appears to be something monstrous, whether it be really monstrous, I do not know; for to endure sins of such heinousness which seem to be worse than adultery or fornication, will appear to be irrational; but again on the other hand to act contrary to the design of the teaching of the Saviour, every one would acknowledge to be impious. I wonder therefore why He did not say, Let no one put away his own wife saving for the cause of fornication, but says, "Whosoever shall put away his own wife, saving for the cause of fornication, makes her an adulteress." [Matthew 5:32] For confessedly he who puts away his wife when she is not a fornicator, makes her an adulteress, so far as it lies with him, for if, "when the husband is living she shall be called an adulteress if she be joined to another man;" [Romans 7:3] and when by putting her away, he gives to her the excuse of a second marriage, very plainly in this way he makes her an adulteress. But as to whether her being caught in the act of poisoning or committing murder, furnishes any defense of his dismissal of her, you can inquire yourselves; for the husband can also in other ways than by putting her away cause his own wife to commit adultery; as, for example, allowing her to do what she wishes beyond what is fitting, and stooping to friendship with what men she wishes, for often from the simplicity of husbands such false steps happen to wives; but whether there is a ground of defense or not for such husbands in the case of such false steps, you will inquire carefully, and deliver your opinion also in regard to the difficult questions raised by us on the passage. And even he who withholds himself from his wife makes her oftentimes to be an adulteress when he does not satisfy her desires, even though he does so under the appearance of greater gravity and self-control. And perhaps this man is more culpable who, so far as it rests with him, makes her an adulteress when he does not satisfy her desires than he who, for other reason than fornication, has sent her away — for poisoning or murder or any of the most grievous sins. But as a woman is an adulteress, even though she seem to be married to a man, while the former husband is still living, so also the man who seems to marry her who has been put away, does not so much marry her as commit adultery with her according to the declaration of our Saviour.
source_title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew (Book XIV), Section 24

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But also to all the saints a contempt of corporeal delights is enjoined, and a hope of spiritual delights is promised in return. Do you wish also to receive authority of the divine Scripture concerning this? There was a certain rich man, and Lazarus a poor man; the rich man was in corporeal delights, Lazarus was wasted with hunger. Each departed from the age, and Lazarus indeed was taken up by the angels into the bosom of Abraham, that there he might rest in delights; but that one who had been in corporeal delights went off into the gehenna of fire, as it is in the Gospel, and hears from Abraham, that "you have obtained good things in your life", that is, you have abused delights, "and Lazarus evil things: but now here he rests, while you are tormented". No one can have delights both in the flesh and in the spirit. But if anyone takes delight in the flesh, like that rich man, he will lack the bosom of Abraham and its delights. But he who in the present age feeds on the bread of affliction, like that poor man, when he has departed hence, will be in delights.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But do you also wish to learn from the Gospels that he who "shall have received in this life his evil things" does not there receive them again, but he who has not received them here, there all things are reserved for him? The example of "poor Lazarus" and of that rich man teaches us, to whom it is said "in the netherworld" by the patriarch Abraham: "Remember, son, that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise the evil things. But now you indeed are tormented, while this one is at rest."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But indeed, when the Savior was asked by the Pharisees about the kingdom of God, "when it would come", he replied: "The kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor do they say: behold, here, or behold, there. For the kingdom of God is within you". The Savior does not say to all: "the kingdom of God is within you", since in sinners there is the kingdom of sin, and without any ambiguity either the kingdom of God rules in our heart or the kingdom of sin. Whence, whether it be the things we do, or the things we speak, or the things we think, let us contemplate them more attentively, and then we shall see whether the dominion of God reigns in us or the dominion of sins. The Apostle, knowing that this diversity exists, admonishes certain people, saying: "let not sin reign in your mortal body". If any one of us desires the kingdom of God, he is ruled by it; if anyone is tormented by the ardor of avarice, he is ruled by avarice. Further, he who is just has justice as his queen; he who is exalted by the ambition of vainglory, the breath of popular favor reigns over him. He who mourns, he who dreads something, he who loves, he who desires — each of these things commands him, according as he is possessed by various disturbances. Recognizing all these things, and how many kinds of kingdoms there are, let us rise up and pray God to take away from us the kingdom of the enemy, that we may be able to be under the kingdom of God almighty, that is, under the kingdom of wisdom, of peace, of justice, of truth — all of which are understood in the only-begotten Son of God: to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 36

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But because "the law is spiritual" and the things that befell the ancients "befell them as a figure," let us see whether perhaps Lot, who did not look back, is the rational sense and the manly spirit, while the wife here holds the image of the flesh. For it is the flesh that always looks back to vices, which, when the spirit strives toward salvation, looks back and seeks after pleasures. Hence indeed the Lord also said: "No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God," and he adds: "Remember Lot's wife." And that "she is made a pillar of salt" seems set forth as an indication of her folly. For salt is put in place of prudence, which she lacked.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Whoever seeks", he says, "to save his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will save it". The martyrs seek "to save their soul"; and for this reason they lose it, in order to save it. But those who wish "to save their soul" and do not "lose" it, these "lose both body and soul" alike "in hell". Wherefore, he says, "do not fear those who can kill the body, but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell". This much we have said briefly on the point at hand, according to the strength of our talent; but "the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit", and therefore he cannot be saved. "A natural body is sown, a spiritual body rises". Further, "he who cleaves to the Lord becomes one spirit" with him. If, then, "he who is joined to the Lord", though he was natural, is by that very thing turned into a spiritual man and "is one spirit", let us too lose our soul, so that, cleaving to the Lord, we may be transformed into one spirit.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 36

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He prays for those who pray and appeals with those who appeal. He does not, however, pray for servants who do not pray continuously through him. He will not be the Advocate with God for his own if they are not obedient to his instructions that they always should pray and not lose heart. It says, "And he told them a parable to the effect that they should always pray and not lose heart. In a certain city there was a judge, etc." … Who would hesitate a moment to be persuaded to pray if he believes that the mouth of Jesus cannot lie, when he says, "Ask, and it will be given you … for everyone who asks, receives"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if you wish also through examples to know how each one is bowed down by his sins, so that he cannot look up nor lift his eyes to heaven, gaze upon that publican who in the Gospel, having entered the temple and standing afar off, not daring to lift his eyes to heaven, but striking his breast and confessing his sins, said: "God, be merciful to me a sinner." To this man surely it is fitting to say, "I am bowed down even to the end, and I went about all the day saddened." And in saying this, he sets forth, as it were, the very disposition and soul of the penitent, who says: From the time I sinned, I have never laughed, I have never been glad, I have never indulged myself in anything of enjoyment, but I have always been in mourning, always in repentance, always in grief.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Interest on the Word of God is having in life and deeds things that the Word of God has commanded. When you hear the Word, if you use it and act according to those words that you hear and live according to these words, then you are preparing interest for the Lord. Each of you can make ten talents from five. You will then hear from the Lord, "Well done, good and faithful servant, you shall have power over ten cities." Beware of this, fearing that any one of you may gather "in a napkin" or bury "in the earth" the money that has been received. You know well the nature of the outcome for this kind of man when the Lord comes.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What you have offered to God you shall receive back multiplied. Something like this, although put in another way, is related in the Gospels when in a parable someone received a pound that he might engage in business, and the master of the house demanded the money. If you have caused five to be multiplied to ten, then they are given to you. Hear what Scripture says, "Take his pound, and give it to him who has ten pounds."We therefore appear at least to engage in business for the Lord, but the profits of the business go to us. We appear to offer sacrifice to the Lord, but the things we offer are given back to us. God does not need anything, but he wants us to be rich. He desires our progress through each, individual thing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And that this may become clearer, let me set down the parable of the minas. He who had received one mina and had made ten and offered it to the Lord, by whom the mina had been entrusted to him, received also another which he had not had before. For the mina of him who had not multiplied what he had received the Lord orders to be taken away and given to the one who has others; "take away", he says, "the mina and give it to him who has ten minas". And in this manner, the things we have given to God he will restore to us, those very things, together with the things we had not had before. God exacts and requires of us, so that he may have occasion for giving, so that he himself may bestow, who paid it out. For by his own grace the mina was doubled, and to each of the worthy more was given than they hoped for.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Bethany is interpreted, the house of obedience, but Bethphage the house of cheek bones, being a place belonging to the priests, for cheek bones in the sacrifices were the right of the priests, as it is commanded in the law. To that place then where obedience is, and where the priests have the possession, our Saviour sends His disciples to loose the ass's colt.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It was read in the Gospel according to Luke how, when the Savior had come "to Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples" to untie "the colt of a donkey", which was tied up, "on which no man had ever sat". This indeed seems to me to pertain to a higher understanding rather than to the simple narrative. The donkey was tied up. Where, then? "Opposite Bethphage and Bethany", of which Bethany is interpreted "house of obedience", while Bethphage means "house of jawbones", a certain priestly place; for the jawbones were given to the priests, as is prescribed in the law. To that place, therefore, where there is "obedience", where there is "a place made over to the priests", the Savior sends his disciples, that they may untie "the colt of a donkey, on which no man had ever sat". Furthermore, what else can sit upon a donkey apart from a man? I wish to take an example for a little while, so that what I am about to say may be understood. It is written in Isaiah: "the vision of the quadrupeds in tribulation and distress", and the rest, up to the place where he says: "the riches of the asps will not profit them". Let each one of us consider how great wealth of asps he has borne before this, how great riches of beasts, and how a rational man never sat upon our donkey — not the word of Moses, not of Isaiah, not of Jeremiah, nor of all the rest of the prophets — and he will see that the word of God and reason then sat upon us, when the Lord Jesus came and commanded his disciples that, going, they should untie "the colt of a donkey", which before had been tied up, so that it might walk free.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (sup. Joan. tom. ii.) Now I think this place is not without reason said to be a small village. For as if it were a village without any further name, in comparison of the whole earth the whole heavenly country is despised.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There were then many masters of this colt, before that the Saviour had need of him. But as soon as He began to be the master, there ceased to be any other. For no one can serve God and mammon.
