(Matt. 6:24.) When we are the servants of wickedness we are subject to many vices and passions, but the Lord has need of the colt, because He would have us loosed from the chain of our sins.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And so the "colt of the donkey", once untied, is led to Jesus, and in sending his disciples to untie it he had said: "If anyone asks you: why do you untie the colt? say to him: because the Lord has need of it". There were many masters of this colt before the Savior had need of it; but after he began to be its "master", they ceased to be many masters; for no one "can serve God and mammon". When we serve wickedness, we are subject to many passions and vices. The colt, therefore, is untied, "because the Lord has need of it". And now the Lord "has need" of the colt. You are the colt of the donkey. What does the Son of God "have need" of that is yours? What does he seek from you? He "has need" of your salvation, he desires that you be loosed from the chains of sins.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Luc. 37.) The disciples next place their garments upon the ass, and cause the Saviour to sit thereon, inasmuch as they take upon themselves the word of God, and make it to rest upon the souls of their hearers. They divest themselves of their garments, and strew them in the way, for the clothing of the Apostles is their good works. And truly does the ass loosened by the disciples and carrying Jesus, walk upon the garments of the Apostles, when it imitates their doctrine. Which of us is so blessed, that Jesus should rest upon him?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then the disciples put "their garments upon the donkey" and make the Savior sit upon it. They take up the Word of God and set it upon the souls of the hearers. They strip off their garments, they "spread" them "in the way". Upon us are the garments of the apostles; their good works are our adornments: the apostles wish their garments to be trodden by us. And indeed the donkey, untied by the disciples and bearing Jesus, walks upon the garments of the apostles when it imitates their teaching and their life.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As long as our Lord was in the mount His Apostles only were with Him, but when He began to be near the descent, then there came to Him a multitude of the people.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Which of us is so blessed that Jesus sits upon him — Jesus, who, as long as he was on the mountain, tarried with the apostles alone, but when he began to be near the descent, then the crowd of peoples met him? If he had not come to the descent, the multitude could not have met him. He came down and sat upon the colt of the donkey, and all the people with one accord praised God.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When we also are silent, (that is, when the love of many waxeth cold,) the stones cry out, for God can from stones raise up children to Abraham.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Seeing this, the Pharisees said to the Lord: "rebuke them"; to whom he answered: "If these keep silent, the stones will cry out". When we speak, the stones are silent; when we keep silent, the stones cry out; "for the Lord is able to raise up from these stones sons of Abraham". At what time shall we keep silent? When "the charity of many shall have grown cold", when that which was foretold by the Savior shall have been fulfilled: "do you think that the Son of man, when he comes, will find faith upon the earth?" Therefore let us entreat the Lord's mercy, lest, while we are silent, the stones cry out, but let us speak and praise God in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
All the blessings which Jesus pronounced in His Gospel He confirms by His own example, as having declared, Blessed are the meek; He afterwards sanctions it by saying, Learn of me, for I am meek; and because He had said, Blessed are they that weep, He Himself also wept over the city.

I do not deny then that the former Jerusalem was destroyed because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, but I ask whether the weeping might not perhaps concern this your spiritual Jerusalem. For if a man has sinned after receiving the mysteries of truth, he will be wept over. Moreover, no Gentile is wept over, but he only who was of Jerusalem, and has ceased to be.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When our Lord and Savior had drawn near to Jerusalem, seeing it he wept and said: "if you too had known, even in this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes: for the days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart". What is said here are mysteries, and we hope, if God opens them, that what lies hidden can be laid open. First, then, we must consider his weeping. All the beatitudes that Jesus spoke in the Gospel he confirms by his own example, and what he taught he proves by his own testimony. "Blessed", he says, "are the meek". Like to this is what he says of himself: "Learn from me", he says, "for I am meek". "Blessed are the peacemakers". And who else is so much a peacemaker as my Lord Jesus, who "is our peace", who "loosed the enmity" and "destroyed it in his own flesh"? "Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake". No one so suffered persecution for righteousness' sake as the Lord Jesus, who was crucified for our sins. All the beatitudes, therefore, the Lord shows forth in himself; and to this likeness belongs also that which he had said: "blessed are they that weep" — he himself wept, that he might lay the foundations of this beatitude too.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 38

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And he wept over Jerusalem, "saying: if you too had known, even in this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes", and the rest, up to the place where it says: "because you have not known the time of your visitation". Let one of the hearers say: What is said here is plain, and has been fulfilled in deed concerning Jerusalem: for the Roman army surrounded it and laid it waste even to utter destruction, and the time will come when a stone shall not be left upon a stone upon it. I do not deny that that Jerusalem too was destroyed because of the crimes of its inhabitants; but I ask whether perhaps this weeping pertains also to this our Jerusalem. For we are the Jerusalem that is wept over, we who seem to ourselves to have the greater vision. For if, after the mysteries of truth, after the word of the Gospel, after the teaching of the Church and after the vision of the sacraments of God, someone among us should sin, he will be lamented and wept over. For no Gentile is wept over, but only he who was of Jerusalem and has ceased to be so. And this our Jerusalem is wept over, because after sins "enemies surround" it — namely the hostile powers, the wicked spirits — and cast "a rampart" around about it and besiege it "and leave not a stone upon a stone", especially if, after much continence, after some years of chastity, someone should be overcome and, enticed by the blandishments of the flesh, should lose the endurance of purity. If you have committed fornication, "they will not leave a stone upon a stone in you". For he says in another place: "I will not remember his former righteous deeds; in his sin, in which he shall be caught, in that very sin will I judge him". This, then, is the Jerusalem that is wept over.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 38

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But our Jerusalem is also wept over, because after sin enemies surround it, (that is, wicked spirits,) and cast a trench round it to besiege it, and leave not a stone behind; especially when a man after long continency, after years of chastity, is overcome, and enticed by the blandishments of the flesh, has lost his fortitude and his modesty, and has committed fornication, they will not leave on him one stone upon another, according to Ezekiel, His former righteousness I will not remember. (Ezek 18:24.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If any then sells, let him be cast out, and especially if he sells doves. For of those things which have been revealed and committed to me by the Holy Spirit, I either sell for money to the people, or do not teach without hire, what else do I but sell a dove, that is, the Holy Spirit?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this it is said: "he entered into the temple", and, when he had entered, "he cast out those who were selling doves". He did not cast out those who buy; for he who buys, possesses what he has bought. Those Jesus cast out of his Father's temple who sell and throw away what they had, after the likeness of that prodigal son who received his substance from his father and lost it all in excessive drinking. If, therefore, anyone sells, he is cast out, especially if he was selling "doves". Why did he name no other birds but doves? This animal is simple and comely. I fear lest this same fault be found in us also. For if the things that have been revealed and entrusted to me by the Holy Spirit, that I might bring them forth to the multitude, I should sell for a price and not teach without wage, what else do I do but sell doves, that is, the Holy Spirit? And when I have sold him, I am cast out of the temple of God. Wherefore let us ask the Lord that we may all rather buy than sell. For if we do not sell, we shall know and understand our salvation; otherwise the enemies will surround our city. And if once the hostile army has encircled us, we shall not deserve the tears of the Lord. Let us therefore rise up at dawn and beseech God that we may at least be able to eat the crumbs that fall from his table. The scripture marvels that the queen of Sheba came "from the ends of the earth, to hear the wisdom of Solomon"; and she, when she had seen the banquet and the furnishing and the ministries of his house, was astonished and was wholly in wonder. If we do not gladly embrace such great riches of our Lord, such furnishing of the word and abundance of teachings, if we do not eat the "bread of life", if we do not feed on the flesh of Jesus and drink his blood, if we despise the feasts of our Savior, we ought to know that God has both "kindness and severity"; and of these we ought rather to pray for his kindness, in Christ Jesus our Lord: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 38

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Furthermore, since something was added about the image of Caesar, we must also touch briefly upon this. Some suppose that it was said by the Savior simply: "render to Caesar what is Caesar's", that is: pay the tribute which you owe. For who among us objects to paying tribute to Caesar? Therefore the passage holds something mystical and hidden. There are two images in man: one, which he received from God when he was made in the beginning, as it is written in Genesis: "according to the image and likeness of God"; the other of the earthy, which afterward, when he had been cast out of paradise because of disobedience and sin, he took on, persuaded by the enticements of "the prince of this world". For just as a coin or denarius bears the image of the emperors of the world, so he who does the works of "the ruler of these darknesses" bears the image of him whose works he has: which image Jesus here commanded to be rendered back and cast off from our face, and that image to be taken up according to which from the beginning we were fashioned to the likeness of God. And thus it comes about that we render "what is Caesar's to Caesar, and what is God's to God". "Show me", he says, "the coin", for which in Matthew is written "denarius". And when he had received it, he said: "whose inscription does it have?" They answering said: "Caesar's". To them again he said: "render what is Caesar's to Caesar, and what is God's to God". The logical sequence of these things Paul too has expressed, saying: "as we have borne the image of the earthy, let us also bear the image of the heavenly". So then, what he says: "render what is Caesar's to Caesar", this he means: lay aside the person of the earthy, cast off the earthly image, so that, putting upon yourselves the person of the heavenly, you may be able to render "what is God's to God". God demands us back. What does he demand back? Read Moses: "and now what does the Lord your God demand back from you?" and the rest that follows. God therefore requires of us and beseeches us, not because he has need of anything that we might bestow upon him, but so that, after we have given it to him, he may bestow that very thing upon us for salvation. And that this may become clearer, let me set down the parable of the minas. He who had received one mina and had made ten and offered it to the Lord, by whom the mina had been entrusted to him, received also another which he had not had before. For the mina of him who had not multiplied what he had received the Lord orders to be taken away and given to the one who has others; "take away", he says, "the mina and give it to him who has ten minas". And in this manner, the things we have given to God he will restore to us, those very things, together with the things we had not had before. God exacts and requires of us, so that he may have occasion for giving, so that he himself may bestow, who paid it out. For by his own grace the mina was doubled, and to each of the worthy more was given than they hoped for. Wherefore, rising up, let us pray to God that we may be worthy to offer him gifts which he may restore to us, and that in exchange for earthly things he may lavish heavenly ones upon us, in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now this place contains a mystery. For there are two images in man, one which he received from God, as it is written, Let us make man in our own image: (Gen. 1:26.) another from the enemy, which he has contracted through disobedience and sin, allured and won by the enticing baits of the prince of this world. For as the penny has the image of the emperor of the world, so he who does the works of the power of darkness, bears the image of Him whose works he doth. He says then, Render unto Cæsar the things which be Cæsar's, that is, cast away the earthly image, that ye may be able, by putting on the heavenly image, to render unto God the things which be God's, namely, to love God. Which things Moses says God requires of us. (Deut. 10:12.) But God makes this demand of us, not because He has need that we should give Him any thing, but that, when we have given, He might grant us this very same gift for our salvation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The heresy of the Sadducees not only denies the resurrection of the dead, but also believes the soul to die with the body. Watching then to entrap our Saviour in His words, they proposed a question just at the time when they observed Him teaching His disciples concerning the resurrection; as it follows, And they asked him, saying, Master, Moses wrote to us, If a brother, &c.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is a sect among the Jews which is called the sect of the Sadducees: this sect denies "the resurrection of the dead" and supposes that the soul perishes together with the body, and that after death no faculty of perception any longer remains. These men, then, in putting a question to the Lord, made up the tale of the woman with seven husbands, who after her first husband, in order to raise up seed for the former, married a second, and when he had died a third also, and again a fourth, and in this manner arrived at the seventh. The question, therefore, is which of the seven brothers will claim her as his wife "in the resurrection of the dead". Now they proposed this problem, laying a snare for the words of the Savior, at that time when they saw him teaching his disciples about the resurrection.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But because the Lord says in Matthew, which is here omitted, Ye do err, not knowing the Scriptures, (Mat. 22:29.) I ask the question, where is it so written, They shall neither marry, nor be given in marriage? for as I conceive there is no such thing to be found either in the Old or New Testament, but the whole of their error had crept in from the reading of the Scriptures without understanding; for it is said in Esaias, My elect shall not have children for a curse. (Isai. 65:23.) Whence they suppose that the like will happen in the resurrection. But Paul interpreting all these blessings as spiritual, knowing them not to be carnal, says to the Ephesians, Ye have blessed us in all spiritual blessings. (Eph. 1:3.)

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Answering them, the Savior said: "You are in error, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection of the dead they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they will be like the angels in heaven". Those who will be like the angels will certainly be angels. And at the same time it must be learned that the angels have no marriages. Here indeed, where there is death, both marriages and children are necessary; but where there is immortality, there is need neither of wedlock nor of sons. Let me set before myself a very troublesome question, one that is not easily solved, in the person of those who are most zealous for the Scriptures and who "meditate day and night in the law of the Lord". Where, they say, is it written that "they will neither marry nor be given in marriage"? Passing through both the Old and the New Testament in memory and mind, I do not recall that anything of the kind is anywhere reported. But if perchance it escapes me, let him who knows more teach me; I gladly learn what I do not know; yet as far as I judge, he will find nothing of the sort in either the Old or the New instrument. All their error, therefore, has crept in from the reading of the prophets, which they do not understand — among which is that passage in Isaiah: "my chosen ones will not have children for a curse", and in Deuteronomy among the blessings: "blessed are the children of your womb" — and they suppose that these things are to be in the resurrection, not understanding that spiritual blessings were foretold. For Paul, "the vessel of election", interpreting spiritually all these blessings that are set down in the law, and knowing that they are not carnal, speaks to the Ephesians: "blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing". And so all these blessings will be spiritual, when, rising from the dead, we attain eternal blessedness. But in the Psalms too, finding something similar, they slip into the same error: "your wife", it says, "like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house, your children like young olive shoots around your table", up to that place where it says: "may the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you see the good things that are of Jerusalem". Therefore, when Jerusalem has been furnished and restored to its ancient state, then the holy one will see the good things which the Scripture mentions. Those who understand Jerusalem spiritually, and know that it is said of her: "which is heavenly, which is above, which is our mother", will see her good things, of which we have often spoken, and that which we have now cited from the psalm: "your wife like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house, your children like young olive shoots around your table". To the Sadducees, who were a portion of the Jews, understanding all these things bodily, the Savior says: "you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God". Let these things be said briefly concerning the question which the Sadducees put to the Lord.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 39

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then, moreover, the Savior too, with the authority of the Lord and King, establishing laws and ordinances at once for priests and for the peoples, says: "Take heed, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with drunkenness and surfeiting and with the cares of this world, and that sudden destruction come upon you". You have heard the edict of the eternal King, and you have learned the lamentable end of "drunkenness" or "surfeiting". If some skilled and wise physician were to prescribe to you in these very words and say: Take heed to yourselves, lest anyone, for example's sake, take too greedily of the juice of this or that herb; for if he does so, sudden destruction will come upon him—I do not doubt that everyone, with regard to his own health, would keep the precepts of the physician who forewarned him. But now the physician of souls and bodies, and at the same time the Lord, bids the herb of "drunkenness" and of "surfeiting" be shunned, and likewise the deadly juices, as it were, of worldly cares be guarded against. And I know not whether any of us is not consumed in these things—not to say wounded. Drunkenness by wine, then, is pernicious in all respects; for it alone is the thing that renders both the body and the soul feeble at once. In other matters indeed it can come to pass that, according to the Apostle, when the body "is weakened", then the spirit "is the more powerful", and where "he who is without, the man, is corrupted, he who is within is renewed". But in the sickness of drunkenness the body and the soul are corrupted together, the spirit is vitiated along with the flesh. All the members are feeble, the feet, the hands, the tongue slackened; darkness veils the eyes, forgetfulness veils the mind, so that a man does not know nor perceive himself to be a man. This, then, drunkenness has first, of bodily disgrace.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And, to come to the things that are written, the "Lord of majesty", Jesus Christ our Savior, was crucified. The author of this crime and the father of the wickedness is without doubt the devil. For thus it is written: "but when the devil had entered into the heart of Judas Iscariot, that he should betray him". The father of the sin, then, is the devil. He, in this wickedness, first begets a son, Judas; but Judas alone could not accomplish this. What, then, is written? "Judas went" it says "to the scribes and Pharisees and to the chief priests, saying to them: What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?" There is born, then, from Judas a third and fourth generation of sin. And you will be able to detect this order in each single sin as well.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: From then on he was seeking an opportunity to hand him over. But what sort of opportunity Judas was seeking, Luke has explained more plainly, saying: "And he was seeking an opportunity to hand him over to them without the crowd," that is, when the people was not about him, but he was apart with his disciples. And this he did, handing him over after the supper, when he was apart in the estate of Gethsemane; for Judas reckoned that the opportunity was his after the bargain which he made, when Jesus was not with the multitude. And see whether even until now this opportunity does not seem the same to the betrayers of the word of truth, who wish to betray Christ, God the Word, in the time of the persecution of Christians, when the multitude of believers is not about the word of truth and cannot hinder or restrain the persecutors, especially where few of the faithful are to be found. And since there is a time for all things, Solomon saying: "a time to give birth, and a time to die," and the rest, this is the time proper to the betrayers of the word of truth, when there are not many faithful about Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (in Matt. 26:18.) But I think that the man who meets the disciples as they enter into the city, carrying a pitcher of water, was some servant of a master of a house, carrying water in an earthen vessel either for washing or for drinking. And this I think is Moses conveying the spiritual doctrine in fleshly histories. But they who follow him not, do not celebrate the Passover with Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But I think that the man who, as the disciples entered the city, met them "carrying a jar of water", whom Jesus willed that his disciples should follow as he went into the house, who was bringing that subtle water to the house, so that it might not only be cleansed, but also more fully washed with waters, was a certain one ministering to the householder (that is, to the understanding), carrying cleansing water in an earthen vessel, "that the sublimity of power may be of God", or certainly he was supplying drinkable water in that earthen vessel, so that the Son of God indeed might furnish the produce of the vine, but that understanding, the minister, might furnish out of the law and the prophets the water that is mingled with the wine of the Gospel word. We therefore who desire to be of the Church, wishing to celebrate the Passover with Jesus, let us follow that man who carries a vessel of water of this kind, whom I think to be Moses the giver of the law, carrying spiritual doctrine in corporal histories. But those who approach the law and the prophets as to the utterances of God himself, yet do not follow spiritually him who carries the vessel of living water, do not celebrate the Passover with Jesus nor drink the cup of the new testament.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us then ascend with the Lord united to us, to the upper part in which is the guestchamber, which is shown by the understanding, that is, the goodman of the house, to every one of the disciples of Christ. But this upper room of our house must be large enough to receive Jesus the Word of God, who is not comprehended but by those who are greater in comprehension. And this chamber must be made ready by the goodman of the house, (that is, the understanding,) for the Son of God, and it must be cleaned, wholly purged of the filth of malice. The master of the house also must not be any common person having a known name. Hence He says mystically in Matthew, Go ye to such a one.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: (ut sup.) But we should know that they who are taken up with banquetings and worldly cares do not ascend into that upper part of the house, and therefore do not keep the Passover with Jesus. For after the words of the disciples wherewith they questioned the goodman of the house, (that is, the understanding,) the Divine Person came into that house to feast there with His disciples.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Concerning the bread a thing similar to what Matthew records of the cup is said in Luke: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you. I say to you that from now on I will not eat it, until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God." Therefore the Savior will eat and drink that bread and paschal drink renewed "in the kingdom of God," and he will eat and drink with his disciples. For just as "he did not deem it robbery to be equal to God, but humbled himself even unto death," so he will eat the bread and drink of the generation of the vine, and he will drink it new, and by reason of his great goodness and his love of men he will eat and drink with his disciples, "when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father." For attend to what he says: when I shall drink it new with you, at no other time, except in the kingdom of my Father. And elsewhere, moreover, "the kingdom of God is not food and drink." For in a bodily sense, and according to the likeness of present food and drink, "the kingdom of God is not food and drink" … to those who have shown themselves worthy of the heavenly bread and the bread of angels and of that food of which the Savior says: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work." But that "in the kingdom of God" we shall eat and drink, it is possible to demonstrate from many places of the Scriptures, especially from that which is written: "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." Therefore this Passover will be fulfilled "in the kingdom of God," and Jesus will eat it with his disciples and will drink; and what the Apostle says, "Let no one judge you in food and in drink and the other things which are a shadow of things to come," has a revelation directed to the future mysteries concerning spiritual foods and drinks, of which the things that had been written in the Law concerning foods and drinks were a shadow. And it is manifest that we shall eat true food and drink true drink "in the kingdom of God," building up and strengthening through them that most true life.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Something in the passage has perhaps escaped our notice. You will find it out by noting how the cup is mentioned in the three Gospels. Matthew writes that the Lord said, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." Luke writes, "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me." Mark writes, "Abba, Father, all things are possible to you, remove this cup from me." Every martyrdom completed by death for whatever motive is called a cup. See whether you cannot say with him, "Let this cup pass from me." ... "The cup of salvation" in Psalms is the death of the martyrs. That is why the verse "I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord" is followed by "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet since the word of God is rich and, according to the judgment of Solomon, is to be "inscribed upon the heart" not simply, but doubly and "triply," let us try even now to add some things to those which were spoken a while ago according to our strength, that we may show how, "in a type of things to come," here too one goat was offered to the Lord as a victim and the other was sent away "alive." Hear in the Gospels Pilate saying to the priests and the people of the Jews: "Which of the two do you wish that I release to you, Jesus who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release "Barabbas," but hand Jesus over to death. Behold, you have the goat which was sent away "alive into the wilderness," bearing with itself the sins of the people that cried out and said: "Crucify, crucify!" This, then, is the goat sent away "alive into the wilderness," and the other is the goat that was offered to the Lord as a victim to make propitiation for sins, and made true propitiation for the peoples who believe in him. And if you should also inquire this — who it is that led this goat "into the wilderness," so that it might be proved in him also that he was washed and made clean — Pilate himself can be taken as the "man made ready." For he was the judge of that very nation, who by his sentence sent him out "into the wilderness." But hear how he was washed and made clean. When he said to the people, "Do you wish that I release to you Jesus, who is called Christ?" and all the people had cried out, saying, "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar," then, it says, "Pilate called for water and washed his hands before the people, saying: I am clean from the blood of this man; see you to it." So then he will be seen, with his hands washed, to have been made clean.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Celsus goes on to say that "those who killed Jesus suffered nothing for a long a time afterwards." We must inform him and all who are prone to learn the truth. The Jewish people called for the crucifixion of Jesus with shouts of "Crucify him, crucify him!" They preferred to set free the robber who had been thrown into prison for sedition and murder. They wanted Jesus, who had been delivered through envy, to be crucified. The city where all these things happened was attacked shortly after this. After a long siege, it was totally overthrown and destroyed. God judged the inhabitants of that place unworthy of living the life of citizens together. Although it may seem incredible to say, God spared this people in delivering them to their enemies. He saw that they were incurably against any improvement and were daily sinking deeper and deeper into evil. All this happened to them because the blood of Jesus was shed at their instigation and on their land. The land was no longer able to bear those who were guilty of so fearful a crime against Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And in commenting on John we have explained, as best we could, concerning the two robbers who were crucified with Christ, who according to Matthew indeed and Mark both reproached him on the cross, but according to Luke, who says that "one of the hanging robbers blasphemed him, saying: You are the Christ; save yourself and us. But the other, answering, rebuked him, saying: Do you not fear God, seeing that you are in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done nothing evil. And he said to Jesus: Remember me when you come into your kingdom. But Jesus, answering, said to him who had rebuked the one blaspheming: "Amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise".

It is fitting, therefore, that at first indeed both robbers should be understood to have blasphemed the Lord, but after this that one of them was converted and believed, pondering within himself both about these miracles which he heard had been done by him, and perhaps also seeing the change of the air and the darkness that came about, unusual and not such as was frequently accustomed to happen.

Or perhaps, as we said in that place too, these two robbers are different — of whom one was blaspheming him while the other rebuked the one blaspheming — and different were those two robbers who both blasphemed.

But that robber who was saved can be a mystery of those who after many iniquities believed in Christ and said: We have been crucified together with Christ and conformed to the death of Christ, and who always say to the Son of God: "Remember" us "when you come into your kingdom, and therefore" they are "in paradise" with him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For just as to that one who confessed he opened the gates of paradise by saying: "today you shall be with me in paradise", and through this gave to all who believe and confess an entrance for entering, which formerly, when Adam sinned, he had shut up — for who else could move aside "the flaming, turning sword which was set to guard the tree of life" and the doors of paradise? Who else could bend the "cherubim" watching with ever-wakeful guard, unless he alone to whom "all power in heaven and on earth has been given"? — so, I say, as none other but he himself could do these things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "I will recall you from there in the end." I think this means that at the end of the ages his only-begotten Son descended even into the nether regions, for the salvation of the world and recalled "the first-formed man" from there. Understand that what he said to the thief, "This day you shall be with me in paradise," was not said to him alone but also to all the saints for whom he had descended into the nether regions. In this man more than in Jacob the words will be fulfilled, "I will recall you from there in the end."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The body in the tomb, the soul in hell, the spirit was given up to the Father. … If it is true that He entrusted the spirit to the Father, then He committed it as a deposit. For it is one thing to give a thing as a gift, another to give it away, and another to give it as a deposit. A depositor places a thing in safekeeping, intending to receive his deposit back. Why then did the Savior entrust His spirit to the Father as a deposit? … just as His body could not descend into hell … so also His spirit could not descend into hell. Therefore He entrusted the spirit to the Father as a deposit, until He should rise from the dead. As He entrusted this deposit, so He took it back again. When did this happen? Not at the very moment of the resurrection, but immediately after the resurrection.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up the spirit.

As far as Matthew is concerned—who says that Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up the spirit, but does not make clear what that loud voice was which he cried out again—one could say that he cried out again the same voice which he had cried out above when he said: "My God, my God." But because Luke clearly writes what voice he cried out when he gave up the spirit, saying: "Into thy hands I commend my spirit,"

it is to be understood also in this place that the voice which he cried out again as he gave up the spirit was this one: "Into thy hands I commend my spirit."

If, therefore, to give up the spirit, or (as John writes) to hand over the "spirit," were the very same thing as to die, then what is said in this place, he gave up the spirit, would have to be understood in a plain sense. But now, since the wise define death to be nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body, let us consider whether perhaps it is one thing simply to die, and another thing to cry out with a loud voice and give up the spirit (as the present passage of Matthew expounds it), or to commend the "spirit" "into the hands" of God and release the "spirit" (according to what Luke says), or to bow the "head" and hand over the "spirit" (as John expounds it). And to die indeed belongs to all men, even the wicked, since the souls of all men are separated from the body, even of the unjust, who cannot say those things which Christ said as he went forth from his body. But to cry out with a loud voice and thus to give up the "spirit"—which is to commend the "spirit" "into the hands" of God and thus to release the "spirit," or to bow the "head" and hand over the "spirit"—belongs only to the saints, who by good works have prepared God for themselves as Christ also did, so that as they go forth from the world they may be able confidently to commend or hand over their spirit into the hands of God.

If, therefore, we have understood what it is to cry out with a loud voice and thus to give up the spirit, that is, to commend it "into the hands of God" (for so we expounded above, setting forth the exposition of the evangelist Luke), if we have understood what it is to bow the "head" and hand over the "spirit," let us hasten to keep our life such that at our departure we too may be able to cry out with a loud voice and thus to give up the spirit, or to bow the "head" and hand over the "spirit," like Jesus who "bowed his head" and, as it were, resting it upon the bosom of the Father, went forth—the Father who was able to cherish and strengthen it in his bosom. But if you wish to hear what it profited Christ to have cried out with a loud voice and thus to have given up the spirit, that is, to have commended the "spirit" "into the hands" of the Lord and thus to have given it up, or to have bowed the "head" upon the bosom of the Father and to have handed over the "spirit," hear what the prophet says: for "on this account" "he did not leave his soul in hell, nor did he give" him "to see corruption." If, therefore, we too conduct ourselves in such a way that we can commend our spirits into the hands of God, or bow our head upon the bosom of God and thus hand over our spirit, then without doubt he will neither leave our souls in hell nor give us to remain in corruption forever. But he who called him back from the dead after the third day will call us back too at the opportune time; and he who granted him that his flesh should not see "corruption" will grant to us—not indeed that our flesh should not see "corruption," but that it should be freed from corruption at the opportune time—since he indeed "did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth," but we shall be just if at least at some time we depart from our sins.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But the centurion, and those who were with him keeping guard over Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, feared greatly, saying: Truly this man was the Son of God.

But Mark writes thus: "The centurion who was standing there, seeing that he expired crying out, said: Truly this man was the Son of God"; but Luke: "When the centurion saw the things that were done, he glorified God, saying: Truly this man was righteous." According to Mark, indeed, the centurion marveled not because "the veil of the temple had been rent from the top even to the bottom," nor because the other signs had come about which Matthew relates (that is, because "the earth was shaken," because "the rocks were split," or "the tombs were opened"). It is therefore worthwhile to consider what happened afterward, over and above what is written in Mark, such that the centurion marveled, saying: "Truly this man was the Son of God." And see whether we may say, according to one manner of understanding, that he marveled at those things which had been spoken by him to God with a great cry and with loftiness of feeling, in accordance with what he was able to understand; … suspecting this, he marveled and said: "Truly this man was the Son of God." But according to another manner, since perhaps Pilate, wishing to gratify the whole people who had said: "Crucify, crucify him," and fearing a tumult of the entire people, did not command — according to the custom of the Romans regarding those who are crucified — that Jesus' body be struck beneath the armpits, which those who condemn men found guilty of the greater crimes sometimes do (for those who are not struck after their fixing to the cross undergo a greater torment, since they go on living with the utmost torture, sometimes indeed the whole night through and still, after it, the whole day). Jesus therefore, since he had not been struck, and it was expected that, hanging long upon the cross, he would suffer greater torments, prayed to the Father and was heard, and immediately, as soon as he cried out to the Father, he was received; or, as one who had "the power" of "laying down" his "soul," he laid it down when he himself willed — which prodigy, when it was done, astonished the centurion, and he said: "Truly this man was the Son of God." For it was a miracle that after three hours he was received who perhaps would have lived two days upon the cross, according to the custom regarding those who are indeed hung up but not struck, so that it might be seen to have been a benefit of God that he expired, and the merit of his prayer rather than the violence of the cross. That which Mark sets forth in what follows also signifies this very thing, when "Joseph" had gone in "to Pilate" and had asked for "the body of Jesus." For he speaks thus, that "Pilate marveled that he was already dead, and calling the centurion he asked him whether he was already dead"; and when he had heard it from the centurion, "he gave his body to Joseph." For if the custom which had been in force among the Romans concerning those crucified and struck through had been observed in the case of Christ, how would Pilate have marveled if he were already dead? See therefore whether it does not point to a new miracle, that he was already dead and that "Pilate called the centurion and asked whether he was already dead." And see whether Matthew too does not show that Christ's torment was of this kind, when he says: the centurion and those who were with him, keeping Jesus. But why were they keeping him, unless it were that, hanging longer on the cross, he might be tormented the more, neither slain nor taken down? Yet the centurion, according to Matthew, not only said of Jesus: truly this was the Son of God, but also feared him, since the earthquake cast him into fear. And perhaps too he knew by experience, from the earthquakes that occur among the nations, that this had been an earthquake, and at this he was astounded as he beheld it.

And observe that in Mark, where the centurion is reported to have seen no miracle, he calls Jesus a man, the son of God; but the one who was astonished at the tearing of the veil or at the earthquake does not say that he was a man but the son of God. Now the wording of Luke's composition also agrees with us as to the treatment we have made concerning Mark's Scripture, since he too writes thus: "truly this man was righteous." With him nothing else is mentioned except the veil: "seeing," he says, "what things were done, the centurion glorified God, saying: truly this man was righteous." And that some such thing happened at the time of Christ's condemnation, and that Pilate did not order the custom to be kept whereby Christ's body should be struck, John too makes plain, writing in this way, that "they asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away." But what necessary would there have been to make a request and offer prayers about this, if it had been done according to custom? The Jews, therefore, took pity after the cruel condemnation of those who, so far as could be judged, were living in a terrible torment; and they broke the legs of the first, and likewise of the second. But Jesus had no need of their intercessions or of the prayers they offered to Pilate, and for this reason, when they came to Jesus, since he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Or perhaps the Jews did this not out of mercy, but chiefly on account of the sabbath, so that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath; for the day of that sabbath was a great one. These things we have discussed because of what is written, that the centurion, and they who were with him keeping watch over Jesus, seeing the earthquake, and the things that were done, feared and the rest. For it is likely that they saw how the veil of the temple was rent from top to bottom, and the other things showing forth the mystery of those matters which we have set forth above, and they feared greatly; for this is what is meant by what is said, greatly.

But see whether perhaps the passage admits a moral exposition also in this manner: since there are certain people who receive Christ and keep him; and if ever they see the veil torn according to what we have handed down, and the rocks split as we have expounded, and the tombs opened according to what we have expounded, and the bodies of the dead saints going forth from the tombs and entering into the holy city (that is, the Church), they are brought to the fear of God and bear witness to him, that he who suffered such things is the Son of God. And it will be no wonder if someone confesses that the Son of God is Word and Wisdom and Truth and all the things whatsoever that the Son of God is called. And praiseworthy is the one who is not troubled at those things which appear to have befallen him in a human manner, and confesses that he was the Son of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When it will be our professed purpose to treat such things, we will explain at greater length on a more suitable occasion the matters of his burial, tomb and the man who buried him. For now, it is sufficient to notice the clean linen in which the pure body of Jesus was wrapped and the new tomb that Joseph had hewn out of the rock, where "no one was yet lying." … It suited him, who was unlike other dead people but who even in death revealed signs of life in the water and the blood. He was, so to speak, a new dead man, laid in a new and clean tomb. His birth was purer than all the others, since he was not born in the ordinary way but of a virgin. At his burial, the new tomb where they deposited his body also symbolically indicated his purity. It was not built from stones gathered from various quarters not having natural unity. It was quarried and hewed out of one rock, united together in all its parts.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore Matthew recorded that the tomb was new, and set forth plainly that it was hewn in the rock. And that it was new, free from every dead body, Luke and John made manifest, one of whom indeed said: "in which no one had yet been laid", and John: "in which no one had yet been laid"—clearly, if never had anyone been laid there, but afterward some were laid there; for what he says: "in which no one had yet been laid", is signified to those who consider this word carefully. We say then (lest perhaps we ought to understand this passage simply), that he who said: "we have been buried together with Christ through baptism" and have risen together with him, was himself also buried together, after Christ, with Christ in a new tomb and an intelligible one hewn in the rock, and all who have been buried together with Christ in baptism, that they may rise with him from the new tomb of the firstborn "from the dead and holding the primacy in all things". And Joseph rolled not many stones to the door of the tomb but one, and a great one. And a greater one than the power of those lying in wait could be, yet not greater than was the power of the angel descending "from heaven" and rolling away from it the "stone", and sitting "upon it"; since all things that are around the body of Jesus are clean and new, and not simply great but all "exceedingly" great.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: By which is implied, that the words uttered by the Saviour inflamed the hearts of the hearers to the love of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Do you wish that I show you how from the words of the Holy Spirit fire goes forth and kindles the hearts of believers? Hear David saying in the psalm: "the word of the Lord set him on fire". And again it is written in the Gospel, after the Lord had spoken to Cleopas: "was not our heart" it says "burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?". Whence therefore will you burn? Whence will "coals of fire" be found in you, who are never set on fire by the word of the Lord, never inflamed by the words of the Holy Spirit? Hear also elsewhere David himself saying: "my heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation a fire blazes forth".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whence it is shown that we must not only apply zeal to learning the sacred letters, but must also entreat the Lord and "day and night" beseech him, that the Lamb "from the tribe of Judah" may come and himself, taking the "sealed book," may deign to open it. For he it is who, "opening the Scriptures," kindled the hearts of the disciples, so that they said: "was not our heart burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that He blessed them with uplifted hands, signifies that it becomes him who blesses any one to be furnished with various works and labours in behalf of others. For in this way are the hands raised up on high.

author: Paschasius of Dumium
quote: Alms and faith must not leave you. Remember that every day death is near and act as if the tomb already enclosed you. Do not care for this world, since anxiety for the world and the desire for riches are thorns that choke the good seed.
source_title: QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS OF THE GREEK FATHERS 43.2

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "The Lord is with you." Why is the Lord with you? Because he is coming to you not merely to pay a visit, but he is coming down into you in a new mystery, that of being born. Fittingly did the angel add, "You are blessed among women." Through the curse she incurred, Eve brought pains upon the wombs of women in childbirth. Now, in this very matter of motherhood, Mary, through the blessing she received, rejoices, is honored, is exalted. Now too womankind has become truly the mother of those who live through grace, just as previously by nature are subject to death.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: She soon realized that she was receiving within herself the heavenly judge, there in that same place where with lingering gaze she had just seen the harbinger from heaven. It was by a soothing motion and holy affection that God transformed the virgin into a mother for himself and made his handmaid into a parent. Nevertheless her bosom was disturbed, her mind recoiled, and her whole state became one of trembling when God, whom the whole of creation does not contain, placed his whole Self inside her bosom and made himself a man.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: You perceive that Christ came to the Pharisee's table not to be filled with food for the body but to carry on the business of heaven while he was in the flesh.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "And behold," it says, "a woman in the town who was a sinner." Who is this woman? Beyond any doubt, she is the church.…She heard that Christ had come to the house of the Pharisee, that is, to the synagogue. She heard that there, that is, at the Jewish Passover, he had instituted the mysteries of his passion, disclosed the sacrament of his body and blood, and revealed the secret of our redemption. She ignored the scribes like contemptible doorkeepers. "Woe to you lawyers! You who have taken away the key of knowledge." She broke open the doors of quarrels and despised the very superiority of the Pharisaical group. Ardent, panting and perspiring, she made her way to the large inner chamber of the banquet of the law. There she learned that Christ was betrayed amid sweet cups and a banquet of love.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: With her hands of good works, she holds the feet of those who preach his kingdom. She washes them with tears of charity, kisses them with praising lips, and pours out the whole ointment of mercy, until he will turn her. This means that he will come back to her and say to Simon, to the Pharisees, to those who deny, to the nation of the Jews, "I came into your house. You gave me no water for my feet."When will he speak these words? He will speak them when he will come in the majesty of his Father and separate the righteous from the unrighteous like a shepherd who separates the sheep from the goats. He will say, "I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat. I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in." This is equivalent to saying, "But this woman, while she was bathing my feet, anointing them and kissing them, did to the servants what you did not do for the Master." She did for the feet what you refused to the Head. She expended upon the lowliest members what you refused to your Creator. Then he will say to the church, "Your sins, many as they are, are forgiven you because you have loved much."

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: The flock is little in the eyes of the world, but great in the eyes of God. It is little—because he calls glorious those whom he has trained to the innocence of sheep and to Christian meekness. The flock is little, not as the remnant of a big one, but as one which has grown from small beginnings. This little flock denotes the infancy of his newborn church, and immediately he promises that through the blessings of heaven this church will soon have the dignity of his kingdom.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: All this is what that treasure brings about. Either through almsgiving it raises the heart of a man into heaven, or through greed it buries it in the earth. That is why he said, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." O man, send your treasure on, send it ahead into heaven, or else your God-given soul will be buried in the earth. Gold comes from the depth of the earth—the soul, from the highest heaven. Clearly it is better to carry the gold to where the soul resides than to bury the soul in the mine of the gold. That is why God orders those who will serve in his army here below to fight as men stripped of concern for riches and unencumbered by anything. To these he has granted the privilege of reigning in heaven.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: As the text says, the kingdom of God is like a grain of mustard seed, because the kingdom is brought by a word from heaven. It is received through hearing and sown by faith. It takes root through belief and grows by hope. It is diffused by profession, and it expands through virtue. It is spread out into branches. To these branches, it invites the birds of heaven, the powers of spiritual insight. In those branches, it receives them in a peaceful abode.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "He had two sons," that is, two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles. Prudent knowledge of the law made the Jewish people his older son, and the folly of paganism made the Gentile world his younger son. Just as surely as wisdom brings distinguished gray hairs, so does foolishness take away the traits of an adult. Morals and not age made the Gentiles the younger son. Not years but understanding of the law made the Jews the older son.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "He divided his means between them." The son is as impatient as the father was kind. He is weary of his father's own life. Since he cannot shorten his father's life, he works to get possession of his property. He was not content to possess his father's wealth in company with his father, and he deserved to lose the privileges of a son.Let us make some inquiries. What reason brought the son to such actions? What bold prospect raised his spirits to make so startling a request? What reason did he have? Clearly the Father in heaven cannot be bounded by any limit, or shut in by any time, or destroyed by any power of death. The son could not await his father's death to get his wealth, so he conceived the desire to get his pleasure from the generosity of his father while he was still alive. The father's bounty proved that the insult lay in his request.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "He went and joined one of the citizens of that country, who sent him to his farm to feed swine." This is the experience that comes to one who refuses to trust himself to his father but delivers himself to a stranger. He flees from a most generous provider and endures a severe judge. A deserter from affection, a refugee from fatherly love, he is assigned to the swine, sentenced to them, and given over to their service.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: He wallows in their muddy fodder. The rush of the restless herd bruises and soils him so he perceives how wretched and bitter it is to have lost the happiness of peaceful life in his father's house.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "He fell on his neck and kissed him." This is how the father judges and corrects his wayward son and gives him not beatings but kisses. The power of love overlooked the transgressions. The father redeemed the sins of his son by his kiss, and covered them by his embrace, in order not to expose the crimes or humiliate the son. The father so healed the son's wounds as not to leave a scar or blemish upon him. "Blessed are they," says Scripture "whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered."

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: The father runs out from far away. "When we were still sinners, Christ died for us." The Father runs out. He runs out in his Son, when through him he descends from heaven and comes down on earth. "With me," the Son says, "is he who sent me, the Father." He "fell upon his neck." He fell, when through Christ the whole divinity came down as ours and rested in human nature. When did he kiss him? When "mercy and truth have met each other, justice and peace have kissed."

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: He now comes back to his Father and cries, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you." Every day in its prayer, the church testifies that the younger son has returned to his Father's house and is calling God his Father. [The church] prays, "Our Father, who art in heaven," "I have sinned against heaven and before you."

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "Give him a ring for his finger." The father's devotion is not content to restore only his innocence. It also brings back his former honor. "And give him sandals for his feet." He was rich when he departed, but how poor he has returned! Of all his substance, he does not even bring back shoes on his feet! "Give him sandals for his feet" that nakedness may not disgrace even a foot and that he may have shoes when he returns to his former course of life.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "He gave the best robe," that which Adam lost, the everlasting glory of immortality. "He put a ring upon his finger." That is the ring of honor, the title of liberty, the outstanding pledge of the spirit, the seal of the faith, and the dowry of the heavenly marriage. Hear the apostle: "I engaged you to one spouse, that I might present you a chaste virgin to Christ." "And sandals on his feet, etc." This is so that his feet might be in shoes when he preached the gospel, for "how beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace."

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "And he killed for him the fattened calf." About that David sang: "And it shall please God better than a young calf, that brings forth horns and hoofs." The calf was slain at this command of the Father, because the Christ, God as the Son of God, could not be slain without the command of his Father. Listen to the apostle: "He who has not spared even his own son but has delivered him for us all." He is the calf who is daily and continually immolated for our food.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: The older brother, the older son coming from the field, the people of the law, hears the music and dancing in the Father's house, yet he does not want to enter. "The harvest indeed is abundant, but the laborers are few." Every day we see this same thing happen with our own eyes. The Jewish people comes to its Father's house, the church. It stands outside because of its jealousy. It hears the harp of David echoing, and the music from the singing of the psalms, and the dancing carried on by so many assembled races. It does not wish to enter. Through jealousy, it remains outside. In horror, it judges its Gentile brother by its own ancient customs, and meanwhile, it is depriving itself of its Father's goods and excluding itself from his joys.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: The Father steps outside and says to his son, "Son, you are always with me." How is he with his son? In the person of Abel, Enoch, Shem, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and all the holy men from which stems Christ's Jewish lineage read in the Gospel when it says, "Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob," and so on.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "All that is mine is yours." How is this? The law, prophecy, temple, priesthood, sacrifices, kingdom, and the gifts are for you. This is the greatest gift of all: Christ was born. Since you through your jealousy wish to destroy your brother, you are no longer worthy to possess your Father's banquets and joys.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: "Send Lazarus." As I see the matter, the rich man's actions spring not from new pain but from ancient envy. This hell does not kindle his jealousy as much as Lazarus's possession of heaven. People find it a serious evil and unbearable fire to see in happiness those whom they once held in contempt. The rich man's ill will does not leave him, although he already endures its punishment. He does not ask to be led to Lazarus but wants Lazarus to be led to him. O rich man, loving Abraham cannot send to the bed of your tortures Lazarus whom you did not condescend to admit to your table. Your respective fortunes have now been reversed. You look at the glory of him whose misery you once spurned. He who wondered at you in your glory sees your tortures.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: Hear the Lord saying, "Woe to the world because of scandals!" A scandal tempts the saints, fatigues the cautious, throws down the incautious, disturbs all things and confuses all people. It is true that in this present passage the Lord is talking about the scandal of his passion.

author: Peter of Alexandria
quote: For thus will they be the rather profited, meditating upon the prophet's words, and saying, "Unto us a child is born, unto us a Son is given; and the government shall be upon His shoulder: and His name shall be called the Messenger of My mighty counsel." Who, as ye know, when another infant in the sixth month of his conception had preached before His coming repentance for the remission of sins, was himself also conceived to preach repentance.

author: Peter of Alexandria
quote: For they gave themselves up to be afflicted for the name of Christ, even though in their dungeon they enjoyed much consolation from their brethren; which, indeed, they shall return many fold, desiring to be set free from that most bitter captivity of the devil, especially remembering Him who said: "The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He hath anointed me to preach the Gospel to the poor; He hath sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised; to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompense unto our God."

author: Peter of Alexandria
quote: Moreover, we hear both also preaching, in the first place, not only repentance, but the kingdom of heaven, which, as we have learned, is within us; for the word which we believe is near us, in our mouth, and in our heart; which they, being put in remembrance of, will learn to confess with their mouths that Jesus is the Christ; believing in their heart that God hath raised him from the dead, and being as those who hear, that "with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation."

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And also it was because the marvellous preacher, John the Baptist, according to the testimony of the Book, lived in the wilderness until the day of his showing himself to the children of Israel, that he was able to receive and to teach Divine mysteries, and to receive the power of the baptism of the Spirit. And of the things which none of the early prophets had perceived, he, through the natural simplicity in which he had been brought up, became a receptacle in the wilderness; and Grace led him forth to the wilderness that he might remain in the simplicity of nature, and be able to receive the knowledge of the mysteries which were above nature.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: He sat among the teachers, and listened unto them, and asked them questions, and He bowed His ear, and received instruction, that thou also mightest hear and ask questions, and incline thine ear continually to the hearing of the divine commandments, and that thou mightest ask questions and learn those things which are beneficial to thy life, even from those who are inferior to thee in knowledge, even as our Lord Himself asked questions of those who were inferior to Him in knowledge, and He received doctrine from those who had gathered together doctrine from the law which He Himself had given.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 8 -- First Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: It is written that before His baptism He was subject unto His parents; "He went back with them to Nazareth, and was subject unto them." But observe that, after the baptism, when He was delivering a rule of life which was more perfect than this to the children of men, He was not persuaded to acknowledge parents after the body. And although He was obedient and subject unto His parents before baptism, in the time which followed, when He was delivering the rule and course of life of spiritual beings, He said, "I know them not"; and they called Him to go forth to them, but He would not be persuaded. Now if our Lord had done this before baptism when He was keeping the law, that is, if He had been called by His mother, and He had not obeyed, He would have transgressed the law; but in this case, He did not transgress except to shew that He was more obedient to the Father of nature than to the parents of grace, and that He might also teach those who are perfect to be more obedient unto the Father of grace than unto natural parents.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 8 -- First Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And He shall come of Whom it is said, "He holdeth His fan in His hand and He will purify His threshing-floors; and He will gather His wheat into the garner, but the straw He will burn up with unquenchable fire." And the Husbandman who planted in the world the tree of our mankind will shew Himself to be the Judge, and He will hold in His hand the axe for cutting down, and every tree which beareth not good fruit He will cut down and cast into the fire.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And since the building itself is fixed in the ground every man can build and raise upon it whatsoever he pleaseth, until the day which shall decide is revealed, and He shall come of Whom it is said, "He holdeth His fan in His hand and He will purify His threshing-floors; and He will gather His wheat into the garner, but the straw He will burn up with unquenchable fire." And the Husbandman who planted in the world the tree of our mankind will shew Himself to be the Judge, and He will hold in His hand the axe for cutting down, and every tree which beareth not good fruit He will cut down and cast into the fire.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word which goeth forth from the mouth of God." Now He said "shall live," and not, "shall be sound," nor, "shall be strong," nor, "shall be filled its lust's need;" and although this word is of little importance in its utterance, yet a great distinction is apparent therein. For He taught us clearly by that word that not by bread alone should man live, but that he should eat only to live, and not for the sake of lust, or strength, or healthy condition.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Others, however, He healed by a command of power, without either looking up to heaven or asking His Father. For by a command of power He raised up the young man, the son of the widow; with a word He called to the daughter of the chief of the congregation and straightway she stood up; He commanded the sea and it was silent, and the wind and it was stilled; He spake only, "Fill the water pots with water and draw out and bear to the governor of the feast," and created matter delayed not [to do] His will. "I say unto thee," He spake to the dumb spirit, and immediately it departed from the man. "I will, be thou clean," He spake to the leper, and as He willed, straightway the leprosy fled from his body.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And who of all the ancients, who were accounted worthy of the sublime and wonderful gift, was like unto John the Baptist? According to the testimony, which Christ spake concerning him, "He was the greatest of all the Prophets"; and again He said, "Verily I say unto you, among those born of women there is none greater than John the Baptist." Now let us understand and see how and what was the rule and conduct of life of this marvellous man who arrived at such greatness as this, and why he was accounted worthy of all this gift, and with what increase and with how great labours, and after what asceticism, and for how long a time he lived a solitary life away from human intercourse; and when we have seen and have understood these matters of his life, let us consider the greatness of the things which were unto him, and let us understand first of all the things which concern the will, and afterwards the things which concern grace, for until the will shewed its fruits the Spirit gave not its gift.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And again, teaching us that we should not only forsake our possessions for the sake of His glory, and deny the world for the sake of confessing Him, but also our transitory life, He said, "Except a man deny himself he cannot be My disciple."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And by the hand of that one feeble disciple, concerning whom it is written in the Gospel of our Redeemer, Jesus hath rebuked this wicked thought in all His foot-soldiers. "And one came and drew nigh and said unto Him, Master, I will follow Thee whithersoever thou goest. Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay His head." "Depart thou from me, O disciple of iniquity, for I have not that to give unto thee which thou desirest, and that which I can give thee thou dost not wish to receive. I know that which thy desire asketh, and that which thou seekest, but I will not give them unto thee, for through the love of the thought of riches thou hast been pleased to come after Me, and being in the light thou hast come forth to seek darkness, and having the true possession, to seek poverty, and having life, to seek death. That which I command every man, to forsake the world and to cleave unto Me, I desire that thou shouldst possess in thy coming unto Me. By the door through which I desire to bring thee out, by that same door thou pressest to come in unto Me, and therefore I will not receive thee. For in My outward appearance I am poor, and for this reason I have not things which are manifest to give in the world into which I have come. I am in appearance a stranger, for I have neither house nor roof, and whosoever seeketh to be My disciple must inherit poverty from Me. Why dost thou wish to inherit from Me that of the possession of which I have made thee destitute?"
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And again in another place He restrained that man who wished to perform two things in one, that is, honour to his parents and discipleship to Himself, and told him that it was impossible that two things which were the opposites of each other could happen at the same time: "Teacher, suffer me to go and bury my father and my mother, and I will come after Thee," that is to say, "I will keep the first commandment which God commanded me, Honour thy parents and be obedient unto them, and then I will come after Thee and minister unto Thee." And what answer did Jesus return to this? "Leave the dead to bury their own dead; and go thou and preach the kingdom of God. It is not necessary for thee to keep the law, for it hath been kept and is dissolved, neither hast thou any need to minister unto natural parents, because I have been obedient unto parents according to the body, and I have ministered unto them on behalf of everyone. The yoke of the law and nature is henceforth lifted from off thee, and thou art left a free man unto thyself, there being no worldly power that can subdue thee, for thou art dead unto the world, and thou art dead unto it. Dead bodies have not service paid unto them, they are only wrapped in shrouds and buried; leave the dead then to bury their dead, and do thou go and preach the kingdom of God."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Behold also we learn from this testimony that the man who becometh a disciple of Jesus hath not even power to minister unto his natural parents, because he hath a true Father, Who by His grace hath enrolled him for Himself as a son, and Who hath set him apart for the ministration of His will. And unto the man who sought to honour his parents according to the body, so long as they were alive, and after their death to become His disciple, He said, "Let the dead bury their dead."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Hear also again another proof, which like the preceding will bring instruction nigh unto thee, and the example of the testimony of which will urge thee to deny thyself everything, and to go forth after Jesus. "And one of His disciples drew nigh and said unto Jesus, Suffer me to bid farewell to them that are at my house, and I will come after Thee." Hear also in this case what the Master answered the disciple, and receive it as if it had been spoken unto thee by that disciple: "No man, having put his hand upon the ploughshare, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "No man, having put his hand upon the ploughshare, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God," that is to say, "Whosoever fulfilleth this work in nature, and who guideth the plough with oxen according to the custom of man, and who suffereth himself to look behind him instead of in front — now in this manner the work would never be completed — is not able to advance, nor are his furrows cut straight, and the oxen also do not travel forwards; and although this work be visible, and one which can be seen, and it taketh place in the very earth itself, yet if the ploughman look behind him, his labour is spoiled. Now as concerning My own discipleship, one labour differeth from another, even as world differeth from world, and life from life, and immortal from mortal beings, and God from the children of men; if then thou takest the yoke of My discipleship upon thy soul and body, thou must perform the service of My commandments, and thou must turn thyself back to the world, and it must not be a care to thee to make peace with thy kinsfolk, and thou must not be anxious to pay unto them the obligation of honour according to the body, and to fulfil unto them the law of the fulness of the world, and then to come after Me. For if thou wouldest pay the obligations of the world, those which are due unto Me cannot be paid; and if thou art anxious not to offend the world in anything, why then shouldst thou set thyself to provoke Me? Let there be no peace between thee and the world, in order that thou thyself mayest have peace with Me."
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "I will go and bid farewell to the children of my house," but Christ said unto him, "Thou hast no peace with them," for "Ye shall salute no man by the way"; and the meaning of this speech is that Christ thereby denied His disciples also that salutation of the peace of the world. These things were said in the person of one disciple unto every man, that is to say, unto all those who have dedicated themselves unto discipleship, for it is better that a man should not be a disciple unto God in name, being in truth a disciple of the world, and that he should not hire himself unto One, and serve the other.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
